NEVER SAY DEE. The_weeds o' this world for a long time aw've worn, An' sin moor ups an' deawns then mooast ROA aw'll be sworn; Aw've bin heigh up Wl' fortune, then low down i' tuck, An aw've varra, oft bed to rely on my pluck. Wl' friends lookin' cowd and relations teen flight, Aw never set deawn to mourn over my plight; Booath riches an' poverty's one advice gi'en— " Never say dee while there's leet yo'r een." Ay, were short o' ten year when aw torn'd eawt to work, An aw roughed Id an' toyled id fro dayleet to derk; I' them days a weyver were nobbut a slave— Iv lie 'wanted to rest he'd to creep into th' grave. After forty years feighten myfeyther 'd to dee, Leoving nine little childer, an' th' owdest were me; Bud he left me one lesson—an' useful id's been— "Lad, never say.dee while tha's leet i• thy een." My mother an me hed to put eawr best bond To eawr werx—id were idle to potter or stond. Through the lesson ov werk aw went page after page, An- though but a lad aw -soon geet a mon's wage; Bud luck were as usual—a rise, then a drop— Th' mill were horned deawn an' left me eawt Bud one lesson aced learnt, thougla aw 're only-sixteen— '" Never say dee while there's leet yo'r een." riot stetted o' hawkin, an; though short o'. cheat, Aw -wed wod would Iteep us, ne'er missing a 'week; I3ud th' frost droove me off id--cowd ured me give o'er, An' aw torned back to th' shuttle an' -weyvin once

more. .Aw worked noosn.so weel for a little at th' fost, Bud in th' cocaine ov a week aw picked up wod aw'd lost; Aw soon geet V:t000.1 fettle—a mon at's mod green • -Need never saydee while there's lest inins een. 'Bud th' war "browt us famine—aved mod much laid bye ; . But 't were terkken things woes to leawr deawn an cry. 'Were geet laheurin'—carried a bed; then ten bob 'Were put onto my wages, aw're footmen o' th' job. Aw've risen *in then among fair luck an' feaw ; Aw've threrrsooarts o' brass? my pocket just neaw. There's only one plank—good an' bad hick between— 'lt's "Never say dee while there's yo'r eon." Cnarties TAVC4STER.

GEN-COTTON.—When gun-cotton or other high explo- sives are freely exposed upon an iron anvil and deto- nated, the explosive 'leaves a deep and permanent impression upon the surface of the metal with which it was in contact. . . The impression produced by the exploding mass is anelmost exact copy of that face of the explosive which was in contact with the metal. This is best observed from gun-cotton, for, from the nature of the material, it can 'he shaped according to fancy, and such figures and designs as one wishes can be stamped upon its surface. Thus, if a disc of gun-cotton, on which the letters "U. S. N." and the date "1884" are indented, be detonated, it will be found that the letters and figures, will be reproduced inthe iron. Gun-cotton constitutes the best military explosive known, for, while its explo- sive force vastly exceeds that of gunpowder and approaches that df nitroglycerine, it is the safest and most stable explosive we possess, since it can be stored and transported wet; and while in this state, though it may be detonated, it cannot be exploded in any other way. As flinch as two thousand pounds of wet com- pressed gun-cotton `have been placed in a fierce bonfire, where it has gradually dried, layer by layer, and been Consumed without exploding. Besides, gun-cotton is the only military eseplosive which can be detonated with certainty when frozen.—Scribner's Magazine for May. EVOLUTION IN A SURREY POND.—The tadpoles, of course, begin life as spawn—big jelly-like masses of round transparent eggs, each with a tiny black speck or nucleus showing through in the centre, the earliest germ of the future frog. 'lf you watch these germs in their slow development, you Will see that each gradually acquires a wee head and tail, and emerges at last from the slowly-absorbed Jelly-bag as a tiny limbless swim- ming creature. It'has big branching gills, very delicate and ramifying, on each side of its throat, by whose means it extracts the floating oxygen dissolved scantily ' in the water about it.l3ut as it grows and grows it acquires with age a more consistent substance and decided form, its little body becoming fat and round and faintly f mg-like, and its long tail showing a sort of intermediate type be- tween the rudder shape of the fish and the lizard model. In process of time a pair of little hind legs begin to bud out in soft outline from its smooth black sides, and then a pair of forelegs, which rapidly assume a more distinctly froggy character. Its head meanwhile acquires'a more decided and intelligent aspect, with inquisitive eyes of the higher type, no longer covered by a fold of ' trans- parent skin, and only the long tail remains to suggest the little animars fish-like origin. But boor by hour the tail now gets shorter, being slowly absorbed by the re- mainder of the body-, and in the fulness of time the re- modelled creature quits the water and steps on dry land in the accomplished dignity of perfect froghood.—Studies from Life, fig Grant Allen, in Good Words for April. A Erssorr IN Boxisio.—A farmer about fifty years old stopped a number of people on Monroe Avenue, Chicago, to inquire his way to a gymnasium, and he was finally asked if he was going to take lessons in boxing. "No, not exactly," he replied, "but I want to see a thumper." Be was directed to the right place, and after looking the • establishments over he said to the proprietor: "I live out here about fourteen miles. I've got a hired man who has got so sassy that I can hardly live with him. ' 'He's too big to lick with a gad, and I've got to cuff him 'tip to a peak. I want to take a lesson with the gloves, ,and when I go home I'll astonish John Henry with a bit ,of science." One of the boxers about the place said he'd give a lesson for a dollar, and the old man peeled down to his undershirt, and put on the gloves. He was shown how to pose and how to hold his guard, and then warned to look out for himself. "'You play you are John Henry the hired man," he said. "All right." "You've been looting your time away, and I've called you a lazy coyotte. "Exactly." "You have sassed me back, and I go for you like ihis—and this'!" And the old man struck right and left and followed the boxer around the ring. He was doing. noble work when something shot •ever his guard and hit his chin, and he went over like a legend laid there until they threwwater on him. Then be sat up, looked about in a dazed way, and feebly inquired: "What was it ? " "John Henry hit you." "He did, eh? Then that settles it! Here's your dollar, young man, and here's the gloves. If I'm liable to get such a lick as that, I'm going home to tell the hired man he can boss the whole ranch and be-hanged to him!" WHAT IS DECORATION ?—iri strictness, to decorate is to add beauty to something by adding to it ornament, or perhaps colour, and implies something to be decorated. It is an inconvenience to have no better name than trinket, ignick-knack, gewgaw, for a thing that exists for its prettiness alone; and so we stretch the more reput- able word to cover such things. So, also, people speak of decorating a slab of wood or stone by painting or carving something on it, when the slab, if it exists only for the sake of what is on it, is no more decorated by this than the painter's canvas is decorated by his picture. Let us use the word now in its true sense, by which decoration exists for the sake of the thing to which it is applied. The distinction concerns us, for 'neglect of it has led decorators into serious faults. It is easy, in the desire to do something called deconttive, te think only of the charm of what we are doing, withottt regard to the thing to which we are doing it This is a besetting sin of amateur decorators. . . . The ...cense for colour of the army of amateur decorators has gained wonderfully within a few years. But this im- .provement in colour of our painted decoration, of our stained glass, of the work of our Societies of Decorative Art, makes their shortcoming in other respects the more conspicuous. There is a tinge of the barbaric in it. It waken the kind of admiring dissatisfaction with which one always sees art that supplements conspicuous beau- ties with conspicuous defects. When we go below the best of it, and look at the things which fill the common shops and attract cheap buyers, we are disheartened, sud long to barter the gaudy ugliness of our day for the quiet ugliness of our fathers. Of course, the present condition of things will not last. As colour becomes popular it also becomes vulgar in any people which has not a, hereditary instinct for it.— WA. P. P. Longfellow, ,Se 'timer's Magazine. "If I learn how to do such things just right I'll grow up into a servant girl, won't I?" "No. dear; if you learn how to do anything just right yoli'll never be a servant girl." A sensible man does not brag, avoids introducing the names of his creditable companions, omits himself as , habitually as another man obtrudes himself in the dis- course, and is content with putting his fact or theme simply on its ground. He was feverishly awaiting her answer. "I have spoken to your father, Miss Clara," he added, by way Of a clincher, " and he will gladly welcome me as a son-in- law." In aloud, sweet tone the answer came: "If you had spoken to me first, Mr. Sampson," she said, "it would have saved you the trouble of speaking to my father?' And then she said something about the weather, which Mr. Sampson found cold and bleak a few moments later. THE PONY BITTER.—A beer traveller went into &public, house at Windy Nook and called for a "pony bitter," which, it may be explained, is a very small glass of beer. A pitman who stood near was asked by the traveller if he would have something to drink. " Wey," was the reply," aa'll have a powney bitter tee." On the liquor being placed on the table, the pitman took up his glass, and, addressing the landlord, said, " Noo, lad, if that's yor powney, tyek him back tiv his steal, and bring me a pit galloway !" A BLIZZARD EPISODE.—The old man, muffled to the ears, was shovelling off the snow; the pitiless blizzard howled dismally through his whiskers, and he was mad all the way through. "My deaf." came a voice from an upper window. "My dear, nothing !" he shrieked back. "Let me alone. I'm busy; !" and he went on shovelling, and down slammed the window. Half an hour later the same voice, from the same window, came in earnest, pleading tones—" My dear !" "Well, what in thunder Ido you want !" he shouted. "Is the house on fire?" "No, John," wailed the voice, "the house Is all right. but You are shovelling off the wrong walk." Then the blizzard turned and fled. REMARKABLE MEMORIES.—An article now going the rounds of the newspapers gives some instances of par- ticularly agile memories hut the following are omitted from the list :—Henry VIII. of England could repeat the names of his wives in their consecutive order without missing one. A school teacher of London, whose name was Dawson, possessed a remarkable memory. Be could repeat the first verse of the Book of Sob, and on a wager of £2OO, he repeated without the aid of a book, the title to Spenser's " Faery Queene," a poem of nearly 400 stanzas of nine lines each. Porson, the Greek scholar, I could repeat the Beautitudes in the original with his eyes closed and one hand tied behind. him. A notocl Scotch divine had such an excellent memory that he used the same grace at table in his 90th year that he used 70 years before. Lord Chesterfield always remembered' to say "Thank your' without the aid of a microscope. Coming down to modern times, we have instances almost as remarkable. The Prince of Wales never forgets to snub Henry of Battenburg when he has an opportunity. General Sherman can recall the strains of " Marching through Georgia" almost involuntary. Grover Cleveland can remember who is Governor of New York without being told. Governor Foraker can remember who is President of the United States when the thermometer is 80edegrees in the shade.—Anzerican. TESTING FOR COLOUR BLINDNESS.—The scene, a village school, far up in the north of England; about forty-five children present; for the dialect of either master or scholars I am far from any wish to apologise; the Eng- lish was, to say the least, of it, more agreeable than that spoken in London. None of the children were more than eight years old. It should be explained that there was a class-room beyond in which was a table covered with skeins of German wool, bits of coloured glass, and silk of all colours. Master: "Now, bairns, back end o' ' lest week I tell'd ye I'd gie ye an ould farrant lesson to- day. You, Josey, ye see this?" holding up a red rose. Josey, a small child of six years," Ay, master." "What I be it, bairn ?" "Why a rose, master, for sure." "Ay, but what kin' o's rose?" "A red un, sir." "Well, now you Kvin t' class room and fetch me out a skein o' wool, the nighest like this rose ever ye can." Josev takes the rose and fetches back a skein just of the same hue. "Now, Mairy lass, thou's got to go and do likewise." "I doon't want t' rose, I can lease (choose) t' skein wi'out it," says Mary rather sulkily. Mary was nearly eight years old, and was surprised at and despised the easiness of the lessen. She brought out a good match. After this about twenty children were sent on the same errand and matched the colour perfectly. The interest of the lesson flags—the children's attention wanders. At last, a little white-faced fellow goes into the class-room, stays some time, and finally comes out with two skeins in his hand. Shouts of surprise and derision fill the rooms. " Sure-ly." "What be ye thinking on ?" "One on 'em's as green as grass, and t'other as grey as a ratten (rat)." The little boy looks frightened. " Thou's done as well as thou knew how," says the master rather gently. "Don't thou be scared, thou's nobbut tried once. Here take and match me this." He gives him the glossy leaf of a laurel. The child goes out again and with a much more cheerful and confident air comes hack and puts into his hand a skein of the brightest scarlet. The other children too much surprised to laugh whisper together," He beant fondy neither "—fond here has the old sense of, foolish. Out of the fifty children two wore found who could not match all colours.—.leas Ingslow, in Good Words.

. HIS EYES.

, Three commercial travellers sat over tiitifi-ifine and cigars one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Tom, Dick, and Harry. After comparing notee on the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around, till, at last. Torn and Dick began chaffing. Harry on the shabby condition of his head, for his hair was fast falling out, and the sparse quantity he still retained was quite gray, and both de- clared he had deceived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Diek declared that he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and anxiously Inquired what it was. Dick told Lim "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hours I" "Nonsense l" tarry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I" Harry secretly resolved to try it, and did. The next day his mischievous friends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered with onions, his eyes full of thef.?juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they set ' up told Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interference Dick's head would have stood in neerl of a plaster. Dick ' apologised; and made amends by informing Harry of the admirable qualities of Mrs. S. A. Allen's,World's Hair Re- storer, which never fails to restore the hair to Its natural colour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the world. It should always be kept on the toilet table for dressing the hair. It is delicate and agreeable. • _ „

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTICUL- TURE. &c.

A Southdown ewe belonging to Mr. J. Glossop, of Ambergate, has produced no less than twenty-two lambs in five years—three fours and two fives. At the present time she has four lambs, and all are doing well. In 1884 she had four, 1885 five, 1888 four, 1887 five, and this year four again. A valuable herd of cattle, belonging to a farmer in , Selside, strayed into private grounds a few days since. and ate a considerable quantity of rhododendron with a little yew for variety. When found shortly afterwards several of theranimals exhibited signs of poisoning, but with prompt veterinary treatment they all recovered within a few hours. LINCOLN GREAT APRIL HORSE FAIR. Trade conti- nued very slow at this fair. Prices all round were con- sidered lower than those of last year. The better Class of agrienitural horses ranged from 60 guineas to 80 guineas per head. The highest price obtained for carriage horses was 600 guineas, given by Mr. Robinson, of Hull, _

for a splendid pair of high-steppers. , Mr. W. P. Young, who occupies a farm in lowa, has lately carried out a series of carefully-conducted experi- ments in cattle feeding, which go to show that whilst a beast between two and three years old grows at the rate of 1-391 b per day, those between 18 and 30 months old increase at the rate of 1•761 b. per day. The balance, therefore, is in favour of early maturity'. Mr. W. H. Smith has stated in the House of Commons, in reply to various questions, (1) that the scheme for the formation of the new Agricultural Department was re- ceiving the careful consideration of the Government, and he hoped it would be made public very shortly; and (2) that the Agricultural Department was not yet in ossession of the £5,000 provided in, the Estimates. Mr. John Handley, Green Head, Milnthorpe, has just sold to Mr. J. A. Argles, Eversley, Milnthorpe, the young red-and-white shorthorn bull Baron Derwent, by Golden Treasure, and out of Derwent Queen 3rd, by Sir Arthur Ingram; also the yearling red-and-white hull Sir Edward 2nd, by Royal Ingram, and out of Elixir by Royal Victor, to Mr. R. Rawlinson, Docker Garths, Kenaal. The Earl of Duninore's rec immendation of Highland r cattle for North-Western ranches has just received valu- able confirmation. Sir Donald Smith has some Highland cattle at his Silver Heights Farm, near Winnipeg, and after a personal inspection he finds them to be doing even better than those bred in Scotland. Moreover, Sir Donald also finds that these cattle can be raised in the North-West, though out of doors every day of the:year. The horse has the smallest stomach in proportion to his size of any animal. Fifteen or sixteen quarts is its utmost capacity. This space is completely filled by four quarts of oats and the saliva that goes into the stomach with it. Hurses are generally overfed and not fed often enough. For a horse with moderate work *fix or eight quarts of bruised oats and 81b. or 101 b. of fine hay a day is sufficient. This should be fed ia at least three meals, and is better if fed in four. A WEED ACT IN AMERICA.—Two years ago an Act MA passed by the Legislature of Wisconsin entitled a "Weed Act," requiring all .persons and corporationato destroy all noxious weeds in such time and marther as would effectually prevent them bearing seeds. Farmers are also required to destroy noxious weeds on roads and lanes that adjoin their lands failing which they are sub- ject to a sharp penalty. There is plenty of room for the application of o similar Act to this Country. William G. Bartle, of St. Louis, who was formerly in the American pork-packing business, has been letting us into the secrets, observes an American paper, of the trade. Cholera hogs, he admits, are packed with other hogs. Hogs, too, are cut into hams, notwithstanding that they are affected with cholera. "If," he added. naively, "the meat of cattle suffering from Texas fever was poisonous, half the people in St. Louis would have been dead long ago." Whenever practicable, horses should have their water always-at hand. Much less will be drunk and with more relish than by the common method of the periodical bucket. Cold water should never be given to a heated horse, nor tepid to a cool one; the latter is as unpleasant to him as itjs to ourselves. Modern stable fittings are complete with every convenience for the renewal of water, its removal, and the cleanliness of its receptacle. Drinking water should be pure, and not too hard. SIVEDIM Boma FOR ENGLAND.—At a recent meeting of the Swedish Agricultural Society, Professor Loven urged the Swedish dairies to mark their casks intended for England with the word "Sweden." The letters should be about Sin. high, and it was advisable not only to mark the lid, but also at the top on the side, as other- wise the cask might be put upside down, or a new lid put on. Although the Merchandise Marks Act demands that an article should be marked by the name of the country where it was produced, the Swedish dairy agent in Manchester has reported that a number of Swedish marks were sold in England as Danish. Professor Loven expressed his opinion that Swedish butter is likely to lose its reputation when the best marks sail under another country's flag. He thought the best plan would be to instruct the Custom House officials to see that all Swedish butter was properly marked "Sweden" before It left the country.

. BEES AND BEE-KEEPING. Mr. Mc.Clure, of the Lancashire and Cheshire Bee- keepers' Association, contributes the following paper to the Journal of the Royal Lancashire Agricultural Society :—" To many of the readers of this journal bee- keeping-Vill be considered an uninteresting pursuit, mainly foi the reason that bees have stings and some- times use them but the sting of the bee is its only pro- tection, and but for this means of defence the insect would have been extinct long ago. To the experienced beekeeper, however, the sting has no terrors, and even a beginner, with a taste for the pursuit, who goes amongst his bees with confidence and a quiet manner, will soon be at home with them. The limited space at my disposal prevents me from giving more than the merest outline of what there is to be said on the subject, though I hope to be able to answer in the affirmative the question, Should farmers encourage bee-keeping? I reply, it is their interest to do so. The question has been asked by practical farmers. Can bees carry away cwts. of honey from my fields without its entailing a loss to me, either in milk or in the flesh-producing properties of the herbage?' To this I unhesitatingly reply—the farmer loses nothing whatever, but is a gainer, though his fields be visited daily by myriads of bees. lam quite ready to admit the force of the reasoning which, on the face of it, seems only a common-sense view, when the farmer refuses to believe that so much actual weight can be carried off by bees without entailing loss to him. I assert, however, that the crop suffers just as much damage through the evaporation of the dews of heaven when dispelled by the morning sun, as it does by the rifling of bees. The honey evaporates' if not gathered, just as does the dew; therefore, I say, there is no loss to anyone. But when we remember that the bee, in its search for honey, carries pollen dust from bloom to bloom, thus ensuring the complete fertilisation of the flower, who can deny that the farmer is a gainer, seeing that without fertilisation there is no increase? As a practical man, he knows that unfertile blooms yield no fruit, while barren clover heads cannot be so nourishing to his cattle as those which are full of seed. Now, if we can but induce the farmer to become a bee-keeper, even in a small way, so that he may add the production of honey to the various crops on which he relies for profit, he will be doubly the gainer, for the cwts. of honey—the loss of which he now deplores—will be garnered i to his own store, and form, in good seasons, a not inconsiderable item in the income of the farm. In addition to this there is the fact that honey, being a vzhoLsome and nutritious article of food, should be on every farmer's table as an article of daily consumption for the household. I also say that "Farmers should encourage bee-keeping" among the labourers at their own cottage homes; it will make them better ser- vants, add to their intelligence, conduce to their comfort, assist in keeping them from the village ale house, and take up none of their master's time, if every farm labourer kept a hive or two of bees. A working man who labours away from home from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day, made a profit from his bees last year which more than paid his rent and procured him a new watch into the bargain. I could name similar cases of successful bee-keeping among working men from last year's bee-work, but one fact is worth a load of argu- ment; and surely there is wisdom in encouraging thrift in this form among the labouring, men employed about a farm; moreover, the practical experience gained by a man in working among the bees at his own home will be of the utmost value to the farmer whose servant he is, seeing that he can turn his knowledge to account in managing the bee department of the farm. Having endeavoured to show—briefly, I must confess, not for lack of argument, but owing to the limited space at my disposal—that 'Farmers should encourage bee-keeping,' I now pass on to the proposition, How is it to be done?' There are two ways of looking at this last question. There is the broad view of it, or that which is supposed to benefit the pursuit at large ; and there is the narrower, but not less important aspect, which has reference to the profit, or personal advantage, the farmer himself will gain by giving his attention to the subject. In regard to the first point—he will aid and assist the cause of bee-keeping 12 enerally by encouraging the bee association of his own county, and that of the central body in London, with which all county associa- tions are affiliated. These associations are formed not only for the diffusion of information regarding bees, and how to keep them successfully, but to assist members in finding a market for their honey, and by giving them timely advice and assistance at certain times in each year. The second view in which bee-keeping presents itself to the farmer is a directly personal one; yet I do not object to his looking at it from thiii latter stand- point, tor he can help the cause for which we plead though he may have no other object save that of profit, by starting a few stocks in a suitable place about his own homestead. If, after a season or two: thaw stocks of bees yield a fair return for the labour bestowed on, them, the farmer may make a gift of a swarm to one of the most likely of his labourers, in' order that he too may benefit in the way already described. It will be quite impossible in this short paper for me to give more than a passing glance at the practical part of bee-keeping. There is a very use- ful little handbook, giving all the needful information, which may be had for 6d. from the hon. sec. of any Bee Association. I may, however, just point out one or two things to be borne in mind by those who, for the first s time, attempt bee-keeping on modern methods, not so

much for the purpose of showing what to do, as what to avoid. In a word, to point out the difference between keeping bees for profit, on modern principles, and the old-time system of the straw skep and the brimstone pit. First then, I would say to the farmer, don't start by adopting the bar-frame hive! Begin with the straw skep, not the old-fashioned dome-shaped article, but what is known to dealers as a fiat-topped one. This has a good-sized hole in its crown, and Can be supered'or fitted with surplus boxes, just as can a bar-framed hive. Then, again, don't keep your stocks in a bee-house; these are generally useful chiefly as harbours for vermin, and are usually a source of annoyance to the bee=keeper who adepts them. Let each stock of bees be placed On itS own separate stand, with free space for passing round about it without disturbing the adjoining stock. Let the stand be firmly fixed %the ground, and adopt some means of not only keeping the skep dry, but of preventing it from being:blown over in,M,orms. Don't let the bees:be interfered with or disturbed unnecessarily. To give them timely room for storing surplus honey, and so. preventing swarming, is a very important matter, an'd not less is it important to see that the bees are well fed up in autumn, if they have been deprived by their owner of the main portion of the year's in-enthering. Lastly, see that they do not perish through starvation in spring, just before a natural supply of food can be had outside, and carefully protect them front wet or damp during the long winter months when they are confined in-doors by severe weather. All the needful details of bee-naanagement will be found in the Bald work I have already named, but I have just hinted above at a few simple, but im- Dortant matters which any one can bear in mind: I therefore close by expressing hope that the farmerswho read these words will be induced to give a small portion of their time pa the subject I have briefly brought under notice. If they will think over this and pursue the subjeg intelligently, they will find that both pleasure and profit may be got out of 'that industrious little labourer, the busy-bee.' Such information as it is hi my power to give regarding bees will be most ,cheerfully, supplied to any applicant who may apply for it.
The Lathams, Prescot, Lancashire."

PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY Huon BETTE. XIII.—PHOTOGRAPHIC PHIZZES. When I used to watch the professional photographer dodge in and out of the black cloth covering of the mysterious box in which he was "drawing likenesses," I tised to wish I was one (a photographer, not a black cloth); but owing to the wheel of fortune turning in the opposite direction, it didn't come off. I don't, mean that the wheel didn't come off my fortune (for if I held to the naked, unvarnished truth I should say that it did), but the important event of my becoming a photographer didn't come off. Since these golden days, when the photographer was a romantic character, I have become intimately acquainted with several professors of the art, and have extracted from conversations on cameras, dry- plates, negatives,/&c., sufficient knowledge to make me grateful that no photographer has a sign with the name " Hugh Bette" on it. At least, if he has, I hereby give •rublic notice that he is an impostor, If I were a photographert would I pander to the self- worship of some photo-idolisers whom I should have for 'customers? No ! Would I have that photographic custom requisite to keep the business on its three legs if I didn't pander? No! Is it ten to one that in a few months I should use the sensitive paper to write to my creditors offering a composition of about two shillings in the pound? It is! Therefore, I trust the reader will forgive me for being glad under the circumstances; if not, of course, I shall be under the painful necessity of rejoicing in unforgiven gladness. I have a very high opinion of the photographer. I regard him as one type of patient humility. Look at the trouble he takes with Ina customers! If you are an individual who would have no chance of winning at a man show, he screws you into positions that you never dreamt of befoile, in order to make you presentable. Take into consideration the difficulties he has to encounter, and you must appreciate his evenness of temper, especially when you consider that he doesn't get paid until he has showed you the negative, and you are satisfied with it. When the doting mother wants a picture of her baby, truly representing it in the sleekness of its fat beauty, the docility of the photographer enables him to be an immense doll, a Jack-in-the-box, and a gigantic squeaker in rapid succession, and as a fond mother doesn't like to see a photograph of\ her baby which gives you the idea that it hadthe bowel, complaint, she at least appreciates the charming good nature of the photographer. I spoke of his patience. I think you will allow that when a man goes to be photographed who has such a decided cast in his eyes, that he shows up on the negative with only one eye, and that right in the middle of his face, I think you must,allow that a photographer is patient who takes the blame upon himself, and spoils plate after plate in the hope that by some means a passable one may he obtained. It is a very hard thing to take a good photograph, and it isn't everybody that knows what a good photograph means. For example, when you hear Mrs. White tell Mrs. Black that she has had a dozen photos of herself taken, and they are such good ones, you will please to understand that the picture of Mrs. White has, by some inexplicable mystery to the uninitiated, been taken without the freckles and pimples, and that she mustered for the occasion the smile that she only ordinarily wears when she is presented with a new bonnet. That is what is considered a good photograph. You will have noticed the graveyard expression on the features in some photographs. This expression is caused by the efforts of the photographer to make it a good one, but they have flashed in the pan. Giles goes to "have his •likeness took." The photo- grapher puts him in the chair, and instructs him to look at a certain article in the room. He then takes a look through the camera to see if the subject is the proper distance from the lens (most probably because the pro- per distance len(d)s enchantment to the view). He then comes back to twist Giles's head round till his neck craoks, places his hands in the approved schoolmistress fashion, and, telling him to look at the article, goes back I and takes another survey. Giles begins to feel by this time as if he had been varnished all over, and was just getting dry. The photographer gives the momentous I word "ready," and Giles stiffens all his muscles, holds his breath, and stares at the top corner of the studio as lif he was trying to decipher the date of a threepenny- piece there deposited, or as though he was awaiting to hear the crack of doom. When Giles showed the photo- graph to his friends, they have the impudence to ask him why he looked so solemn. They ought to know I that the solemnity was a compliment to the photo- grapher's excessive attention. Perhaps you have heard of the lady who went to be photographed, and who evidently didn't " seem " the ghastly look usually imparted to the sitter, for the photographer, after looking through the camera, requested her to smile. She " smole !" Whereupon he came from under the black cloth more rapidly than before, exclaiming, "Too large! Far too large! The machine won't take it all at once." He must have lost his patience when he said that. A friend of mine in the " perfesh" told me a very pathetic story. A widow waited upon him, and gave him the order to photograph the grave and surroundings of her "dear departed." When he had done so (having had to make a journey of six miles to do so), she brought him a photograph of herself, with the order that it be worked in, to appear standing beside the gravestone. When he told her it couldn't be done, she threw the grim Work of art on his hands, and he will perhaps have to keep it a long time before he can sell it to someone else as the photograph of their grave. In common justice to photographer, I ought, perhaps, to state that the latter portion of the painful history, having reference to selling the photo, is only a reasonable surmise of my ova. "I want my portrait taken," said a pompous coun- cillor, entering a photographer's. "Do you require a small carte, or one of the large ones, sir ?" asked the pro, prietor. "This is no joking affair," said the councillor, with dignity; "what use have I for a cart ? What do you take me for ?" "I take you for thirty shillings a dozen in the large size, cash in advance," answered the photographer. It is an interesting study to look into a photographer's window and criticise the various forms of phisiognemy there displayed; more especially if you have seen much of the actual "taking." The family group is one of the best specimens. It would puzzle some of those men who profess to read character by a photograph to delineate the characters in some family groups. The father, instead of having that look of calm dignity and serenity proper to the 'pater familias," has his eyes fixed on vacancy, and the expression of his face would lead you to think that someone was standing on his toes, and he was trying his level best not to notice it. The mother looked as if she had smiled sometime during the frost without giving her features time to thaw, and the youngsters seem as though they had been glued against an unseen board in various positions, and had their Sunday clothes put over them to hide the supports. This effect may be due to one of three things. It may be owing to the subjects trying -to look unnaturally dignified; to the constrained position for some ten minutes while the ph° ograpber manipulated a third- rate lot of apparatus; or to the kindness and care of the photographer in trying to take the creases out of them. I rather favour the latter theory, for if you go to a photographer and 'throw yourself into a chair, saying that you want a photo without any stiffening, and with something like a natural appearance about it, he will either thinkyou are crazy, or that you intend it as a personal insult to himself. At any rate, he will be grieved, and will think that you don't know anything about the higher ptrrposes of the art. I think there must be a photographer somewhere in th,s country who doesn't 'lnsist upon trussing his customers up like gees', because now and then we do see a photograph that is the likeness of a human being. I intend to look that photographer up, and when I have found him I shall severely reprimand him for not advertising himself.

COTTAGE GARDENING.

Tun CAUROT.—If the ground is unsuitable to this vegetable it becomes the least profitable crop in the garden, but if, on the other hand, matters are to its liking, very few give better returns. Deep sandy loam as a rule has been found to yield the best results, and from such soils the roots come out straight and clean. . . .

Sowing is either made broadcast or in 'thins, but by adopting the latter method much more may be got from the ground, if the drills are drawn much closer than is usually done. The common distance is 8 to 10 inchfis for large-growing sorts, such as Long ,urray, and Altringham, but if half the distance were allowed, and Early Horn or Early Nantes sown alternately, these would be fit for uge and out of the way long before the others are ready, and they would have the full space to develope themselves. With crops of this kind much time is taken up in weeding and thinning, and in this particular case the thinnings would be thrown away if sown on the broad cast plan. It is very annoying to those who are in the habit of exhibiting when they find that they can grow all crops of vegetables fairly well but the carrot, but it has baffled them, so that they can- not present a decent specimen on the exhibition table. Now as a good dish of carrots would carry as many points as any other vegetable it may be worth while to deviate s,little from the ordinary methods of culture in order to attain the desired results. If a piece of ground 4ft. wide is excavated the depth of the spade and placed on each side Until the cavity is filled with decayed leaves or a mixture of decayed, as well burnt vegetable matter, yvhich must be well pressed with the feet, then about six or eight inches of the most friable of the •floil thrown out must be placed on the top to sow the seeds in, which : should be covered over with half-an-inch of fine soil. For exhibition purposes James's Intermediate would be ! more likely to suit under this artificial treatment, and if I sown in drills Early Horn might be sown alternately as ; with the other sorts. Treated well, two or three yards in length served in this way would give several dishes for exhibition as well as for home use. As the seeds, from their tendency to adhere together, give some trouble to the sower, it will be as well to mix them with _

sand, which will cause them to separate. Our ground has been ready for sowing for some days, but there has been too much wind for to get such feathery articles as , carrot seed to drop where they are wanted, so we have to wait for calmer weather. Broccoli, Boreeole, Savoys, and Cauliflowers may now be sown, and it is advisable to divide the contents of the seed packets, leaving a portion to be sown later on, for the two-fold reason that an accident may happen to the first sowing, which greater vigilance may avert on a second attempt, and that as frequently hawens from adverse circumstances, the plants of one sowing cannot be planted out at the right time; or may be after they are planted dry hot weather prevails, and in spite of watering the plants become shrivelled and frightfully crippled, whilst those planted may be a fort- night later will go on unchecked. Sowing In drills ii preferable/to the broadcast plan when several sorts are Own, as it iS much easier to keep the gods distinct. The drills ate net made Mute than two inches deep and about six inches apart. There are about a score of varieties of Brocoli, but the following will give a supply from March to June or July, according to the season :—Adam's Early, Knight's Protecting, Cattell's Eclipse, and Ledsharn's Latest of All. Under the head of Boracole may be placed the Curled or Scotch Kale. Cottager's Kale, and Aspar- agus, or Buda Kale, all of which, as well as the Brocoli, are giving us abundance of vegetables just now. Of Savoys there are only two distinct kinds, the small and the large, and it is an advantage .to have both, as Early Ulm turns in some considerable time before the Drum- head. The following Cauliflowers come in in the order they are named, and will yield a supply from July until destroyed by frost: Early London Walcheren and Veitch's Autumn Giant, the latter being most valuable for exhi- bition.'

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Hardy Periennials There are a few of these that may be raised from seed, and the manner of sowing is similar to that described last week for annuals.. There are four kinds of Campanulas that may be so raised, also about the same number of Colum- bines. - Thefl Everlasting Pea, single and double Canter- bury Bells, four sorts of Delphiniums (lark spurs), Phlox in varity. Lupin (Lupines Polyphyllus), and the beauti- ful Pyrethrums. Last week, as already intimated, we gave instructions how to sow hardy annuals, but for want of space a list of cheap suitable kinds was omitted. To a novice it is of as much importance to know what to select as to know how to sow them. Collinsiapf Sorts, Erysimum, Arkansaunium, Candvtuft, crimson mid white, probably the two best hardy annuals grown; Gilia Tricolor, Larkspurs, Lo+e-lies-Bleeding, Lupins, Sweet Peas, Nemophilla, Silene pink and white, Virginia Stock, and Nasturtiums. The above, with a few others, may be bought in penny packets, which will be found suffi- cient for two patches of each. The following plants are now in flower in the front garden. Primroses in variety, also Polyanthus, Auriculas, Aubretia, Arabis, Muscari, Double Daisies, Hyacinths various, and Narcissus. •

M. tiLADSTONE AND THE NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB.— 1 Mr. Gladstone opened the Library of the National Liberal Club on Wednesday night. Some 2,000 ladie, and geatlemen were present, and gave the ex-Premier, who was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone and Mrs. Drew, a hearty reception. Mr. Gladstone, in his, ad- dress, paid a high tribute to the memory of the late Mr. Chesson, who had done so much for the club, and went on to say that they did not look upon that library as a mere place of lounging or as a simple repository for novels and romances, but as a treasure house of all that could fertilise and ennoble the human mind. The right hon. gentleman next dwelt upon the paramount impor- tance of a well-stored mind in the discharge of public. political, and other duties, and quoted from Macaulay and ether authors who spoke of the tranquillising in- fluences of commune with spirits of the great dead. He was glad to see the national mind taking a turn to the study of history, which would enable people be form better judgments for the wellbeing and happiness of men women and children all over the world.

. CHAPTER XVI HE IS DEAD. • Ceoffrey Stanhope is sittiog alone in the painting room on the morning succeeding his somewhat disagreeable conversation with his mother. He has not met her since, for neither she nor Irene have appeared at .breakfast. Perhaps therpurposely, left him to a fete 4 fete with his father, thinking that, petticoat influence having failed, the head of. the house might be able to talk him into reason. Never, however, were they more mistaken, if this was their object, for the few words that passed between the father and son scarcely amounted to conversation, and even to an outside observer it must have been apparent that Mr. Stanhope was very shy of Geoffrey. , He evidently had not the slightest in- tention Of asking him to help in the family trouble; nor did he even allude in the most distant manner to the revelation which Simon 'Knight had made him, grave though he thought it. For Mr. Stanhope was much more inclined to give it full credence than was .Lady Fedora, and there was little doubt that Geoffrey's marriage with Phyllis would rank side by side in his mind with Ferdinand's delinquencies, and., yet he did .not seem as if he dared say one angrt word to Geoffrey on the subject. Was it that he was utterly cowed by his children's self-will and seeming determination to carve out their own destinies for themselves, or was it that some hidden and strong secret power was laying its •heavy hand on Henry Stanhope, and forbidding him to move one step without permission. Of his inmost feelings it were difficult to give an account; suffice it to say that ,but few men. would have cared to change places with him at that moment, and that if a strong faith and belief in the Great Unseen Deity, on Whom from childhood he, had been taught to rely, had not en- veloped him as in a mystic cloud he would have rid himself of the troubles of life by seeking without More ado "that country from whose bourne no traveller returns." And yet this man was frequently quoted in London clubs as one with Whom places might be changed with advantage. Was he not endowed with riches, a pleasing countenance, and courtly manners,And had. --he not a wife and children of whom any man might be prowl? Alas for the shallowficss of a calculation founded on mere externallseeming! • NO? -Was triere a ninan being to Whom 'Henry Stanhope cared to confide the true story of his life. As his son had hinted when refusing to accede to his Mother's wishes, Henry Stanhope had been sailing for many years under false colours. He had not the strength of character to haul them down; he would rather his barque were carried away into deep wapr by the force of the current, and then what mattered It to him even if it foundered altogether? Only. one Man in London could keep him more or less straight, and that was the man whom he feared the most of all, Sergius Lenskoff. • ' Why had Sergius Lenskoff stridden out of the almost foraotten past and appeared once more in his life? Why had, lie, of all the millions who dwell on the cis,' ised earth, been selected by fate to love and be loved by. Irene? , Sergius Lenskoff loved by Irene! Oh, God, the thought was maddening; and Henry Stanhope,cower- ing before it, eould have wept like a little child; for he, too, loved Irene with that deep holy paternal love which her brothers had never evoked in his heart; and, to see her happy and prosperous had been his prayer' ever since she was laid an infant in his arms. She, his beautiful, sweet innocent Irene, Sergius Lenskoff's wife! No, it could never be. The full array of the Russian's shortcomings—Henry Stanhope called them crimes—rose up in glaring, guilty horror before him as he contemplated such a contingency, and yet he dared not cry out to forbid the march of events, but must sit placidly by and _watch for the issue destiny might have in store. Such being the sort of constant nightmare in which Henry Stanhope was compelled to exist no wonder that the furrows on his brow had deepened. the hair on his temples grown more grizzled •of late; or that Geoffrey, sipping his tea and contem• plating his father over the top of the Times, while he pretended to read, should come to the con- clusion that he was looking terribly old and worn. "And," Geoffrey went on to decide, "if I were to give in to my mother, and consent to further in.! volve the estates' I shall deserve to look at thirty as my father does to-day. No, no, ,I may be hard and disagreeable in my resolution, but I must be firm." And, so determining, he set down his cup and strolled away up to his painting. "In a* world of his own creating he would forget all unpleasant family discussions. Pity his father did not take to painting or: reading instead of dwelling over Ferdinand's follies till he made himself and every one else miserable." Once in the painting room and his work set on the easel, his palette prepared, Geoffrey did not find it so easy to concentrate his mind. ' He was painting in the crimson dress in which Phyllis had sat for her picture, and naturally, as he gazed on her face, his thoughts reverted to her, iis beautiful Phyllis whom he adored. Of course, he adored her; there was no doubt on that subject. Never had he seen any woman so lovely as Phyllis,not even Irene, about whom London raved; she was- too pale and lily- like to suit Geoffrey's taste. No. Phyllis was exactly what he liked--quiteof the Reuben's type. And he laid down his brush and looked at her, he did not feel industrious to-day, it was pleasanter to gaze than work. Married to Phyllis ! What greater bliss could tlaa Virmici have in store? Married to Phyllis!" ATM' the first time the three words' seemed to stagger him. He had refused to burden the estate with the sum of £4,000 to save his father's honour and his brother's name; yet he contemplated a Marriage with. Phyllis Knight! Was not his idea of what- itkwas right and loyal and true for an Englialz gentleman to do just a little, bit of an anomaly! When he talked grandly about walking along heat erect, on straight if narrow paths as a Stanhope should walk, would not folk think he was rather illogical? • What matter if they, did; he had asked Phyllis to be his wife, and she had consented; 'it would be most dastardly and' base to hark back now. Besides he had no wish to do ea, was she not his beautiful darling, his very own? But the. conflicting thoughts worried him none the less, and his work for that day was so bad that he was coupelled to paint out quite as much as he painted in. Ah, if he were only a great artist and could get big sums -for his picture,' he would give his father that four thousand,. but—involve the estates? no that would never do. . Why did not Irene come and talk to him? He wanted to discuss Prince Sergitts:w4h her, and try to make her promise quit she would not think of marriage with. him ; then he looked once more on Phyllis' face, and decided that he had no right to take such an initiative. Still he wished the little sister would eome, and be opened the door. and. listened for her' fOotfill, but only heard that of old Purvis, to whom he caned out, asking What had become of Irene. "Miss Stanhope has had a bad night, and is not up," was the answer, which did not serve to reassure Geoffrey, who, .generally a steady' worker, had never felt more unsettled than he did. that morning. . . There was something; wrong ; the air felt mesmerid and it made his head ache. So he threw down his brush and wandered for a while up and dawn the room, his hands in his trouser's sockets, whistling as men are wont to whistle When'thinking Oppresses them. What it can .be that bother S him he does not know. • "One of Geoff's cranks," Irene would have said '" dear old Geoff, he had a tile loose sometimes." Perhaps she guesses that something of this sort is the matter now, for she comes flying downstairs in her dressing-gown, her lovely hair lying loose in rip- pling curls about her shoulders, her pretty white, stockingless feet encasei in 'a pair of Turkish em- broidered mulcts. She holds a pink paper in her hand, which shews more or less the object of this sudden rush to find her

• brother. "Simon Knilit is dead !" she announces breath- lessly. "Here is a telegram from Phyllis." Geoffrey' took it from her with a trembling, hand, and the brother and sister looked at each other. They both seemed. intuitively to know that :with Simon Kni,k,lit'S death a crisis had arisen in their lives, though they could not have defined in what form it would manifest itself. Geoffrey, at once tossed off his painting blouse and without even stopping to put away his colours ran, briskly downstairs. In the hall he met his father. "What is the matter, • Geoffrey ? " asked the elder man in some surprise,- on noting his son's perturbation. , "Simon Knight is dead, and I am going to Wandsworth to see if I can be of any assistance." "Sinn Knight dead " And it was as if a ray

denoting something akin to joy passed athwart Mr.- Stanhope's usually grave features. Then he pulled!. himself together,as though fearing it might be rots marked and asked,., "When did he die? He was here last evening." , "Here hat evening! Simon Knight! I did ness know he was doing any work for you." "Nor was ke.. He came to consult .tne on Matter conneeied With his daughter." , • But Geoffrey did not seem to think it expedient to'• ask any further question, so he set his hat solidly' on his brow and proceeded to open the street door. The announcement of Simon Knight's death had 'evidently lifted some portion at least, of a heavy load from Mr. Stanhope's mind, for advancing to,Wards•She doer, he gave it a little push. "You will not go to Wandsworth! r win not hive you always with these Knights," he said With more withority than he had used in speaking to Geoffrey RA late. ; , There was no . disrespect in the young man's Manner, but he answered very'firmly, "I arm sorry;to disobey you but I must go; I cannot- desert theta , now when are in trouble." . . "Geoffrey I lea me that it ,is not true ;that you been making love and, engaging yourself,. to that girl: •Do not.. let me be :disappointed in both my eons. . Do not kill me with the know le,pe that you, Married a 10-w, good-for-nothing girl. „ ' Therapp,eal In-light have had some effect but for the! -epithets at the end of it; which were most injudicious and stuns. Geoffrey to the quick, rousing his temper 9 • and making him answer very roughly; -f!..Lani of age, to do as I please, and I . suppose I 'Shall carve out my, fortunes as I choose, even .as . you did before me. . The words struck the father far more surely ,- than Geoffrey could have expected. I‘ll. .-StanhoprEf' fell just two steps backward, and With something alnioSt like an abject tone in his voice said, "Oh, Geoffrey! do not hurl 'my own past at MY head,' but be Warned .before it is too late about your future ; if you make this low marriage you will never gems) toree•ret it." „ ' But the word " low " kept Geoffrey dorstsd , • in a- • great measnre perhaps because it was its, justice that rankled, • had been , rankling in his heart all that. morning, :though he had been strenuously seeking' not to acknowledge it to hinufelf.. Mr. Stanhope's appeal • without the intervention of hard • words , would have been xi* in a different spirit. - Geoffrey would not perhaps have yielded - the love that-4b6 believed, and truly, that he felt ,fos. cancelled the engagement he had made with her— at his father's bidding ; but saye for those un- diploniatie e-eifliets, he would not have met Mr.. . sfaiihop4 well-meritod reproofs and warnings such a violently anttwenfstlo way. • : is useless td lalk to me in this tone," luf • answered, "If -Phyllis is IoW, then so is all the, world. .There can be no caste, prejlidice in this in- stanee; She' sears above it." " My_ son,. you are deceiving yourself, and you will find it out to your cost if yen ever attempt to take Phyllis into the society in which We moire." "A fig for soeiety ! " cried Geoffrey angrily. " Ain I to ruin my happiness for the sa'ke of a society Which has never done anything for me ?Let be marry. Sergias Lenskoff though he is a Prince Darkness ; that is • what you and my mother a,r. aiming. at. - One sacrifice in a family is. surely enou&.;. You can let me be happy.in my own way." A protestation, which might perhaps have startiL4 -Geoffrey had he ._ stopped, to hear it, rose to Mt. Stanhope's ; bitt Geoffrey hail opened the door and Was gone. He was longing to be by Phyllis's side,. to , console and • seethe her in her trouble ; and AO at this particular moment any home opposition irritated him in 'a way which it Would not have done - under Ordinary ciremnstances. To reach the Victoria Station and take a .ticket for Wandsworth was only the work of a'fevi minutes, but there was a quarter-of-an-hour to wait before the train started, and this Geoffrey' employed in walking restlessly about the station, Ile was thoroughly at odds with circumstance, The two conversations he had recently had .with his family worried and annoyed hint more than h° ever remembered to have been annoyed before, it seemed more as if lie wanted to be soothed bY Phyllis's caressing voice; than that he was in a 0 state to offer consolation. Nor was tho Cup of Geoffrey's vexations by all means full. Strolling along the principalplatforn though the d was i ay young, was no leas an ndiVidue: than Sergius Lenskoff. 'THE EUROPEAN SITUATION.-THE • AUS- TRIAN ARMY BILL.-GREECE AND TURKEY.-ENORMOUS ARMIES. VIENNA, MONDAY.—In Hungary, the new Arms,- Bill, which gives the Emperor powers to call out 100.000 men ef the reserve without asking for the sanction of Parlia- ment, has been voted by a large majority. The semi- official Praise to-day discusses the question of war or. Peace, and, after taking into consideration every even- tuality, comes to the conclusion that there is no cause for fear, while at the same time deprecating over-conft- , deuce. It says in effect, "Let us hope that the art of the diplomatist and the military commander will ward otT danger, but lot us keep our powder dry." ATHENS, Motinss ND:MT.—We have had another cur- Prise. The Turkish Minister at Athens, who for the last two weeks has worked heartily to strengthen the rela- tions between Greece and Turkey, has been suddenly recalled, and ordered to return to Con-tantinople at once, 'Without presenting his letters of recall to the King. Beaux, MONDAY Nioirr. The Panslavists have resumed their attack on Germany, and Russia has never Slackened her military preparations. On this point Russia proposes to raise the strength of the troops on her western frontier to 800,000 men. A conflict is there- fore, inevitable, and this compels Germany to act with the greatest. care and wariness, so that it may be clear to all the world that she is not the aggressor. This attitude on the pert of Germany is so much the more necessary the more threatening the situation becomes in France, 'Where the crisis, according to opinion prevalent here, DMA become acute in a few months at latest Under such circumstances Germany has to keep a most careful watch in order not to be surprised, but to arrangs matters in the manner most advantageous to herself. THE GERMAN EMPEROR'S CONDITION. BERLIN, MONDAY.—A bulletin this morning states that the Emperor has reseed a quiet night, and 's almost free ! from fever. Professor Von Bergmann has ceased to visit the Emperor, and there is reason to believe that, The eminent physician will not again participate in his Majesty's treatment This mernine's bulletin was signed by Professor Von Bardeleben, a well-known practitioner, who is for the present, at any rate, railing at the palace. BERLIN, TUESDAY MORNINCL—The temperature of the Emperor this afternoon was 102 degrees, but decreased again to-nieht to 101-6 degrees, and is therefore some- what higher than it has been during the past. three days. With regard to the withdrawal of Professor Bergmann from attendance on the Emperor the following authentic farts have been ascerteined:—On Thursday last, heron, the usual morning consultation, Professor Beremann . handed to Sir Morel! Mackenzie a letter stating, "I wish to inform you that in consequence of your attack upon ; me in the Kreaz Zeitung I desire to have no further conversation with you except upon the state and the treatment of the august patient." A Consultation was afterwards held RS usual, and as Boon as Sir Mdrell Mackenzie had performed his duties as medical attendant on the Emperor Frederick he wrote a Setter to Professor Bergmann, in which he formally acknowledged the receipt, of the Professor's le! ter, vrh;cli had been personally handed to him, and at the same time remarked that he failed to see that his relations with Professor Bergmann in future shnuld he in any Way altered, AS he was not aware that he bad ever with hi rn any conversation except as regarded the condition mid the treatment of the august patient.. The article in the Krell:" Zeitung was it correction sent by Sir Morell Mackenzie of the statements contained in as anonymous attack unon him in the /Unix/Le 7:elbow_ The following bulletin was issued on Thursday Morning With a very low state of fever, the general condition of the Emperor to-day is relatively satis- factory."

REPORTED ASS ASSTNATION OF THE MA HD'. CAITIO, SUNDAY NH-MT.—A considerable number of re- fugees from Omdurman are said to have arrived nt Wady Haifa, although the reports on the subject are Somewhat con holing. Natives who have escaped from the Mandist headquarters state that the Mandi has been assassinated by his lieutenant, who has assumcd power. It is cortein, however, that a bombastic proelamation, Purporting to come from the Mandi. has been issued. In this all believers are enjoined to make common cause With the dervishes. The proclamation which declares that the Mandists have conquered Abyssinia and have forced the foreigners to fly, is beieg extensively circu- lated in Upper Egypt, and ha.s, it is said, made a great impression upon the natives, owing in chief part to the references to the Italians leaving Massowah. PANIC IN A MENAGERIE. VIENNA, MONDAY NIOHT.—A terrible panic occurred in a menagerie at Prague last night. The structure is a 'Wooden one, and is capable of holding about 1,500 per- as. Suddenly, when the building was tolerably full, a cry of "lire" was raised, it is said by pickpockets, when there was a wild rush to the doors. Men, women, and children were knocked down and trampled under Soot, and the scene for some time was terrible in the ' extreme. At length, when quiet was restored, it was , found that six persons had been killed, and a very large *umber more or less seriously injured. PRISON REVOLT IN EGYPT.—DESPERATE FIGHT IN A MOSQUE. CAIDO, SUNDAY NIGIIT.—A serious prison revolt, whice was vet quelled without much bloodshed, took place yesterday at Damanhour, a place 12 miles from Alexan- dria. Two prisoners in the gaol who were under sen- tence of death, aided by 18 other convicts, managed to :z eisrtt iee their escape from the orison. 'rite police at once d in pursuit, but before they could come up with !them, the prisoners took refuge in a mosque, 11: ere a ;desperate fight took place, in which 15 of the prisoners were killed and two were wounded, while the police had four killed and wounded.
THE STABBING OUTRAGE AT WARRINGTON.

In connection With the stabbing case that oc- curred last week in Crostield-st., particulars in re- gard to which were given in the last issue of the "Examiner," the borough police have succeeded in effecting the apprehension of a young man named Arthur Massey (21), of 3.5, Town Hill, Warrington, who is suspected of having committed the outrage on Walls, the man who was stabbed. At the Borough Court, on Wednesday morning, Massey was brought before the magistrates and was charged With unlawfully and maliciously cutting and wound- ing William Walls with a knife, on the 25th of April, in Crostield-st., with intent !to do him bodily harm. The prosecutor, who appeared with his head bandaged and one hand in a sling, gave formal evi- dence to the effect that on the evening of the day in question he was walking along Crosfield-st., to the Post Office, when he met two men, who were walk- ing quickly. As soon as he got up to them the shorter of the men told him "to stand," at the same Ume raising his hand and stabbing him in the ear. The man attempted to strike him again, but prose- cutor warded off the blow with his hand. Witness then ran to see a doctor. Prisoner was a stranger to him, as he had never previously seen him. He seemed to be " neither sober nor drunk." Prisoner Was then remanded until next Monday,

div.head: IRISH PUBLIC WORKS.
div.p: IRISH PUBLIC WORKS.

Lord MONTEAGLE of BRAWDON inquired whether the overriment proposed to take any steps towards carry- ing out the recommendations of the Commission on Public Works in Ireland. He instanced the subjects of ,ITsinage, fisheries, and harbours, as urgently requiring ttention.

Lord Emly. the Earl of Leitrim, the Earl of North- brook, and Earl Spencer spoke on the question.—Eari Spasms stated that it was impossible to form a decisive opinion as to the measures which ought to be taken until the evidence given before the Commissioners was made public. He defended the action of the late Liberal Government.

. The Earl of CADOGAN, replying for the Government, stated that the Chief Secretary proposed to lay two hills on the table of the Flouse of Commons before the Whit- suntide Recess, dealing with the drainage question With regard to the questions of fisheries and harbours, te amalgamation of railways, and Government guar- .latees for railways—these were matters which were now wider the serious consideration of her Majesty's Govern- ;:lent, with a view to speedy legislation. The LORD CHANCELLOR nominated a Select Committee • o consider the Land Transfer Bill.
The House adjourned at 6 30 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MONDAY.

The POSTMASTER-GENERAL promised to consider th, elaims of friendly societies to bave their notices to men - beta in arrears of subscription sent for id. postage, in- -tead of ld, as at present, pointing out, however, that such notices were not circulars in the departmental sens - of the term.

Mr. RITCHTR, replying to Mr. Theodore Fry, said th. ffect of the compensation clauses of the Local Govern- ment Bill would be that in the event of the renewal of n license being refused, compensation would have ;to h, determined with reference to the value -of the prem liv- existing before, and not after, the passing of the Act The basis on which compensation vrould be given wool,: he the value of premises with the license as against the value of premises without the license.

div.head: NEW MEMBER.
div.p: NEW MEMBER.

The SPRAKTiR having ordered meinbcrs entitled to tak, t heir seats so to do, Mr. Phillips, the new member for Mid-Lanark, came up the floor of the House, accompanied hy Mr. D. Crawford and Mr. M. Fergusson, amid loud Opposition cheers.
COL. KING-HARMAN'S SALARY. 'rhe CHIEF SECRETARY for IRELAND moved the second reading of the bill providing for payment of a salary In the Under Secretary for Ireland.

Mr. Jon, MORLEY. who was loudly cheered, formally moved the rejection of the measure. He im- peached the Government for introducing a wholly unnecessary and inopportune proposal. It appeared to him that the new Minister was intended to answer (pep- tions in the HOUSP, but he affirmed that no method of, answering questions relating to Irish administration could be satisfactory unless the responsibility was fixed upon the proper person, who was the Chief, and not the Under Secretary. The only means the Irish members in Parliament had of criticising the Irish administration was by asking questions in the House. so that it was obvious that they ought to have opportunities of address ing their inquiries to a responsible and important official. The bill, said Mr. Morley, was an absurd and irmtioted one, and was only brought in for the purpose of creatine an office for a Minister who had already been appointed. He assured the Government that the measure and the appointment were alike intensely distasteful to the Mill people. Sir Jung SIMOIsT challenged the right of the Govern- ment to create an office without consulting Parliament, and accused the Chief Secretary of practising deception upon the House, when he stated in the first instance that the office was to be unpaid. Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR asserted that the Chief Secretary had practised equivocation, and that at all events he had no need of special assistance.—Colonel SAUNDURSON asked whether it was possible to find a man who was in sympathy with all Irish parties—Mr. T. W. Rosstu. declared that the appointment would be regarded prac- tically as a declaration of war against the tenantry of Ireland.--Mr. BALFOUR replied. Mr. CAMPRFLL-BANNRRMAN expressed his astonishment that precedence should have been given to this bill over the Budget Bill. The Government, with re,gard to this appointment, had been performing a sort of conjuring trick; and a most unfavourable impression must be created on the public mind by the association of three active, militant, and aggressive landowners in the dis- posal of Irish matters in which the interests of the land- lords were largely concerned. After further discussicn the House divided. For the second reading Against . . _ . _ .
The announcement was received with Opposition cheers. The bill was read a second time. TFIE BUDGET.

The Committee on the Budget Bill was resumed. Mr. SYDNEY GEDGR obtained an assurance from the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer that he was really desirous to help in any attempt to cheapen the transfer of land.-- Several formal amendments were made in the schedules, and the &11 nassed thrniiah committee. IRISH LAND LAWS. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL resumed the adjourned debate on the second reading of the Irish Land Commission Bill, of which he moved the rejection. He held it to be a monstrous thing that £lOO,OOO per annum should be spent to compel the landlords in Ireland to do what the English and Scotch landlords did from choice. tie submitted that the bill would take away the option of the Irish tenants as to which court they would gm to for an adjustment of their rents, and compel them to go into the County Court. Mr. BALFOUR promised to consider any proposal that Was likely to be acceptable. The Government were anxious that any modifications that might be made should have the confidence of the tenants in Ireland, and his proposal was to associate with the county court judge two lay commissioners on equal terms, and that the judge should have the alma position as the legal com- missioner in the sub-commission court. If the landlord and tenant agreed to do so, a fair rent might he fixed by the lay Commissioner going over the land and valuing it without the intervention of the court. That would be a cheaper process. Mr. PARNELL said the Government had failed to make out a case for the bill, and he suggested that the method should remain as at present with the appointment of ad- ditional sub-commissioners.

- The SOLICITOR-GENERAL or IRELAND said the bill was not introduced as the hest possible solution, butsas an honest attempt to solve a difficult problem. The House divided, and the second reading was carried by 228 to 139. The bill was read a second time. Other business baying been disposed of, the Rouse ad- journed at 1 a.m. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TimsnAr. •
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at. 4 15 p.m.

THE CHURCH DISCIPLINE BlLL—This bill passed pro forma through Committees, and was recommitted for the 11th inst. CATHEDRAL CHURCHES BlLL—This bill was read a third time and passed. DURATION OF SPEECHES RILL.—Lord DENMAN moved the second reading of a bill similar in its provisions to the bill which he introduced last year for limiting the duration of speeches in Parliament. The bill provided that, with the exception of ministers, ordinary members of Parliament,except for special occasions, should be limited to ten minute speeches. The noble lord com- plained that a lot of time was wasted in long speeches. —Lord CRANI3ROOIC thought the bill was quite un- necessary in the House of Peers. The bill sought to regulate the speeches in another place, which was clearly beyond their province. He, therefore, moved the rejection of the bill.—The motion to reed the bill a second time was negatived without further discussion.
Tbe Westminster Abey Bill and the Customs (We of Man) Bill were read a second time.
On the motion of Lord KINTORE, Lord Thurlow and Lord Hartsmere were added to the Select Committee on the Land Transfer Bill.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Mr. 11. MArtnEws, in answer to Mr. Bradlaugh, said it was fact that breaches of the Truck Act had recently been reported in the Bristol district, and that the In- spector of Factories had been directed to make full in- quiries into the circumstances. Mr. Cana called the attention of Mr. Ritchie to the judgment given on Monday, in the Court of Queen's Bench, in respect to the appeal of a publican from the refusal of the Westmorland magistrates to renew his license for reasons other than offences against the law; and asked whether, in consequence, he intended to press the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill?

Mr. lerrcnni reminded the House that this decision was not given by a final court of appeal. The Govern- ment believed that the compensation clauses of the bill were just—(Conservative cheers) and consequently would not withdraw them. Mr. Ritchio afterwards added, in reply to another question, that he was aware, and did not believe that the value of public-house pro- perty had vastly increased since the announcement of the compensation clauses of the bill.

div.head: CROFTERS' GRIEVANCES.
div.p: CROFTERS' GRIEVANCES.

At 4 30, Dr. CLAIZK moved the adjournment of the House, in order to call attention to the danger to law and order in the Highlands of Scotland, arising from the complete breakdown of the Crofter Act as the remedy for the Crofters' grievances. The SPEAZER put the usual question, and asked whether the hon. member was supported. A large num- ber of members rose on the Opposition side of the House, but several Conservatives asked that they should be counted. The SPRAYER complied, and cried "Forty "; and this number being sufficient for his purpose, Dr. CLana formally moved the adjournment, and criticised the work of the Crofters Act, urging the necessity of reazethe Crofters' Commission power to compulsorily the holdtars.—blr maid ia_wee

The writ for the St. Stephen's Green Division reached Dublin on Thursday. The Sheriff has fixed Monday next for the nomination, and the following Thursday for the polling. A receiving order was on Thursday granted at Liverpool Bankruptcy Court against Mrs. Saker, of the Alexandra Theatre, whose liabilities are said to be be- tween £5OOO and £6OOO, and assets about £2OOO. Tine EARLY CLOSING BILL.— Fifty-three Gladsto- nians including Mr. John Morley and Sir George Trevelyan ; 21 Parnellites, 12 Liberal Unionists, and 11 Conservatives supported the Early Closing Bill on Wednesday. ANOTHER DISCOVERY OF GOLD IN WALES—For some time a number of men have been engaged in removing the rocks at the approach to Holyhead Harbour. During the operation the divers, Guthrie and Moncas, struck a vein of rock glittering with golden particles. A portion of quartz has been submitted to a chemise for analysis, and pronounced to be gold. SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT —A melancholy accident was reported from Galway on Thursday. Miss Noel Persse, a young lady, sister of the High Sheriff, was out riding, when the pony made a sudden start and threw her. She was unable to extricate herself, and hung by the stirrup. When the pony was stopped the young lady was unconscious, and only lived five minutes. WEr.sn Gors, Alms. A deputation consisting of several Welsh members and others waited upon the Chancellor of the Exchequer at the Treasury, on Wed- nesday, in reference to the Welsh gold mines. Mr. Pritchard Morgan pointed out that it would be impos- sible for all gold mines in Wales to pay the heavy royalty a3O per cent to the Crown. and that the development of the Welsh goldfields would be retarded by its imposi- tions. In reply, the Chancellor of the Exchequer said he was desirous of doing everything he could to aid in the development of this national industry. The views of the deputation would be carefully considered by the Government.
