The LORD ADVOCATE saw no vason to depart from the views be expressed at the commencement of the session on the subject. No scheme of migration could have a very salutary effect on account of the rapid growth of the population, and it was also an undisputed fact that Crofters could not maintain themselve out of their crofts alone. Without the removal of a portion of the con- gested population no hope existed of really relieving that part of Scotland, and he thought there was no cruelty in inducing those people to settle elsewhere. The li. CaTHOB ELLIOTT hoped that the strong statement.. the Lord Advocate as to the desirability of assisting emigration would be followed by aCtion which would prevent a recurrence cf the scenes witnessed last winter in the Western Islands.—Dr. R. MACDONALD asked why the crofters should be expatriated, while so many acres were devoted to deer forests.--Dr. Cameron having followed, Mr. J. 0/UNDERLAIN said when he visited the western Highlands he spoke personally to many hundreds of crofters, and in every case the account they gave of their condition and wants was almost precisely the same. No doubt the great difficulty was the deficiency of the lind they cultivated. He had convinced himself that emigration would never have a fair chance till the Crofters were satisfied that. the legislature had done all it could in the direction oi giving them reasonable opportunities of obtaining larger portions of land intheir own country. Mr. Aimus BTITH/MLA/7D said that when the resources pf the country were exhausted the crofters might migrate, but that they refused to do so in order to leave their homes to deer and sheep. After further discussion, Mr. W. H. %writ said he was sorry to state that, the answer given by the Lord- Advocate was the answer of the Government. The Government would not be justified if they sought to deceive the House, and the unfortunate Crofter popula- tion, by holffintg out fallacious promises. Dr. CLARK wished to withdraw the motion for adjourn- ment, but this the House refused to allow, and a division VMS taken— For the Adjournment ...... 99 Against
IR !WAND.

On Monday, the Queen's Bench, Dublin, delivered judg- ment on the status of Mr. Sexton, M.P., as a citizen of Dublin, 'and therefore involving his qualification to be Lord Mayor, the question turning upon whether he was a householder or only a lodger. The Court unanimously decided in favour of Mr. Sexton, and dismissed the appeal. Mr. Wilfrid Blunt, in thanking the subscribers of his defence fund, which has reached a total of £1,365, says the further pressing of his case in the Dublin courts would not advance to a full result, as there would always be some one person amenable to Castle ••,quences able to defeat a unanimous verdict, an. .ven were a verdict obtained the Govern- ment has Mexhau.stible resources to carry the case to the House of Lords, and protract the proceedings over •cent-ha, or vears.• He suggested that the balance of the f., nd should be made a nucleus Of a political prisoners defence fund.
DOUBLE EXECUTION.-EXTRAORDINARY SCENES

„..,...—. .. - Daniel Moriarty and Daniel Hayes were hanged at Tralee Gaol, on Saturday, for the murder of James Fitzmaurice. at Lixnaw, county Kerry, on January 21st last. The morning was bright and fine, and many people from the town and neighbourhood gathered near the gaol shortly before eight o'clock. at. which hour a black flag, hoisted near the scaffold-yard, conveyed the intelligence that the sentence of the law had been :•arriecl out. The circumstances of the murder of Fits- maurice—an aged farmer, living at Ahabeg—who wa by the two men named, with revolvers, in the pre- ence of his daughter, on a public road close to the ell- lage of Lixnaw, on the morning of the date named, aro well known. Since their conviction, at Wicklow o.esires, last month, the prison had been guarded ',37 day and night (by military at night). bu' • here was little interested manifested in the fat, .at the criminals; and there had been no effor' to obtain a reprieve. t M Saturday, a knot of poop!” were assembled in a field adjoining that portion of the ruison where the scaffold-yard is, and among these wet-- ,yme of the relations of the culprits. A mournful dire - -was raised by them as the hour of execution approached- In front of the gaol there were not more than MO persons congregated. Moriarty WAS a farm labourer, who came to the Llama:se district from another part 0, Kerry, and was married there, little mpre than a year ago. Hayes was an itinerant shoemaker. a native of Tralee, who occasionally worked through the northern l‘ortion of the county. He had been several times cen• victed of assaults, and was addicted to drink. Both men appeared very penitent. Hayes particularly so. Tlf. visiting justices, in their discretion, refused to admit th.. Press representatives to the execution. Moriarty is the man who was stated to have partly: confessed the murder. Hayes made no attempt t.c• speak. The bolt was speedily drawn, and Moriarty died I mmediately ; but tour minutes elapsed before Dr. Fal- vey, the prison surgeon, pronounced life to be,extinct in Hayes. The bodies were afterwards cut down, ant' buried in the scaffold yard.

div.head: WASTE AND VACANT LANDS..
div.p: WASTE AND VACANT LANDS..

Mr. BRAD '''That in the opinion of the !louse. ownership of land in the United Kingdom should carry with it the duty of cultivation or utilisation, and that in all eases where land capable of cultivation, or utilisation with profit, and not devoted to some purpose of public utility or enjoyment, is held in a vacant, waste, or uncultivated state, the local authorities ought to have the power to compulsorily acquire such land by payment to the owner of a sum representing the capital agricultural value of such lands, in order that such local authorities may, in their discretion, let the said lands to tenant cultivators, with such conditions as to terms of tenancy, rent, reelan.ation, drainage, utilisation, or cultivation respectively, as shall afford reasonable en- couragement, opportunities, facilities, and security for due utilisation, cultivation, and development of the said land&" His simple proposit ion was that the ownership Mr. MuNno PRRGRSON seconded the motion, confining hie remarks chietly to the question of waste lands in Scotland. . .

Mr. Serox-Raett pronoced en amendment to the effect that, owing to agricultural and industrial depression. these lands could not be profitably cultivated, and were, therefere, unable to support their increasing populations; and the House was of opinion that conferring powers of compulsory purchase on local authorities was not an effectual or desirable remedy for that state of things. Mr. R. G. Webster caught the Speaker's eye before the interval for dinner, and on the House resuming was in his place to continue the debate, but a count was called, and at 8 5 the Speaker loft the chair, there not being a quorum present. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. EARLY CLOSING BILL, &C. A number of petitions were presented against the licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill. A new writ was ordered for the St. Stephen's Green Division of Dublin, after which Sir J. LUBBOCK moved the second reading of the Early Closing Bill, urging that it was impossible for persons working such long hours as he quoted to pay any attention to moral, intellectual, and spiritual welfare. Mr. Blundell Mee= moved that the bill be read a second time that day sbc months, and Mr. C. W. R. COOKE seconded.— Sir W. FOSTER supported the principle of the bill, while admitting that some of its details were open to exception, and Mr. W. F. LAWRENCE opposed it.—Mr. Smerricx SMITH said that among the shopkeepers and assistants in Liverpool there was absolute unanimity In favour of compulsory shortening of the hours of labour among them.—The second reading was negatived by a majority of 183. _ .

VICTORIA UrnvEnsrry. BILL.—On the motion of Mr. BRYCE, the Victoria University Bill was read a second time amidst loud cheers. The House adjourned at ten minutes to sixo'elock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnuasnay, The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. _ .

- LORD CARNARVON AND MR. PA RNELL.—The Earl of Cantianvow asked leave to make a personal explanation regarding statements made concerning himself during his absence. He deprecated making such statements when he was not present to answer them, and then pro- ceeded to complain that Mr. Parnell had represented him as having promised to liberate every one Of a gang of Irish prisoners then in custody, the truth being that lie had only undertaken to consider the case of one pri- soner. He described an interview he had with Mr. Par- nell regarding an Irish Parliament, and said Mr. Parnell's account of this interview was absolutely without founda- tion. - HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. .

In the a-ceiTe-e—of the speaker, who is unwell, the chair was taken at five minutes past three o'clock by Mr. Courtney, the Chairman of Committees. PETlTlONS.—Petitions were presented against the com- pensation to publicans and other licensing clauses of the Local Government Bill, by Mr. Hardcastle, from the Gravel-lane Working Men's Institute, Salford: Colonel Bridgeman, from the Methodist Band of Hope and Sons of Temperance, Bolton; Mr. Allison, from the Cumber- land and Westmoreland Grand Division of the Sons of Temperance; Mr. Shepherd Cross, from Rechabites, Bol- ton; Mr. Slagg, from Good Templars, Burnley • Mr. Brunner, from Winsford ; Mr. Sidebottom, from Comp- stall; Sir U. Kay Shuttleworth, from Nonconformist congregations of Nelson and Opine; and Mr. Ainslie, from Bealand ; for a clear definition of the term "main road," by Mr. For wood, from the Upholland Local Board; against the exemption of large towns from coun- ty contributions which they have hitherto paid, by Mr. Forwood, from the Upholland Local Board ' • that all towns of over 50,000 inhabitants be dealt with as separ- ate counties, by Mr. Seton-Karr, from the Mayor and Corporation of St. Helens. THE COMPENSATION OE LICENCE HOLDERS.—Among the questions asked was one put by Mr. BONSOR, who wished to know whether Mr. Ritchie, instead of making the compensation of licence holders a charge on the countyrates, would accept an amendment to the Local Government Bill authorising the County Council to allocate to a fund to be used for compensation purposes any additions which might be made to the existing licence duties. The President of the Local Government Board undertook to give consideration to such an amend- ment, presuming it was moved. THE GOLD MmEs.—ln reply to questions, Mr. SMITH said that, with a view to the development of goldmining in Wales, leases or licenses were being granted at moderate royalties to such persons as desired to take them. The amount of royalty was under consideration, and the Government would do everything in their power to encourage the industry. THE PAPAL DECREE.—Efforts were made by Mr. Labouchere and Sir George Campbell to elicit whether communications had passed between the Government, the Duke of Norfolk, and the Pope recently upon Irish affairs • but Sir J. Ferguson was exceedingly reticent, and wished to have notice given of one of the ques- tions. _ _ _

THE BUDGET—On the report stage of the Budget Bill, the clause dealing with bottled wines was carried by 207 votes against 115, though Sir W. Harcourt and many hon. members spoke strongly against it because of the disturbing effect the tax was likely to have upon our trade relations with France.

div.head: PAPAL CONDEMNATION OF THE , PLAN OF CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE PAPAL CONDEMNATION OF THE , PLAN OF CAMPAIGN.

The following text of the there° has been for- warded to the Irish Rishops, accompanied by a cir- cular from Cardinal Simeoni :—On several occasions Ihe Apostolic See has given to the people of Ire- land (whom it has always regarded with special benevolence) suitable admonitions and advice when circumstances required as to how they might de- fend their rights without injury to justice or to public peace. Our Holy Father Leo XIII., fearing lest in that species of warfare that has been introducen. amongst the Irish people into the contest between land- lords and tenants, and which is commonly called the. "Plan of Campaign," and in that kind of social inter- dict called boycotting, arising from the same contests. True sense of justice and charity might ho perverted. ordered the supreme Congregation of the Inquisition to subject the matter to serious and careful examina- tion. Hence the following question was proposed to the Cardinals of that Congregation. "Is it permis- sible, in the disputes between landowners and tenants in Ireland, to use the means known as the " Plan of Campaign" and "Boycotting ?" After long and mature deliberation, their Eminences unanimously answered in the negative, and the decision was con- firmed by the Holy Father on Wednesday, the 18th of the present month. The justice of this decisaon will be readily seen byl'anyone who applies his mind to con- sider that a rent agreed on by mutual ccnsent cannot, without, violation of a contract, be diminished at the mere will of a tenant, especially when there are tribunal 9 appointed for settling such controversies and reducing unjust rents within the bounds of equity after taking into account the causes which diminish the value of the land. Neither can it be considered permissible that rents be extorted from tenants and deposited in the hands of unknown Rerson§,t9 the detriment ef the land- owners. Finally, it Is contrary to justice and charity to persecute by a social interdict those who are satisfied to pay the rents they agreed to, or those who, in the exer- cise Of their right, take vacant farms. It will therefore 134 PH lordship's duty prudently, but effeettaily, advise and exhort the clergy and the laity not to films- gress the bounds of Christian charity and justice whilst they are striving for a remedy for their distressed con- dition. At a meeting of English and Irish Roman Catholics, at Aldershot. on Sunday. it was resolved to support the Plan of Campaign, to form a branch of the Home Rule League, and to abstain from contributing to Peter's Pence. The Pope's action was strongly denounced as supporting rack-renting and evicting Irish landlords against the only protection the tenants nave.

_ NEW Yong, Tnrsnam—Mr. Fitzgerald,president of the Irish National League of Ameiica, alluding to the Papal decree, states that Irishmen will now step backward, being satisfied that their cause is inst.

A telegram from Rome announces that the Pope has decided that Dr. Walsh shall return to his post as Arch- bishop of Dublin. The weekly reports of the National League, published on Thursday, show the opinion of the League of the Pope's pronouncement on the Irish question. An atti- tude of hostility to the interference of the Papacy in a political matter of this.kind is manifested.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Up to the present time Lord Cross has been unable to draft a report which the whole of the members of the Royal Commission on Education, over which he presides, are willing to sign. It is probable the difficulty will be got over by the issue of two reports, one signed by the minority. Mr. Mundella, speaking on Monday at Whitechapel, de- scribed the .Irish policy of the present Government as the meanest, pettiest tyranny ever perpetrated by a strong upon a weak people, and Lord Randolph Churchill se an honourable man could not stand the broken pledge of the Government to concede local government to Ireland. The Local government Bill falsified Sir Michael Hicks-Beach's boast that Conservatives trusted the People, for by this measure the people were not trusted with the control of their own police. The bill was full of checks and hindrances to prevent popular control, which it would be the object of the Opposition to elimi- nate. Ile condemned the taxation proposals of the Chaneollor of the Exchequer, and advocated the equilisa- t ion of the death duties. _

Mr. Gladstone, replying to a correspondent who drew attention to previous utterances on the purchase of the Sner. Canal Shares, writes:—" I do not, on tie evidence before me, find much fault with my memory, though the word financial seems to have been used in two senses. As an operation of British finance, I consider the purchase of the canal shares tot* worse than ridicu- lous. It was wrong and it was dangerous. As a money speculation I am not aware of having ever said or thought it would prove a bad one. As I think it has to do with the imprudent engagements subsequently con- tracted in Egypt and the vast cost they entailed, I think in its ultimate effect the purchase entailed or helped to entail great pecuniary loss upon the country.";

COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL.-SAD - - -

div.head: LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: LOSS OF LIFE.

A collision took place in the Channel on Sunday morn- ing about ten o'clock, off the Isle of Wight, between the British ships Smyrna, from London to Sydney, and the Mob), from Bilboa to Newenstle. The Smyrna, which was n full rigged ship, sank almost immediately after the collision, taking down with her 12 of her crew. The Moto put into Southampton for repairs, her fore compartment being full of water and her bows damaged and stove in. She landed the sur- vivors of the Smyrna's crew, seventeen in number. The Smyrna belonged to Aberdeen, and the captain was Thomas Taylor. She was bound from London to Sydney with a general cargo. The Moto, a screw steamer, Cap- tain Dig,man, of Newcastle, was from Bilbao with iron ore. About 16 miles south-east of Anvil Point, Captain Digman and the look-out man saw the Smyrna under full sail on the port bow. There was a good sailing breeze, and the weather was thick. The engines of the Mot() were reversed for three or four minutes, and the vessel VMS almost stopped when the Smyrna collided with her. She grazed the port bow of the Moto, which then struck her near the main rigging with great force, causing her to sink very quickly. The bows of the Moto were badly stove, and the vessel was kept from sinking by the watertight bulkheads. The second mate of the Smyrna, named Walker, jumped on board the Moto, ad two men were hauled on board. Three boats were also immedi- ately lowered from the steamer, and succeeded in saving 15 others; but the London pilot, Mr. Colby; Thomas Taylor, captain; Fowler, third mate: and carpenter, cook, and seven able seamen of the Smyrna were drowned. Johnson, chief mate of the Somas, was badly
GENERAL NEWS.

A London policeman, named Samuel Parish, died at the Royal Free Hospital, on Monday, from concussion of the brain, caused by attempting to alight from a tram- way car in motion. The death is announced of Mr. Charles Sturge, of Bir- mingham, who was prominently associated, in conjunc- tion with his brother, Mr. Joseph Sturge, with the Anti-Corn Law and Reform movenrent. _ .

„-... At Sandbach (Cheshire), on Monday, Samuel Shaw, miner,Kidsgrove, was committed for trial on a eharge of attempting to murder his sweetheart, at the Bull's Head, Holmes Chanel, on the 29th February, when he also shot himself with a pistol. At the-Central Criminal Court, on Saturday, upon the application of Mr. Forrest Fulton, M.P., Mr. Justice Smith postponed until the next session the case of Hunter, wha was convicted of perjury in connection with the Salford gas scandal at the last session. FATAL FALL FROM A CLIFF.---011.SlaU1'day night, Jas. Francis Dottin Souper, eon of the Rev. F. A. Souper, Head Master of St. Andrew's College, Eastbourne, was collecting wild flowers on the rocks at Beachy Head, when he missed his footing and fell over the precipice. He died almost immediately from the result of his injuries. ALLEGED MIIRDF.R BY A WIFR.—At Worcester Police Court, on Saturday, Eleanor Powell, widow, and Ellen Humphreys. servant, were remanded on a charge of murdering Henry Powell, publican, husband of the first- named prisoner, whose death is attributed to narcotic poisoning. A man named Keatley, who is now in prison, will be brought up on the same charge. THR UNEMPLOYED.—The Duke of Cambridge on Satur- day afternoon opened a new recreation-ground for Pad- dington. Lord Randolph Churchill delivered a brief address• on the occasion, and said that the committee for the relief of the unemployed had been enabled to find work for a considerable number of men in utilising the public space, which had been laid out as a recreation- ground. . MR. SPIIROFX)N AND THR BAPTIST UNION.—MY. Spur- -1808, it is stated, has determined not to rejoin the Bap- tist Union. Regarding the action of the Union he writes: "All has been done that can be done, and yet without violence to conscience we cannot unite; let us not attempt it any more,-but each one go his own way in quiet, each striving honestly for that which he believes to be the revealed truth of Clod.”

A distressing occurrence is reported from Newport, Monmouthshire. A plumber, named William Morris, Cell from the roof of a provision market And sustained fatal injuries. A workman, named Beer, had a narrow escape. An acquaintance ran to the house of Mrs. Beer and told her that her husband had been killed. She was daily expecting the birth of a child, and the fright had such an effect on her that she died.

SNOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN ART/LLIIRTMAN.— on Saturday evening, a private in the Lancashire Artil- lery Volunteers, named Robert Guy, was killed while employed in firing a gun. He was at pmetice at Seaforth battery, and when the gun was being run up it caught him and crushed him against the wall of the batViry, breaking several of his ribs and inflicting severe internal injures, from which he died immediately. TIMER WonxmEN 10mm—A shocking accident was on Monday reported from Tredegar, South Wales. It ap- pears that two masons, Frederick Baldwin and William Evans, were arching a dangerous pl7..ce at the Shirhowy Mines, when the roof gave way, crushing the two men to death on the spot. An old man, named Thomas Kinsey, was shortly afterwards killed near the colliery, by a runaway train of trucks passing over his body.

- _ PAYING t:ws. A Garnum.—At Hrentiord, on Saturday, '-zarah Ellen Proctor was brought wp for final examina- tion on the charge of having muritlered a young woman named Charlotte Whale, by striking her on the head with a jug, at their lodgings, in Worton-road, Isleworth. Prisoner, after the murder, said she had owed deceased a grudge, and that she "knew she would swing." The woman, who did not raise her head during the hearing and seemed ill, was committed for trial. TErtruntat CRIME.—On Saturday night a terrible crime was committed at Lincoln. James Carter, a labouring man, had enticed away his brother's wife, but after a time she returned to her husband. In spite ef frequent attempts she reinsert to renew her intimacy with James, and in consequence he met her on Saturday night and cut her throat with a razor. Her injuries are of such a nature that her life is despaired of. Her assailant is in custody.

TIM FAILURE OF' TAR CARDIFF SAVINGS BANK.—A communication of a semi-official character has been received at Cardiff, to the effect that all the depositors in the Trustees' Savings Bank, which collapsed about 12 months ago, will be paid in full, with interest to date, and it is added that the trustees and managers of the bank, who are mostly men of position, will be called 'mon to pay the amount necessary to satisfy the depo- sitors. The bank failed owing to the defalcations of the actuary, which were discovered after his death. The Manchester Chamber of Commerce, on Monday, passed a resolution, by a large majority, that as foreign nations, formerly our best customers, are extend- ing their manufarturing instries and restrict.- Ing MO sale of out Akio s mareasing tariffs, the Government should be urged to foster the systematic creation of new markets by enabling our surplus population to be drafted into Canada. Australia, and South Africa, on rational self-supporting principles, and so increase the purchasing power of the colonies.

ArFRAY n ALIMANDRIA—BRITISIT SEAI,EN STIOT.—A serious affray has just occurred at Alexandria between a number of British sailors and soldiers and some men belonging to a French mail steamship. A quarrel arose in a cafe, and the brawlers were driven into the streets by the native police. Here a free fight took place, in the midst of which some unknown person fired a revolver several times in succession, and when the police had cleared the streets it was found that four English sea- men had been seriously wounded, and they were removed to the hospital.

REGISTRATION OF HORSES FOR THE ARMY. -- Notice was issued from the War Office on Mouday inviting owners of 20 horses and upwards within the Metropolitan area to register such number of horses as they would be willing to sell to the Government on the occasion of a great national emergency. The Govern- ment are prepared to pay in case of taking the horses such a price as would represent what., it would cost to replace them and the estimated loss which might accrue pending their being replaced. A retaining fee of 10s. per horse per annum will be paid.

A WARD OF COURT CASE.—Mr. Justice North had before him, on Saturday, the case of Kettlewell v. Bowyer Lane. Some time ago a criminal charge of sending a fictitious telegram was made against Colonel Bowyer Lane, and it was also suggested that he had allowed his ward to contract an imprudent marriage, and that he had personally benefited in a pecuniary sense. It was now stated that the Chancery litigation was settled, the charges being withdrawn, and Mr. Justice North refused the request of the defendant's counsel to allow the terms to be read in court in order to refute the allegations made against him. MURDER OF AN EMIGRANT FAMILY TN VIRGINIA.— American mails on Sunday brought particulars of a terrible murder of an English emigrant family in Calhoun County, West Virginia. A farmer named Haller, recently emigrated from Staffordshire, went to market selling stock, leaving his wife and three children at home. Re- turning about midnight with a neighbour named Tweed, they saw a light in the house. Looking through the window, they were horrified to see Mrs. Haller and her children dead on the floor, and four men plundering the room. Tweed stood at the front door, while Haller went to the rear of the house and made a noise. As the mur- derers rushed out, Tweed shot them, killing two and wounding the other two severely.

MURDER OF A BROTHER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. --A shocking crime was committed in Wolverhamp- ton on Monday morning. A young man, named Ernest Harper, aged 21, son of a publican, got out o bed, and attacked his brother Thomas, aged 17, with a knife. A desperate struggle ensued, in the course lf which the elder one stabbed his brother in the throat, in- flicting so terrible a wound that the young man died a few minutes after. The murderer then jumped through the bedroom window, and sustained such serious in- juries that he now lies in the hospital in a critical condition. The murderer has been a sailor about six years, and since his return home he has been somewhat reserved in his manner, but he and Thomas were ap- parently on friendly terms. The weapon with which the deed WAS committed was a large carving knife, with heavy brass handle, and blade about 15in. long by 3m. broad. It is thought he was seized by a fit of insanity.

SHRIOUS RAILWAY COLLISTON.—Much excitement and some anxiety were caused in Harrogate on Saturday evening, when it became known that the through express from Newcastle to Liverpool had been run into while standing in the station by a train from Pateley Bridge. The express was crowded, on account of Thirsk races, and several passengers were thrown about and cut and bruised. All, however, with one exception (a man named Green, Manchester), were able to continue their journey. The driver of the Pateley Bridge train had, it is Stated, instructions to draw up his train at the tictet-platform immediately behind the express, so that an of his pas- sengers going with the latter might the more readily change carriages. On Saturday he did not notice the express standing in the station, and when he discovered the danger he was unable to pull up in time to prevent the "pitch-in."l notwithstanding that his engine was fitted with the Westinghouse brake. INHUMAN CONDUCT OF A STEPMOTHER.—At the Central Criminal Court, on Saturday, Joan 13arratt was indicted for maliciously wounding a girl, aged ten years. The girl lived with the prisoner, who is her stepmother, at Lewis- ham, and it was alleged that on several occasions the prisoner severely beat her, and also that she struck her several times with a red-hot poker. The relieving-officer was eventually called in, and he took the child to the workhouse. Dr. Gabe examined the child on behalf of the society prosecuting, and found severe scars on both legs, the result of burns evidently inflicted with some red-hot instrument. The tongue was also severely bitten in three or four places. His (Dr. Gabe's) evidence went to show that the child had been most cruelly ill-treated, and that the accused had been guilty of the most inhuman con- duct —ln defence, it was urged that the Injuries were the result of accident, the child having fallen against the bars of the grate.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and she was sentenced to twelve months' bard labour.

div.head: FIGHT WITH A SLAVE DHOW.
div.p: FIGHT WITH A SLAVE DHOW.
OVER 100 SLAVES DROWNED.

Letters received from the East COast of Africa contain particulars of an exciting chase and sharp engagement with an armed slave dhow by officers and men of H.M.S. Garnet. Chase was given in the cutter Olga, which is attached to the Garnet and armed with a Gardner gun, and on the dhow being overhauled its crew jumped into the sea, but they were nearly all caught and made prisoners. On board the dhow were nearly forty slaves, several of whom had received rifle wounds during the chase, and the whole of them when rescued cried piteously for water. They were taken on board the Garnet. On the same evening, while the Garnet was chasing another dhow, a gust of wind capsized the slaver. Of a total of 108 slaves, besides a crew of twenty armed Arabs, over 100 were drowned, the rest being rescued by the Garnet's boats.
WORKINGTON COLI.I EIZY EXPLOSION.

A descent was on Monday made into the pit, with view to ascertaining whet her it wonld be safe to Make an effort to recover the bodies of the 17 men'who are still in the pit. A party of eight men first went down to make an exploration, and report upon the safety or otherwise of the mine before attempting to recover the bodies. Five of the partrare managers of neighbouring collieries. Since the outbreak of the fire on the 19th inst. 7,500,000 gaPons of water have been pumped into the pit: but as this would flow into the deep dip where the fire occurred, it would not inter- fere with the recovery of the bodies, and would not need e be pumped out before the bodies could be lied. Several of the horses in the low bottom, luch were all expected to be dead. have been found alive, having broken loose from their fastenings. A number of boxes in which to !dace the corpses have been prepared, and a quantity of disinfectants were taken down the pit. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., has received a letter from .the Lord Mayor of London, enclosing a cheque for £lO from himself towards the relief cf the 'widows and orphans of the colliers who lost their lives in the distressing accident at Workington. His lordship says: "If you think that an announcement that I shall he very happy to receive and to forward to the local committee any donations which the charitable public mar like to remit to the Mansion House would aid the fund, you are quite at liberty to say so. I ob- serve that the necessity for a relief fund is the greater nasnitieh as the Cumberland miners are not so far advanced in the measures for insuring against these accidents which are now in successful operation in other mining communities. Should this be the case, tho recent accident may possibly draw attention to the de- airability of imitating the Lancashire and 'Welsh miners in the steps they take by means of their unions and pro- vident funds to mitigate the distress when such sudden :Yalamities arise."

div.head: TIIB LOCAL GOVERNMENT PITA,
div.p: TIIB LOCAL GOVERNMENT PITA,

Earl Cowper. Speaking at a meeting of the Chamber of Agriculture. Hereford, on Saturday, approved the principle of the Local Government Bill, but considered the dual control of the police objectionable, and the licensing proposals opett,,,e ature, At the adjourned Court of Quarter Sessions for Glouces- tershire on Saturday, Sir John Poringtcni, M.P., chairman, it resolution was adopted recommending,. among other chimers in the Local Government Bill, that the elective councillors should hold office six years, one-third retiring every second year; that electoral divisions return not less han three members each; that the control of the police remain with the quarter sessions; and that the licensing clauses be omitted or compensation proposals withdrawn. MR. J. HOWES AT PA HIRAM.

On Sunday, Mr. J. Howes, Rochdale, delivered a lecture at the Liberal Club, in connection with the Blue Ribbon Union, on the. subject. of "Compensation."—Mr. J. Hart- ley presided over a crowded attendance.—Mr. HOWES, in an able address, characterised the Local Government Bill as a fraud, because there was not an hottest clause in it. He did not care whether publicans had a vested interest in their licenses or not, because the onl right upon which the traffic should exist was the stiptve:ed wants of the people. The Government were inakie;.; large areas as possible for the purpose of preventing poor men be- coming members of the County Councils. Having re- ferred to:the fact that magistrates often granted liceases in spite of the protest of the people of the neighbour hood, the lecturer said he was in favour of granting com- pensation—not to the publican, but to those who had suffered through the existence of public-houses. Vested interests were powerful because of the apathy of the people ; and he urged:them to look at the history of liquor- dotn for its commencement and see whether it had pro- duced more'good than evil, or more evil than good. When the owner of a public-house demanded compensation, it was the most impudent demand that had ever been made upon the people, and it was wonderful that the people could tolerate the Government that could make such a proposal or a traffic which could cause so much misery. If the public-houses existed for the public good, the people must have the power to judge. The wish of the people should be the supreme law. That was the platform of political liberty. He urged them to do all in their power to cripple this drink trade, and to declare that these publicans shall have no compensation, because the people could not afford to be bled any longer.—ln the evening another crowded meeting was held. Mr. J. J. Leak presided, and Mr. Howes spoke of many of the im- portant revolutions which had been brought about by the temperance movement during the lost fifty years.— addresses were also given by Mi. Liagard and Mr. Foster.

div.head: – A SHAM NOBLEMAN AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: - A SHAM NOBLEMAN AT ST. HELENS.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Wednesday, be- fore Dr. Gaskell, a German, named Fritz von Weis- senberg, of no fixed abode, a convict on licence, was charged with neglecting to report himself; he was further charged with obtaining by false pretences food and lodgings from Mrs. Brownley, widow, 53, Claughton-street. Mr. Mood (chief-constable) stated that on the 10th April, prisoner, by representing he was a wealthy man obtained food and lodgings from Mrs. Brownley to the amount of 15s 90, and then absconded. He was a convict on licence, and was apprehended ia Liverpool. The Chief-constable called Ann Jane Brown- ley, who said the prisoner engaged apartments with her at lOs a week on the 10th ult. He then left the house, and returned about 10-45 p.m., producing a bundle of papers, which he said were Bank of England notes. Mr_ Wood (chief-constable) produced the bundle, and exhi- bited one of the papers, which witness recognised. The Deputy Magistrates: What is the paper P—Mr. Wood: An advertisement for Dunville's Irish whisky. (Laugh- ter.) Witness (continuing) said the papers appeared at a distance to be bank notes. On the following morn- ing prisoner told her he had £50,000 in chancery, which was coming to him on his marriage. He also said he had a warehouse in Leeds and a large mansion, contain- ing twenty-four rooms, as well as a number of servants and a carriage and pair. She agreed to find him lodg- ings. and he remained with her till the 14th ult., when he owed her 15s 91. Having her suspicions aroused,she asked him on that day for the amount due to her, and he went into the parlour for his hat, and left the house. She did not see him again till he was in custedy. On Tuesday, the 17th ult. witness took the bundle of , papers which prisoner had left in her house to the police station. Amongst them were two advertisements of Dunville's whisky, printed in the shape of Bank of Eng- land notes, and three other papers which showed that Ithe prisoner was a convict on licence. When prisoner I left witness's house he left some clothes behind him which were iaot worth more than ss, but were quite worthless to her. Police-sergeant Strong proved receiv- ing prisoner from the Liverpool police on the 30th, ult., charging him with obtaining food and lodgings under false pretences. Prisoner replied that he did not intend to defraud Mrs. Brownley. Witness further charged him with failing to report himself, and he replied that he was told by thc private police inspector at Sheffield that he need not report himself. His license did not expire till February, 1889. Prisoner, who told the magistrate that it was quite true he had had a large house and a carriage in Leeds and could prove it. was er,Anmitteo to the assizes, which commence on Friday.

Warrants were issued on Wednesday. at Warwick, for the arrest of liclynge Orem:may ,and George Cattea Ni Greenway, the late Town Clerk of arwick,in connection with Greenways' bank failure. Lord Salisbury, on Wednesday, received a deputation of English hop growers, who asked that a duty should be imposed upon all foreign hops imported into this country. The Premier, in reply, said such a proposal would be rejected not only by the Opposition, but by tho the Liberal Unionists and at least one-third or one-half of the Conservative members.

A most important decision with respect to licenses was given, on Monday, in an appeal case which was heard at the COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH, before Mr. Jusrics FIELD and Mr. JuerricE WILL& It is not too much to say of it that it completely disposes of the legal title to compensation which brewers and publicans have been endeavouring to

aet up in view of the provisions of the Local . Government Bill which is now before Parliament.' We have sought at various times to make it clear to our readers that, inasmuch as a licence to sell intoxicating liquors is a privilege which lasts for twelve months only, it is absurd on the face of it to set up a claim for compensation when the privi-! ceases to be granted. But the ground taken of late by the defenders of the traffic has'beenthat a license once granted could be held as a right so long as there was no breach of the law; the re- newal was a matter of form only, since, it was con- tended, the licensing justices had no power to re- fuse to renew a license, except in the case of a breach of its provisions. It would seem that the, • licensing clauses of the Local Government .13ill have been framed on the supposition that pub- licans had legal title to 'demand the renewal of their licenses, and therefore a legal title to corn- I Pensation, in case of an alteration of the law. In introducing the bill, Mr. Ritchie said :—"Although these licenses are technically renewable year by Year, it has again and againbeen held by the courts of law that renewals of these licenses cannot be refused unless for fault shown. We therefore Propose that compensation Shall be paid to those Whose licenses are not renewed." The SOLICITOR-. GENERAL (Sir Edward Clarke), took up the same Position, later on, much to the surprise of other legal authorities in Parliament.' He based his contention on what is known as the Market Bosworth case, in which, in an ap- peal against the decision of the licensing justices, the hearing had resulted in a license being granted, notwithstanding the refusal of the magistrates. He admitted that this was " the only case" he could quote in support of his contention that the licensing justices had no power to refuse to renew a license. But it transpired, when the Market Bosworth case was inquired into, that the 'Some...nos- GENERAL had misinterpreted the at issue, which was not whether the magistrates had an absolute poWerr of refusal; but whether they were entitled to treat an application for a renewal as if it were a nevi application. Referring to the Market Bos- worth appeal, on Monday, both Mr. Jusrlca FIELD and Mr. JUSTICE WILLS agrlied in stating that it did not affect the authority of the licensing- justices to refuse an application either for a new license or for a renewal. The mistake the magis- trates had made was that they refused the applica- tion as if it were a new license, whereas, being an application for a renewal, the applicant was en- titled to an adjournment of the case so that it might be heard at length. The error was not as to the basis of the law, but as to procedure under • the law. Sir EDWARD CLARKE'S "only case" thus falls to the ground; it is a broken reed. But if there were any doubt as to the new (and bad) reading of the law on the part of the SOLICITOR-GENERAL, that doubt WKS effectually removed by the strictly pertinent issue which was decided on Monday. In this case, the owner of ' the Low Bridge Inn, Kentmere, Westmorland, ap- plied for the renewal of a license, and was refused. Be appealed to the Quarter Sessions, and the refusal was confirmed, the bench basing their 'refusal upon the ground of "the remoteness of the house from police supervision, and the character and necessities of the locality and neighbourhood." As a matter of fact, the magistrates were not corn-' polled to give any reason for their refusal; but having stated their reasons, it was open to the ap- pellant to have them considered in a higher court. He accordingly applied, as stated, to the Court of Queen's Bench; and the case was heard at length on Monday. There was no question of procedure invoLved ; the issue was a plain and straightforward 'One; and that was, briefly and simply, whether the licensing justices, and Quarter Sessions, had- rower to refuse the renewal of a license except for breach of the law. Beth Mr. Justice FIELD and Mr. Janice Wm's, having re- gard to the importance of the issue, gave what may be described as elaborate judgments. They traced the operation of the various statutes, showing, step by step, that the intention and pro- vision of the Legislature was that the licensing justices should have full power to refuse either a new license or a renewal ; and the effect of their judgment was, of course, to confirm the decision of the magistrates and of Quarter Sessions in re- fusing to renew the license previously held in connection with the Low Bridge Inn. Mr. Justice FIELD said :----" In granting or refusing a new •• lieense, or a renewal, the justices had an absolute discretion ;" and Mr. Justice Wrms' words were— It followed that there was no limit to the dia., eretion of' the justices in the case of the renewal • arty more than in the case of the grant for the first license." Lord Chief Justice COLERIDGE takes a Similar view of the law; for a few days ago he said—" It has been decided again and again that the discretion of the magistrates is absolute." It may be taken, therefore, as settle'd now beyond question that no class of license holders have a vested interest in their licenses beyond the twelve months for which each license is granted;' and, that being the case, it is a matter nf course to say that having no vested interest they have no title • ,to compensation. The Bill to grant compensation ilas been founded upon a misconception of the law; "(1 if the electors are, alive to their Intereati they will lUist upon it theirthe provide:ins of the Local J..- ;

div.p: Government Bill in so far as they relate to com- pensation shall be swept away. Strugglingtrades- men, artisans, and professional men are sufficiently burdened with rates and taxes, without being plundered to enrich ,brewers and publicans, who have no title to a penny from the public, either in equity or law. '

ONE of the most wretched episodes in the life of the present wretched Government is that of the appointment of Mr. Knio-ILkum.A.N as Assistant' Secretary to the Chief Secretary for Ireland. Whew the question was first broached, it was stated that, although he was being appointed to assist Mr. BALFOUR, he would not be a paid assistant. The Irish members were naturally suspicious of. move Of this kind, and they plied questionii on the subject pretty freely; but they were always beaten off with the answer that nO objection could be taken on tip ground of cost, seeing that there would be no charge on the Treasury. It was thus that the thin end of the wedge was introduced'; and the wedge was being driven home in the House of Commons, On Monday, when Mr.' i3ALvotra moved the second reading of a bill drawn for the very purpose of providing Mr. KING Hs,Juinor with a salary! Mr. BALFOUR professed to be quite hurt at the way in which' Mr. JOHN MORLEY had re- ferred to what he called the "trifling with the House" on the part of the Irish Secretary and the First Lord of the Treasury. But it is Mr. BAL- FOUR'S custom to show the white of his eyes when he is doing something more than ordinarily un- scrupulous and mean. When Sir WurziAls HAR- COURT reminded him the other day that he had broken his .word in the matter of a promised appeal under the Coercion Act, he said the accusation hEa been refuted a thousand times. He used,the same expression on Monday as to the charge of trifling with the House; it had, he said, "been a thousand times refuted." But this trick of expression has I become stale. When •a grave charge ,is made, those who are looking on wish to see one refutation—not to be told of a thousand. AS a matter of feet, no refutation is possible; for Nr. MORLEY was unc'hallenged when he 'quoted Mr. &mu as having said, on behalf of the Government so far back as May last! year :—" It is right to state distinctly that no salary will be asked for." The fact would seem to-be that the Irish Secretary found himself unable.' to stand the questioning of the Irish members; and so he put Mr. KING HAR- aux up as a buffer between riimself and them. In plain terms, he was not equal to the post which he had accepted. It is quite a new thing, it need hardly be said, to have an Under-Secretary for Ire- land, for, if it were-not so, there would be noneed to waste the time of the Parliament and the money of the country, by the bill discussed on Monday, which provides for a new payment of £lOOO per year. It was like Mr. BALFOUR, of course, when he had an/offensive thing to do, to do it in the most offensive way; hence the selection of Mr. KING HARMAN, who is notorious as a renegade Home Ruler, and a rack-renting landlord. Even Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, a Liberal Unionist and an Ulster re- presentative, was constrained to speak against the bill, and in doing so, he did not hesitate to, declare. that Ulster farmers, both Liberal and Orangemen, looked upon the appointment of Mr. KING HAR- MAN as "a practical declaration of war against the tenantry of Ireland." He appealed, in conclusion, to Liberal Unionists to vote against the measure. He knew that they were ashamed of the whole business. There was not one of them to say a word in favour of the . bill, but they could not allow the Government to be defeated; so the second. reading was carried, but with a majority of forty-nine only. The Government have therefore for the present escaped punishment for their breach of faith and bad policy. But they can- not always escape. "The mills of God grind slowly, but they grind exceeding small." The day of reckoning may be long deferred; but it will come,; and meantime they are undoubtedly filling up the cup of their iniquity.

THE, Liberation Society is neither dead nor sleeping; and, as soon as the Irish question ia'out of the way, it will be seen that the active work which is being done will bear fruit in a measure for the disestablishment in Wales, of the English Church. On Tuesday, there was a meeting of the Council of the Society in London, and this was followed in the evening by a crowded assembly in the Memorial Hall. Sir WALTEIRTOSTBR, WhO pre- sided,made a speech which was of special value and interest; for he gave an account of the experience he had undergone as one who had been "brought --up in that straightest sect of Protestantism--the Irish Church." He was alarmed when it was pro- posed to disestablish the Irish Church, and he had grave doubts as to the ultimate issue. "But what," he asked, "had been the results of that I great measure? He found that Protestantism was in no wise suffering. He found that new life had been given to a slumbering Church, and had found an Irish bishop using these words, Dises- tablishment, which, according to the prophets of evil, was to have been the ruin of the Irish Church, had in fact been the means of its salvation." The lesson is one to be taken to heart ; people reason from analogy; and when the Church-people of Wales, of Scotland, and of England express their fears that Disestablishment would be the ruin a the Church, the answer is that it is more likely, as was the case with Ireland, to prove its salvation. In the course of the evening, Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN addressed the audience in a; style' which showed that his temporary separation from his party on the question of Home Rule for Ire- land had not been the means of deteriorating his Liberalism, as has been the case with some of the Dissentients. tie dwelt on the fact that Disestab- lishment in Wales was now an acknowledged plank in the Liberal platfcrm ; and, as evidence of the growth of opinion en the question, he stated that, while in 1856 two only of the representatives of Wales were in favour of the principle of religious equality, at the pre- sent time no less than 26 out of the 30 Welsh members were ready to vote for the disestablish- ment of the English Church in Wales., Surely if the voice of a nation is of .any moment, and we have acknowledged that by extending our repre- sentative institutions, it must be admitted that Wales has declared in the most unequivocal man- ner that the time has COMO when ,Welshmen should no longer be afflicted by the incubus of an English Church. Touching the plea that is some- times put forward that the Established Church in Wales is doing something, although in a minority, to convert the people, Sir GEORGE said : In this argument there was a fatal fallacy, and there was a most cruel injustice. The fallacy was the same fallacy that was used in defence of the in- defensible Irish Church twenty years ago, the fallacy that • a Church that was founded upon injustice, that was founded upon the htimilia- tion of the majority of the people of a country, could be a persuading Church. a con-, ciliating Church, and, in the true sense of the word, a converting Church. They must disassociate and disconnect the idea of a religion from the ideas of privilege, inequlity, and exclusiveness before they could make that religibb attFaCtive to peor- who were outside its pale.
"TouCli AND GO." Next week, the " Examiner " will contain a fine view of Pool Hall in the Eastham section of the Ship Canal.

A London milliner, who is making £7,000 a year, is about—so the story goes—to marry a duke. That opens out an encouraging field for young ladies ; but perhaps when they get to net- ting £7,000 they will feel independent of either 'dukes sr drayrnen.

. , . -, The hop-growers want a duty imposing on im- ported hops; but Lord Salisbury, instead of com- plying with the proposal made by the deputation which waited on him, on Wednesday; read them 'a lecture on Fair Trade. The Protectionists, in this instance were fairly caught—" on the hop." -

At the anniversary services of Wycliffe Congre- gational Sunday Schools, at Warrington, on Sun- day, the total collections amounted to £65 10s 9d. Well done, Wycliffe 1 If this is to be taken as evidence of the decay of dissent," it is to be hoped that next year them will be more of ;it.

There was a collision, the other day, on the Ship Canal works, near Weaste, in consequence, it is stated, of two drivers of ballast engines competing as to which could gain "the points" first. If this be true, those drivers ought to be compelled to-47 which can leave the works first—at a momenta notice.

There are all sorts of ideas as to what consti- tutes temperance. At Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, one defendant pleaded that he had "signed teetotal to one pint of beer a day." The best part of the jolp was that he was unconscious of his own humour. He was perfectly serious, and was inclined to be angry when the court laughed at the new teetotal pledge.%

Lord Stanley of Preston leaves for Canada, as successor to Lord Lansdowne, on the 18th of June. Th 4 is how he has been disposod of. Could not Lord Cross be sent away somewhere P If rumour, speaks truly, he is playing pranks with the Report of the Royal Commission on Education. He would be more usefully employed in doing nothing at some place "far, far away."

Connelllor Dixon, if we understand 'him rightly, affirms that the cost of gas consumed in the streets of Wartingrton is £2 14s : per light now, as com- pared with a is id in 1860; and, further, that Warrington is an exceptional town in this respect. How was it that no member of . the Gas Commit- tee dealt with the statement? If correct, an ex- planation is required; if incorrect, the statement should be refuted. Silence may be very dignified, lint it is not very convincing.

Mr. Thomas Beecham, the manufacturer at St. Helens of the celebrated Beechani's Pills, has had to apply for an injunction to restrain a person cal- ling himself Richard Beecham Pritchard from selling pills of his own make as Beecham's Pills. He wanted to get thebenefit of the repute and exten- sive advertising of the St. Helens firm. It is a de- lightful thing with some people to be able to milk another man's cow; but Pritchard reckoned With- out the Court of Chancery, who have granted an injunction which will put an epdto his little game.

A London correspondent says :—" Mr. Chamber- lain took the opportunity, at a large dinner which he gave on Saturday of denying emphatically that he was engaged to Miss Endacott. Around , the hosPiyible board of the ex-Radical member for Birmingham, on that occasion, were Mr. Arthur Balfour, Colonel Saunderson, and Lord Randolph Churchill—birth, bigotry, and brass—in its Moral sense; under its material, toped that metal was represented by Mr. Vanderbilt, who is worth about thirty-eight million pounds sterling."

It is significant that the leaders of the Liberal Unionists did not vote with the Government on Monday in support of the King Harman Salary Bill. They left it to fifteen of their smaller fry to save the Ministry from defeat. The names of the now famous fifteen are as follows :—Sir Julian Goldsmid, the Hon. Arthur Elliot, General Cross- man, Mr. Hobhouse, Mr. H. F. Beaumont, Mr. Biddulph, Mr. Alexander Brown, Mr. Richard Campbell, Mr. Coghill, Mr. Finlay, Mr. Mackin- tosh, Mr. More, Mr. Thomas Richardson, Mr. Craig Sellar, and Mr. Wodehouse. "When found make a note of." The note will be worth re-pro- ducing at the next election.

George Jones, of Ditton, saved the life of a lad nine years of age, on Sunday afternoon, by jump- ing into a brook ten feet deep, and bringing him to the shore when he was drowning. It is stated that this is the third life which the brave fellow has saved. There can be no question that the Royal Humane Society, will favourably consider the application for a medal, which, we are glad to see, it to be made on his behalf. As to the brook, it ought to be fenced off; that was the opinion ex- pressed by the coroner's jury no later than last month, when a child two years of age was drowned at this dangerous spot.

The Warrington and Distrkt Teachers' Associa- tion were usefully occupied, on Saturday, in lis- tening to an interesting address by Mr. Corney, the president, on Technical Education. There is room for diversity of opinion on the question; and it is to be hoped the Teachers' Association will see to it that they are well represented in the local branch of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Education. Discussion is needed, for the nation may be said to be groping its way as to the right course to take. May Day—whew! what a May Day, it was Goldsmith speaks of winter chillin "the lap of May " ; but on Tuesday it was filled as well ,as chilled with a heavy downpour. Old Chaucer says as to May— The seson priketh every gentil herte, And make9l him out of his slepe to sterte. If the " gentil he'rte " started at all, in the early hours of Tuesday morning, it would be to put on an extra blanket; for it was "a nipping and an

eager air." They kept up the May Day celebration atKnuts- ford, of course. How would Knutsford be remem- bered otherwise? There was as usual a large num- ber of people; the wind slapped their faces, and the rain damped their ardour and their clothes. On such a May Day, "man never is but always to be blest." There was some delay at the commence- ment, and some curtailment later on; but "the Queen" was crowned despite the weather. The Committee were determined that should be done "whether or not." •

no evidence given at the trial of Mr.W. O'Brien, M.P., shows how stupid the Government have been in assuming tluit the National League was almost spark out in the neighbourhood or Loughrea. It transpired that all the Town Commissioners had been engaged in promoting Mr. O'Brien's meeting; and the Chairman went so far as to say there was not a respectable man in Loughrea who was not a member of the League. This is turning the tables on Mr. Balfour with a vengeance. It is evident that the League will survive his attacks.

It is noteworthy in connection with the decree issued by the Vatican that nothing is said about the National League. The decree with the Plan of Campaign and boycotting, and even as to these it is as, gentle in its roar as a sucking dove. There is no condemnation in the old style; it is a case of advice and exhortation to which even Mr. O'Brien himself may patiently listen, leaving him- self at liberty as to each particular case, to do that which seenieth good in his own eyes. Mr. Brunner put a question as to the Weaver Trust, in the House of Comtrions, on Tuesday, which was really an indictment of that body. Sir Michael Hicks Beach gave an answer which is curi- ously ambiguous. " Any proposal for the reconsti- tution of the trust must come from those in- terested." By "those interested," does he mean the members of the trust, or the public? We are all interested in getting rid of a self-eleeted body that has been repeatedly condemned by the Board of Trade. Mr. Brunner has begun the attack and must keep it up. He must peg away until this self-elected body becomes a representative body.

ROBBING A NAVVY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Ruasell, a middle-aged man was charged with stealing a pair of boots, worth 6s 61, the property of William Smith, a navvy on the Ship Carial,Works, who lodges in• Zion-place. The pri- soner pleaded guilty fo "larking With the boots." Super- intendent Hollingsworth said the prisoner had been five times convicted of poaching, and he was now fined £l, and costs,,2ss, or in default -a month's hard labour. WALKER'S BnEwirla ' Hircii.—The "Standard" of Tuesday says:—" A hitch has occurred over the projected launching of Walker's Liverpool brewery and public-house busi- ness as a limited company, with a capital of three 'million pounds. Messrs. Baring Brothers have, for the present, at all events, declined to proceed, so no prospectus will be issued by them on Wednesday, as • the market had expected. The business has. credi- ble reports allege, risen more than half a million in price to the public since first the idea of selling it to. it company was broached. A correspondent writes that the conversion scheme has been given up, and adds :—Durieg 04 progress of the negotiations with Messrs. Baring Bros., the divergence of views be- tween that firm and Sir A. B. Walker as to the floating of the company became so great that Sir Andrew declined to proceed. The project has, there- fore been abandoned for the present. It may be added that the reasons which have led to the with- drawal of the scheme are regarded locally as highly honourable to Sir A. B. Walker."

RUNCORN SCFIOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday mght. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. Mac- Dougall; Messrs. E.'ltnison, S C. Beckett, and F. A. Lake, with G. Moss (clerk). , SCIWOL ATTENDANCE,-TUE NEGLECT OF PARENTS. The minutes of the School Attendance Committee showed that during the past month 63 parents were sum- moned before the committee to explain the cause of their irregular attendance at school. Sixty attended, and were suitably dealt with. There were 19 parents prosecuted before the magistrates. The attendance officer's report showed an increase in the average attendance.—Dr. McDougall said the number of parents who were sum- moned before the committee, and the frequency with which they were summoned. was a terrible commentary upon the way in which some parents neglected the in- terests of their children. There were some who did not seem to have any respect for the authority of the Board, or for the natural obligations which attached to having children, and educating them properly.—The Chairman said it was unfortunate that people did not see the necessity of paying their children's school fees, but were willing to pay repeatedly fines which might be considerably more than the school fees would amount to if the children went to school regularly.— Dr. McDougall : Ass fine would pay for 20 weeks edu- cation.—Mr. Lake gave as an explanation of the chair- h man's remarks that the fine was paid by the father while the onus of sending the children to school lay upon the mother. It was the fault of the mother and not the father that children in many instances did not go to school.—Dr. McDougall thought something should be said as to the risks that parents ran in allowing their Aildren to run wild. If the board chose to put in force the great powers they possessed with respect to habitual absentees from school, they could send these children to a. truant school. The minutes were then adopted on the motion of Mr. Imison, seconded by Mr. Lake.—At a later period Dr. Gastaldi said there was an evil connected with :his school, and that was that the attendance on Monday mornings and on Friday afternoons was very small. •He knew as a positive fact that many parents kept their :children away on a Friday afternoon to help in the housework, but he could not ascribe any reason why they were kept away on Monday mornings. No r doubt other schools had a similar experience. Be suggested that the school attendance officers should look after the children a little more at r the, times he had mentioned.—The Chairman did r•not think it was possible that the officers could do more than they.were doing at the present time.—The Clerk r said want of fees was a great reason for absence on ,Monday morning.—Dr. McDougall did not think the ques- tion of fees could apply on Monday mornings, as the men received their wages on the previous Friday.—Mr. r Beckett said other schools had suffered in the same way, and this plan had been adapted. The children were al- 4bwed to go to dinner at twelve o'clock on Fridays, and lessons commenced inthe afternoon at one o'clock, and k concluded at three o'clock.—Dr. GastaAdi thought this a good suggestion.—Dr. MacDougall said if the women %would look after their own affairs instead of gossiping, being generally idle,. these complaints would not arise.

*** A REPLY Ai o Crteimman.--On Saturday;{ . April 14th the Warrington Guardian said as to its circulation that it was "many times greattr than that of all our local contemporaries combined." As we _have good reason to doubt .so extraordinary . a statement, we are willing to pnt this trumpet- blowing tea, practical test. We, theretme, offer to submit our books .to any firm of accountants agreed upon, on the understanding that the pro- prietors ()Utile Warrington Guardian do the same ;. and we undertake to ',subscribe. £lO to the War- rington Infirmag if, as the result of the investiga- . lion,. it is not shown that the Warrington awl - Cheshire Examiner has a LARGER SALE iu the borotih of Warrington than ourboastfal contem- porary.. We mention the borough of Warrington because it is a distinct and definite area, the cen- tre of local population, and the head quarters of • both newspapers. The further condition stipula- ted is that the proprietors of the Warringrof • Guardian- shall ,engage to subscribe .£lO 'to .the Infirmary if they, on their side, fail to make gned . A similar claim. By SALE, we mean the tOtal 'number of papers for whichs payment can. be. shown to have been received; the time covered to be the first three months of the present year. As the Warrington Guardian is a bi-weekly journal, either the Wednesday's-or the Saturday:s. issue can be taken for comparison. It is time the publie ascertained,. beyond 'cavil, what there is behind this bounce on the part of our local con- temporary, aiukwhether it will be able to boaA, when it has been brought to. book. We have only . to add. that this challenge will be open for ac- ceptance for four weeks from the date of its issue (April 21). POOR BATES FOIL RUNCORN DISTRICT, The Runcorn magistrates on Monday sanctioned the laying of a poor, rate of is in the £ for the township of Stockham, to rea- lise £42 2s 2d; and of is in the £ for the township of Clifton to realise £2lO 8s 6d. UNLAWFUL USE OF WATER AT WIDNES. --- Thomas Catterall, a plumber, of Liverpool, (appeared, before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, to answer a charge of unlawfully using, for building purposes, the water of the Widnes Local Beard. Mr. .1. T. Allen, the clerk, prose- cuted.—The defendant admitt,ed that one of his men had used a bucketful of water, but he was ignoiant that he was committing an offence. , A,fine of 5s and costs was

imposed. LIVERPOOL COLLEGE OF CHEMISTRY.-011 Saturday morning a party of students attending the chemistry classes of DrMeo. Tate visited,by permission of the firm, the chemical works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., at Widnes. The party was conducted over the works by Mr. Carey;who clearly explained the various operations involved in the manufacture of soda ash or carbonate of soda. The party returned to Liverpool early in , the afternoon after thoroughly enjoying their instructive visit • to these noted works. SAD DEATH OF A WOMAN AT WIDNES.—The cirum- stances of the death of ,Martha Dalton, 21 years o age, wife of Samuel Dalton, of 98, Cholmondeley-street, formed the .subject of an inquiry by Deputy Coroner Husband, on Monday. It appeared from the evidence that on the 23rd December last, Mrs. Dalton was stand- ing on a chair arranging the curtains to one of the win- dows, when she slipped and fell to the ground. She was enciente at the time, and the effect of the fall was to cause her to suffer great pain, which ended in her death on Friday last. A child had been born in the meantime. and is at present doing well. The medical men in at- tendance were Dr. Neaten and Mr. Richards. A verdict of accidental death was returned. , , A! WIDNES SAILOR DROWNED AT BANGOR —On Thursday Mr. L. R. Thomas, deputy coroner for Carnarvonshire, held an inquest at the Bangor Infirmary upon the body of Patrick Stokes, aged twenty-one, a sailor, of Widnes, who was accidentally drownea in the Menai Straits, near Bangor, on Tuesday night. Henry Peacock, master of the coasting flat Edward Whitley, of Runcorn, stated that he and the deceased were coming in the ship from Beaumaris to Banger on the day in question. About two o'clock, when the vessel was opposite the Bangor Weir, they let go the anchor in order to get on another tack. When about weighing the anchor again, the de- ceased's foot slipped and he fell overboard, the ship lay- ing very much at the same time. lie had the winch handle in his hand when he fell. Deceased went under the vessel. The jury returned a verdict of "Acciden- tally drowned." THE DROWNING FATALITY AT ACTON GRANGE.--MP Worsley, coroner, held an enquiry at the Walton Arm Inn, Walton Superior, on Saturday, touching the death of Richard Lea,dbetter, aged 16, whose body was found in the canal at Acton Grange, yesterday week. Ann Leadbetter domestic servant, living with Mrs. Massey at Nicholson-St., Warrington, said the deceased was her brother. He was errand boy to Mrs. Massey. She last saw him on the 24th April, when he had to go on an errand along the towing path of the canal. He was learning a recitation he had to give on the day but one after, from a book which he carried. Her opinion was that while he was reading he accidently walked into the canal.—Richard Massey, 23, Nicholson-st., gardener, deposed, to finding the body in the canal at Acton Grange, on the 27th April.—P.C. Dutton, of Moore, said there were no marks of violence on the body. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." SHOCKING DEATH QF AN OLD WOMAN AT WIDNEEL-011 Wednesday, at Widnes, Mr. W. T. Husband, the-deputy coroner, held an inquest upon the body of Hannah Attch‘ ison, wife of John Aitchison, of 20, Milton-st., Widnes., From the evidence it appeared that about nine o'clock on the night of the 17th April the deceased and her hus- band were walking upstairs to bed. After the deceased had ascended about four steps she caught her foot in her dress, and stumbling, fell backwards. She alighted with her head upon the floor, and a comb, which she wag wearing, was driven into her head, inflicting alarge con-' tused wound that penetrated to the skull. She was nicked up in a state of unconsciousness,andMr.Richards, assistant to Dr. McDonnell, was called in, and he attee- ded to her injuries. Afterwards erysipelas set in, and death occurred on the 30th ult. The deceased was 79 years of age, and several witnesses, stated that at the tittle of the accident both :the and her husband were under the influence of drink. The latter, who is about 69 years of age, is now an inmate of the Workhouse Hospital. The jury returned a verdict that the woman fell whilst drunk, and came to her "death accidentally, and not otherwise."

INcThENTsO Taa RIVER AT Rtmeons.--On Friday after- noon, whilst a high wind was blowing and the tide was running strongly, the flat Sarah went afoul" of one .of the pillars of Runcorn Bridge. The captain, William Leeson, was caught by the foresail and knocked ,over - beard, but the two men who•were assisting him to work the boat, threw him a rope, and with great difficulty succeeded in hauling him on deck. He was little' the 'Work for his wetting.—Shortly afterwards the Weston Point steam tug.Begulator VMS towing three flats out Of West Bank Dock, when the last one, which was deeply laden, collided with the north pillar of Runcorn Bridge. Fortunately very little damage was done. Had the flat been sunk, a not improbable occurrence, the three men on board would have been irra perilous position, as not ,one ot the three flats was provided with a small boat, and the lantines of the pillars have net tuty Chains attached., to which a'drowning, man might cling, A few chains might be fixed at a small cost, and might prOve of great service on many Occasions.—On Tuesday a gale blew from the west, and the river traffic was conducted with difficulty and danger. The tide commenced to flow some time before it was due, and the water rose to A, height of over 18 feet, fully three feet More tha'n marked on the tide table. The large steamer Camel, chattered by Mr. Walker, contractor to the Ship Canal ' Company, and piloted by Mr. H. Hill, .was' in consequence enabled to get to -Old Quay Docks before high water with a cargo of material for the works. The Sailing flats from Widnes experienced much difficulty in beatin through Runcorn Bridge, as the wind blew through the arches with terrific violence. The flat Ann, belonging to Messrs. elt. Evans and Co., of Haydock, had her sails blown away, and the anchor being dropped, the chain parted, and the vessel was in a position of danger. The captain, however;succeecied in bringing his vessel safely to Mr. Speakman's •
