The Finance Committee reported that the amoUrit -of school fees received during the past month was £l9 Os 11d. The balance in the bank was £94 ss.
RUNCORN BOARD OF CONIAISiIONERS.:,'

The monthly meeting was held at the Town on Thursday morning. Mr. James Dobson presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, W. Fisher, H. White, S. Taylor, W. Mellor, J. MeadOw— croft, P. Smith, W. Hankinson, E. I misou, H. J. Grice, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secreto7), Dr. MacDougall (medical officer), and M!' Barker (surveyor).

HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-IMPORTANT STITHMENIT The Medical Officer reported that the number of daths registered dhring April amounted to 20; of these one was an inquest case, and of the remaining 19 deaths eight were due to bronchitis, two to inflammation of the lungs, &c. The 20 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 14.2 per 1,000 of the estimated population, and, exclusive of the inquest case, of 13.7.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of a copy of the report recently made to the Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority on the prevalence of fever in their district. The Board regretted that so any conditions obviously tending to injure health and to spread disease were not dealt with before the occurtienc,e of the preventible sickness and death recorded in the report.—The Chairman moved, and Mr. Taylor seaopded, a proposition that the letter be left to the Health Com- mittee.—Mr. Speakman said a report like that going to the public would naturally tend to disquietude, and he suggested that the medical officer should state the position of affairs.—Dr. MacDougall said the report referred to five months of last year ending December 31st. The conditions that then existed; and were supposed to be the origin of typhoid fever, had been dealt with, ibut as to what extent the same condition of things might exist in other parts of the town, he was unable to say, be- cause it was a trotter that came under the special pro- vince of the Surveyor and Nuisance Inspector. It the present time, so far as he was able to gather, there was, not a single case of typhoid fever in the district.; there was no measles and no scarleti fever. There had not beei a death through scarlet fever since 1885, a condi4nn of things which was extremely satisfactory, considering that prior to that time scarlet fever was of almost con- stant duration in the town. At present the hearth of the town was extremely good, as the fact that the death rate had been reduced from 19 per cent to 13.7. • The town was singularly free from preventible diseases. He had on former occasions brought the question before the Commissioners, and the people themselves should make inquiries into the sanitary arrangements of their own homes. With regard to small pox they had so far es- caped, but it would be necessary for the officers to exer- cise great care and watchfulness to prevent the disease invading the district. He did not remember such a sharp attack of typhoid fever as they had last year for 12 or 14 years past. The Chairman said it was satisfactory to learn that the town was free from fever.—The matter , was referred to the Health Committee.

HIGHWAY AND Bump IMO COMMITTEE. . The minutes of this committee recorded that the Sur- veyor having reported that the notices served.on the respective owners of premises fronting, adjoining, or abutting on Egerton-st., Handley-st., and Briscoe-st. to sewer, metal, &c., such streets had not been complied with, it is recommended that the Authority execute the works mentioned or referred to in such notices, and that the expenses so incurred be recovered from the respec- tive owners. Recommended that the tender of Messrs. T. Kirkham and Co., for the excavation of the upper portion of Egerton-st ,at the undermentioned rates, be r accepted :—Excavating carriage-way, 9d per superficial yard; excavating foot-way, per superficial yard. Recommended that Mr. J. Ham let's price for Stafford- shire paving bricks, 12 by 6by 2, at 80s per 1,000 net, be accepted. Recommendation that Mason-st.f be re- constructed, and that the Eas% side of Wellington-st. foot- way be refiagged. The following plans of new buildings were approved :—Mrs. Handley, for the erection of a bedroom over each scullery at the rear of six houses in Greenway-road ; Mr. James Ditchfield, for the construc- tion of a small coal place at the rear of house in Green- way-road • Mr. E. Prince, for the erection of three houses in Halton-road, at the corner of Porterst. ; the Runcorn Property and Investment Co., amended plan of one of four houses in York-st., approved on April sth last, showing wash-house and extended window.—The minu- tes were approved, on the motion of Mr. Taylor, secon- ded by Mr. Grice.
A TENDER.
The tender of Mr W. Blythe, of High-st., to supply the nuisance inspector with clothing was accepted, on the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee.

FINANCE, The Finance Committee reported that during April the receipts amounted to £27 us Bd, and accounts amount- ing to £309 us 7d, were passed. With respect to the assessment and levying of the general dist- rict rate for the year ending --25th March, 1889, it is recommended that the owner, instead of the occupier, be rated, under the prevision of • section 211 of the Public Health Act, 1875, where the rateable value of any premises liable to assessment does not exceed the sum of ten pounds; and that he be assessed on a reduced estimate of three-fourths of the net annual value of such property. It was recommended that the exterior of the Town Hall be painted and the chimneys pointed, and that tenders for executing the work be obtained.—Mr Fisher moved, and Mr Taylor seconded, the adoption of the minutss.—The Secretary said his expenses had increased during the past week ius consequence of the Board having undertaken part of the , work of the nightsoil contractor. He should have to pay the men, and would require a cheque for .£2s.—The minutes were passed, and a cheque drawn for the secre- tary as requested.

div.head: MONSTRE LODGING HOUSE.
div.p: A MONSTRE LODGING HOUSE.

The Health Committee reOommended that G. C. Duckett be registered as the keeper of a common lodging house, situated at 38, Church-st. ; maximum number of lodgers, 51. It was also recommended that the night- soil contractor's cheque be drawn, but withheld until such time as the Inspector of Nuisances may report to • the committee that the work is properly carried out.— Mr. Grice moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes.—The Law Clerk advised that in such an important and vital matter as registering a house to accommodate 51 lodgers, a committee of the Board should make an inspection and see that the Act of Par- liament was properly complied with.—lt was decided to adopt tkis suggestion, and the minute was referred back. —lt war further resolved to allow the nightsoil contrac- tor £2O on account.
THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

At the request of the Parliamentary and Legal Com- mittee the Law Clerk had prepared a written report upon how the Board of Commissioners would be affected by the Local Government Bill, should it pass. In a great part the report was a repetition of the verbal statement he had made at the last monthly meeting.—Mr. Speak- man moved that the report be added to the minutes. He was, he said, in London a short time ago, and Mr. Brun- ner informed him that he would be happy indeed to de anything he could for the Board. He proposed that the Law Clerk's report be communicated to Mr. Brunner, and his special attention drawn to the paragraph relating to the question of returning officers.—Mr. Imison asked whether under this bill the Manchester Ship Canal Co. (Bridgewater Undertaking) would continue to nominate two members on the Board.—The Law Clerk said these rights would cease. Perhaps if the matter were laid be- fore Mr. Ritchie he would preserve the rights.—Mr. Meadowcroft dissented to this. During some further. conversation he said there was a strong feeling that selected councillors should be called Aldermen' as at present.—The Law Clerk: I think that will be struck out. Many of the Unionist supporters of the Govern- ment are against that clause.—Mr. Meadowcroft : I don't know about that.—The Law Clerk: And‘l think they will have a great deal to do with passing the bill.—Mr. Speakman's proposition was carried, and the meeting concluded.
GALLANT CONDUCT AT DITTON.

An official report has been made to Superinten- dent Johnston, at Widnes, in reference to the gal- lant conduct of a young man, named George Jones, of 4. Harrison-st., Ditton, with a view to having the case brought under the notice of the Royal Humane Society, more particularly as this is not the first time that Jones has been the means of saving life in the same dangerous place—Ditton Brook. From the report made by Sergeant Ross, it appears that about two o'clock on Sunday afternoon Jones was passing over Ditton Junction Railway Bridge, when he heard shouts from the direction of the brook that a boy was in the water. On looking over the wall he saw the boy, and hastened to the spot. It was then high tide, and the water in the brook. which is very dirty, was about ten feet deep. A crowd had assembled, but no one offered to rescue the boy, whose name .was Patrick O'Neil, about nine years of age. Jones swam to his assistance, and after O'Neil had disappeared several times, and was apparently drowning, Jones grasped him with one hand, and sans with the other to the side of the brook, where he was helped out by the bystanders. The boy was taken home, and Jones, who seemed much exhausted, was taken to the Railway Hotel, where stimulants were administered. Jones and the boy afterwards quite recovered. Three years ago a boy, named William Reyes, was rescued from drowning by Jones, and again, two years ago, him young brother was saved by him from a watery- grave after a hard struggle. It will be remembered that on Sunday, the 15th April, a child two years of age, son of Mr. Lee, of the Railway Hotel, Ditton,. was drowned in the brook at this very'place, and- the jury at the inquest added a presentment that the London and North-Western ltailwaT Company should be asked to fence off that part ot the brook with a sleeper fence, as in other places. „.

WINNINGTON PARK V. RUNCORN.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturdav, and resulted in a decisive victory for the visitors. Winning the toss, the visitors elected to bat, Wright (captain) and Tickle facing the bowling of Brock and Freeman Despite the efforts of the bowlers, these batsmen could not be separated until Roughley substituted Freeman, Tickle then being dismissed by a splendid catch in long field. Woods and Robertson batted well, the latter's score including 13 singles. Runcorn continued to score rapidly, and afterseven changes of bowlers there was quite a collapse, Bickerton being very destructive, taking six wickets for five runs, the last wicket eventually falling with the score at 90. Winnington then went to the wickets, but could do nothing with the bowling of Woods and Gatley, the whole of the eleven being dismissed for 10 runs, Bickerton, Brock, and Shaw only being able to make anything like a stay. Woods' bowling was superb, taking eight wickets for six runs, including the 'hat trick." It should be mentioned that Winnington -were minus their captain, Rhodes-Denton. Score:— RUNCORN. RUGBY RULES.

RUNCORN v. MANCHESTER DISTRICT.—This match was ' played on the Irwell-lane ground, on Saturday, in the presence of 2,000 spectators. The weather was fine, but a stiff breeze was blowing. The home club were without the services of H. Hughes (captain), Cookson and W. Hughes, but were able, notwithstanding, to pile on the big score of three goals, two tries, and twelve minors to one minor. The winning team had the best of the play all through the game, and had it not been for the wind would have made the score even larger, as often when the forwards dribbled up splendidly and looked like scoring the wind carried the ball dead. The try- getters were Faulkner, Dolan, Gayter, Hampson, and W. Riley, but the victory was earned by unselfish play and the skilful combination. Teams :—Runcorn: Brazendale, full back: W. Riley, Crompton, and Davies, three-quarter-backs; Whitby and Holling-worth, halves; Broady (captain), Faulkner, P. Riley, Dolan Hancock, Gayter, Hampson, Clarke, and Stubbs, forwards. WIDNES AND WARRINGTON.—A match be-

tween a team selected by Mr. G. Wainwright, of the Runcorn Club, and a team selected by Mr. W. Grice, of Widnes Club, took place at Runcorn on Mmday evening. The proceeds were to be added to the funds of the Run- corn Volunteer Band, and there were about 3,000 specta- tors present. Neither side was as originally chosen, the vacant places being filled up by players from the second teams. Wainwright winning the toss, elected to play with the advantage of the wind. During the first ,half play was chiefly confined in the territory of the visitors, and both Faulkner and Hampson se red tries for. ?Run- corn, the game at half-time being—Runcorn, 2 tries, 3 touchdowns, and 1 dead ball, to Widnes 1 touchdown. In the second half the visitors showed up better, but they could make make little impression upon theibril- lia.nt defence of the home team, who by the aid of Faulk- ner and Wainwright added a third try to their score. Jolley and Parkinson had hard lines for dropped goals. Score—Runcorn, 3 tries, 4 minors, to Widnes and War- rington 6 minors. Early in the second half Whitby had the misfortune to have his lip terribly split open, and he had to retire from the field. Teams :—Runcorn : Brazen- dale, full back; Davies, Crompton, and Cawley, three- quarters; Whitby and Antrobus, half backs; Wainwright (captain), Broady, Faulkner Hampson, Clarke, Stubbs, Hancock, Dolan, and Gavier, forwards. Widnes and Warrington: Owen, full back; Hartles, Parkinson, and Jolley (Warrington), three-quarters; Farrell and Howard, half backs; J. H. Smith (captain), H. Ashton (Warring- ton), Woods, Barber, Gandy, Howard, J. Bingham, J. Fairley, and F. Wright, forwards. WARREIGTON V. HALIFAX.

This being the last match of the season, a large crowd assembled on the Wilderspool enclosure to witness the encounter between the Warringtonians and what was thought to be the holders of the Yorkshire Challenge Cup. On both teams appearing in the arena it was ap- parent that the visitors had only provided their "A' team, and indignation was expressed on all sides at the shabby action of the Halifax Committee. It was some time before the Warrington team could be persuaded to play, but after the difficulty had been overcome, the home team started operations against a strong wind, Frank Turner kicking off, Hurst returning into touch at centre. Thorp broke away for the visitors, and Speakman passed to Barns, who was brought down by Sharmin. East kicked to Sanson who was charged off his kick, but he regained possession, thus averting further danger, the ball being scrimmaged in the home 25. The home forwards carried the pack, but Robinson got hold and kicked, the ball going dead. Frank Turner dropped out, the visitors again kicking a dead ball. From the drop out, Fair. Turner and Warren made a „grand dribble, Sharmin getting the oval away with a good kick, Barns returned with interest into touch. Povey and Littlewood headed a dribble by the home for- . wards,Randles making a short run and kick. Warren passed to Barns, this player kicking to the visitors' full back, who was pushed into touch by Warren. The Halifax forwards relieved with a dribble, but Fair. Tur- ner secured from a line out, and kicked up the field, Littlewood preventing any return. East WAS allowed a fair catch, and sent the oval into touch. Hurst passed to Sbarmon, who got in a good punt, Sanson saving smartly by running the leather into touch. Massey re- ceiving a pass from Warren, landed the ball near the -visitors' quarter flag,and the Warrington forwards, led 'by Ashton and Frank Turner, dribbled over the line, the , latter player completing the try. Barnes took the place kick, and succeeded in kicking a goal. Thorp restarted from centre, Massey returning to Cope, who made his rnit, k, Sanson sending the ball in touch near the War- rington quarter flag. From the line out Handles dribbled to centre, but Bromwich intercepting a pass ran across `he field, being brought down by Sanson. Davies 1, vie away with a dribble, Bromwich making a '33.1. kick, the ball again going dead. From the 'l°llC lilt Thorpe secured, and dropped a goal. -drop ~. -.11 re-started from centre, and Warren passed Warn/10. -to ran and kicked, Jolley carrying the ball 'to Barnes, "Varren again passed to Hams, who trans: :into, touch. who was pushed into touch by East ferred to Jolley, lag. Half-time was called, the score near the quarter-L 1 goal ; Halifax, 1 goal and 2 minor • being_warrington, -nds Cope kicked off for Halifax, , Points. on el:411r 4;f ,ed at mid-field, from which BCIIMInage 154411 g f .ed into touch in the visitors' yea /man secured,aml

25. Bromwich took a pass intended for Massey, and transferred to centre. Halifax were now placed on the defensive, and Barnes made his mark in a favourable position, but nothing came of it. Passing between Speakman, Barnes, and Massey ended in the latter drop- ping at goal, the oval being got away by Armstrong. Davies made a fair catch in front of goal, Warrington almost scoring from the kick, the ball going a little wide. Both teams added a minor to their score, then Fair. Tur- ner charged Bromwich off the ball, and Massey, running up, ran in at the corner flag. No goal resulted. From the kick-off the ball was scrimmaged in centre; Warren getting away with a splendid run, being brought down by the full back. A minor was added to the hometeam's score. After the drop-out Barnes got in along kick, and Donohue following up collared Robinson before he could return. From a scrimmage in the visitors' territory Warren passed to Speakman, who ran and safely groun- ded the leather over the line, Turner failing at goal. Speakman again almost scored, and then the same player kicked across the field to Massey, who, after dodging his man in brilliant style, dropped a goal from half-way amidst loud cheering. Time was soon after called, the score standing—Warrington,two goals, two tries, and six minors: Halifax, one goal and three minor points. After the grand display shown by Warrington in their recent matches the spectators were 'sorely- disappointed at seeing their local club pitted against such a paltry team. All expressed wrath at the Halifax Commit- tee's conduct, and the way their men seconded their Executive's efforts was admirable. They delayed and wasted time as much as possible, and this, coupled with the disgust at playing an" A "team, must be ac- counted the reason of the poor exhibition shown on Saturday. The following were the teams: Warrington--Sanson, back; Massey, Barnes, and Jolley, three-quarter backs; Warren and Speakman, half backs ;Fair. Turner Frank Turner, Ashton, Hayes, Randles, Littlewood, Donohue, Povey, and Davies' forwards. Halifax—W. Fletcher, back; Bromwich. Sharman, and East, three-quarter backs; Hurst and Robinson, half backs; Cope, Miller, Clay, Jenkinson, Thorpe, Garside, Bedford, Ellsworth, and Armstrong, forwards. THE ENGLISH FOOTBALL TEAM IN NEW ZEALAND. —Shaw and Shrewsbury's team beat Otago at Dunedin, on Friday, last week, by two goals and two tries to one goal. Speakman, of the Runcorn Football Club, kicked both goals for England. The match caused tremen- dous excitement in Dunedin, 10,000 spectators being present.

WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The annual meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Derbyshire, J. Houghton, Jolley, W. Houghton, Pennington, Grange, Kilshall, Swinton, W. Long, S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Ker- f oot (inspector.) ELECTION 01. CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.—Mr. JOLLEY moved, and Mr. W. HOUGHTON seconded, and Mr. DARBYSHIRE supported, that the Rev. G. F. Roberts be re-elected chairman of the Authority for the ensuing year, and this proposal was agreed to unanimously.— The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS, in taking the chair, said that was probably about the last time that Authority would have the privilege of electing a 'chairman, constituted as ,it was at present. How the matter would precisely work in the future seemed to him somewhat in the dark at present. He did not understand why in dealing with those district councils it did not occur to Mr. Ritchie in the firainstance that he might with advantage consti- tute Boards of Guardians and District Councils under the 'County Council, and constitute different committees of that Board as Rural Sanitary Authorities, Highway Dis- trict Boards, and so on; but he thought that practically it would after all come to the same thing. He did not think that Boards of Guardians and District Councils would long continue side by side. The one would pro- bably absorb the other, and as Boards of Guardians were not to be constituted, District Councils would swallow up Boards of Guardians. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JOLLET, in a few complimentary remarks, proposed that Mr. Darbyshire be re-elected vice-chairman of the Authority. —Mr. PENNINGTON seconded, and Mr. LONG supported, this proposal, which was agreed to unanimously, and Mr. DARBYSIIIRE suitably responded. TIME OF MEETING.—It was decided that the meetings of the Authority should, for the ensuing year, be held on the same day and at the same time as heretofore, viz. :—the first Friday in each month at 10.30 in the morning. PENNETII SEWERAGE.—The agreement with Mr. John Taylor, of Garston, for the execution of the sewerage works of Penketh, for £2OO, was submitted and signed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORTS.—Dr. SEPHTON submitted his annual report as to the health and sanitary condition of the Authority's district. • The registrars had returned to him 401 births and 251 deaths during the year. Tak- ing the population as 14,113, an increase of 445 over the previous year, the birth rate would be 28.4 per 1,000, and the death rate 171 per 1,000. In his report for the month ended April 30,Dr. Sephton stated that there were 34 births and 12 deaths, the death rate from all causes being equal to 10.5 per 1,000, as compared with 19.1 in the corresponding month last year. The district was remarkably healthy for the time of the year. APPLICATION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY—The lIISpeCtOF (Mr. Kerfoot) applied for an increase of his salary (at present £80), but consideration of the matter was left over till next meeting. This was the principal business.

The Speaker of the House of Commons is indisposed, and was not able to take the chair on. the assembling of the House on Thursday. On Thursday morning the new railway station at Blackburn was completed, and the• whole structure was opened for public traffic-. Colour-sergeant Barker, of the East Kent Regiment, committed suicide at Canterbury, on Thursday, by tiring a rifle bullet into his head.. Replying, on Wednesday, to a deputation from the Off-license Holders' Association, Mr., Ititchie sal it was not the intention of the Government to compensate the landlord when a. license was taken away without regard to the tenant's interests. _

THE TRIAL OR MR- W. O'BRLEX.—A Loughrea corres- pondent tekgraphs that when the magistrates entered the courthouse on. Wednesday to resume Mr. William O'Brien's trial, Mr. Paul announced that a most auda- cious robbery had taken place. The court-house had been broken into and all the documents and depositions connected with the trial stolen. The Crown counsel strongly commented. on the outrage. The case had to be recommenced at 2sazo, and the proceedings will last another week. -On Thursday the case for the Crown closed, and Head Constable Kielty was reproved for some remarks made in court concerning Mr. Bodkin, the soli- citor for the defence. All the witnesses to be called will be fresh ones. The court-keeper has been dismissed. The magistrates at Loughrea decided, on Thursday, that the meeting in that town on the Bth April was a National League meeting, and they sentenced Mr. if to three month's imprisonment, without hard labour. They agreed to erant a case on certain points of law, and Mr. O'Brien entered into bail. A further charge against Mr. O'Brien—inciting persons to take part in an unlawful assembly—was opened before the court rose.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
No. 16.— NORTON.

The township of Norton, which, in its lower- lying parts near the Mersey, has already been in- vaded by navvies—human and mechanical—is endued with great historic interest. Considering that it has never been a centre of population, it seems to have shared to an unusual extent in the great Changes and vicissitudes of national life. So long ago as the time of Camden there were dug out of what was known as Norton Marsh about twenty pieces of lead, bearing Latin inscriptions, and sup- posed to be Roman remains. From the somewhat dubious interpretations of these inscriptions— which, as usual; are as laconic, though not so ex- plicit, as Czesar's famous despatch—it is inferred that the low marshes which bordered the Mersey hereabouts were in pre-Roman times populated by a tribe or clan of shepherds named Ceangi. Amongst these Agricola seems to have appeared with his invincible legionaries about the year 79 of the Christian era, and, after scouring the woods and estuaries of the river with his detachments, quickly established the Roman dominion. Coming to later, but still pretty remote times, we find it recorded that this township was given by William, constable of Cheshire, and Son of William Fitznigel, to the canons of Runcorn in exchange for land in Runcorn, and that the canons were removed from Runcorn to Norton about the reign of King Stephen. The land of the township remained in the possession of its ecclesiastic landowners till the dissolution of the abbeys in England by Henry VIII. The monks did not give up their lands with a very good grace, and as they were backed up by the country people living round about, who assem- bled to the number of two or three hundred, and put the king's commissioners in some hazard, Sir Piers Dutton, sheriff of Cheshire at the time, 'sow- ever, hastily came to the rescue of the government's emissaries, and, taking the abbot and his canons in- to custody, lodged them in Halton castle. Henry, in his rough Tudor fashion, directed that their heads be cut off, but it is not known whether this sanguinary edict was carried out, or whether the ab- bot and his fellow prisoners derived benefit from an amnesty which was soon afterwards issued. The monks hafting been thoroughly expropriated, the manor of Norton and its appurtenances was sold by the king to Richard Brooks, Esquire, in whose family it still remains.

div.head: RUNCORN CANAL.
div.p: THE RUNCORN CANAL.

In previous articles we have mentioned that be- tween Twenty-step Bridge at Stockton Heath, and Tom Payne's Bridge on the Chester and Warring- ton main road, the Ship Canal channel will break into and absorb part of the existing Runcorn and Latchford canal. , From this point, westward, the two canals will in the future—sup?osing the older and smaller canal to still exist, which it is not likely to do—will run parallel with each other, at, in most places, a few hundred yards apart, through the townships of Lower Walton, Acton Grange, and Moore; but a little to the eastward of Bob's turn- bridge, in the last-named township, the Runcorn canal, owing to a corresponding bend in the Mersey, begins to deviate to the southward, with the result that by the time Norton township is reached it again crosses the intended route of the Ship Canal and will, consequently, as at Stockton Heath, be, for a short distance absorbed in the greater water- way. Near the most southerly point in this bend of the Runcorn canal there is at present one ot the numerous turnbridges which span this canal, known as Old Handle's turnbridge—whether in vague re- membrance of Randle, a prior of Norton, who flourished in King John's time, or of one of the several other Randles who figure in local re— cords, it would be rash to say. However that may be Handles turnbridge, like its compeers, will disappear under the hand of innovation, and so far as we can ascertain it is not designed that any- thing in the nature of a larger turnbridge or a ferry should take its place, It is evidently not intended . .

to provide any means of crossing the canal at this point, and consequently the bye-road which now leads down from the Runcorn and Warrington high- way to Randle's turnbridge will in the future come to an end on the south bank of the Ship Canal. A NEW ROAD.

Evidently intended as a substitute for the turn- bridges which are to be done away with on this part of the Runcorn Canal, it is laid down in the Canal Act, as a protection of Sir Richard Brooke, that the Canal Company shall construct on the northerly side of the canal—that is between the canal and the Mersey—a road at least fifteen feet wide running westward from the ferry that, as we mentioned last week, is to be provided in place of Bob's turnbridge. This road is to be maintained in a suitable condition by the Canal Company and "Sir Richard Brooke and his tenants, agents, and work- men, and all other persons employed by him for his and their own personal use, and for the purposes of transferring from one part of the Norton Priory estate to another, all live or dead stock, agricultural produce, manure, or materials to be fed upon or used in connexion with the said estates, shall for ever hereafter be entitled free from all dues,and charges to pass and re-pass along such road, and along all other roads 7 constructed by and for the time being belonging to the company alongside the canal." A "SPOIL" DEPOSIT..

It rimy easily be imagined that in the construc- tion of so gigantic a work as the Ship Canal one of the minor dilficulties to be met and overcome will be found in the disposal of the millions of tons of

earth that will have to be displaced. In anticipa- tion of this difficulty we find that the Cbmpany have secured powers under which they mayrequire Sir Richard Brooke to provide them, out of the ' Norton Priory estates, with convenient land, not exceeding seventy statute acres, adjacent to the canal, forthe purpose of depositing thereon spoil from the- canal works. This land is to remain the property of Sir-Richard Brooke, and the Cbrupany are to deposit the spoil within such period,. at such level, and make good the surface in such manner, with a minimum depth of twelve inches of surface soil, and otherwise upon such terms as may be agned upon between them and Sii•Richard!Brooke ; or, in case of dispute, the terms are to be settled by arbitration under the Lands Clauses Aes.

div.head: TILE NORTON ESTATE.
div.p: TILE NORTON ESTATE.

The late Sit' Richard Brook.. like many other landowners whose lands are to be inteeered with by the nanal works, showed a natural solicitude to preserve intact, as., far as possible, his ancestral estates. In additiol, therefore, to the clauses for his protection, which we advlrted to.last week, we find that the Canal Company can not, without the consent of the owner of the Norton Priory estates, put in force the powers conferred upon them by their act, to acquire any part of the estates except the portions which they are expressly authorised to, sc.:quire. These portions, are, first, the lands situate within the limi of deviation of the cand, that is land which lies within certain speci- fied, limits on both sides of the ittended ' channel; second, that land situated within the limits of deviation of the two railways which run through Moore and Dare,sbury stations: and, third, astrin of /and on the noith side of the canal not exceeding fifty yards in width, and to be contiguous to the land to be acquiredwithin the limits of devia- tion of the canal. The owner of thwNorton estates is also to have a first right of pre-emption over all lands situate in Halton, Norton, Moore, Acton Grange, and ,Reckwick, purchased from him by the Canal Com- pany, which the company lawfialy sell and which are not required for the purposes of the company. Sir Richard Brook has likewise a right of pre— emption, next after the original ownei., over all land, situate in the townships named, which have been purchased from other persons. Further pro- visions enact that all works to be executed by the company for the protection of the Norton Priory estates shall be done under the supervision and to th e reasonable satisfaction of the agent or engineer of Sir Richard Brooke, and that the company shall construct, and for ever afterwards maintain, on each side of the land acquired by them, within the limits of deviation of the canal works, a good and sufficient post and rail, or other fence, not less than four feet six inches high, having proper gates for the purpose of providing access to the several roads, wharves, and fences. (To be continued.)

div.head: ALONG THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: ALONG THE SHIP CANAL.

FROM WARRINGTON TO MOORE. (From the "Manchester City News.") Warrington is one of the many towns which are ;oing to have their fortunes made by the Ship Canal. Not that it is an unprosperous town even now; but it has certainly not increased and multi- plied either in population or trade at the rapid rate of its big Lancashire relatives, Manchester and Liverpool. Yet there was a time when it was of more importance in some respects than either of them. Leland. writing in the first half of the six- teenth century, says that it has a better market than Manchester, and describes it as "a paved town of pretty bigness, with an Augustine friary at the town's end, and the parish church at the tail of all the town." The friary has long ago disappeared, and the chief part of the town now runs away ro- wards the bridge. The town is of very old stand- ing as a trading place; and Aikin, whose book was published in 1793, particularly mentions that it had long been noted for its malt and ale. In 1781, the population was stated to be 8,791; the figures now given are 45,257. Leaving the Warrington Central Station :v've are immediately and forcibly reminded that the town's reputation for brewing of good ale—to say nothing of its equally great reputation as a consumer there- of—has continued to the present day. The air is filled with perfume from the breweries. Au old Lancashire versifier says : The physic that cures all diseases, Is a bumper of Warrington ale. The town's claims to consideration are, however, not confined to beer ; it is stated that the first news- paper printed in Lancashire was issued from a War- rington press. We pass along the narrow principal street of this "paved town of pretty bigness,' and so on to the bridge, said to have been erected by the first Earl of Derby for the purpose of accommoda- ting Henry VII., when the Ring was on a visit to I him. Here we stop to have a look at the beautiful river, which winds and bends hereabout and in the neighbourhood of the town like a gigantic water boa-constrictor. The Ship Canal as planned, touches the extreme outward curve of a great bend not a great way from the bridge; and here will presently be constructed docks of twenty-two acres in extent, I the work upon which, so far as we can ascertain, is- not yet begun. We stand upon the bridge, gazing upon the lovely stream, and feel somewhat com-1 forted. L has been an article of faith with us that there is nothing to compare with our own Irwell ;-1 but here we have something nearly as perfect in colour and consistence, with the added advantage that there is very much more of it. There is the same blackness, the same pretty white KUM drift- ing and eddying over its surface. AT LATCHFORD. As we cannot see the unmade dock, we cross, to the Cheshire side, and turn our steps in the upward direction of the Canal to the village of Latch- ford, and after a walk of two or three miles find the works in progress in that neighbourhood and near Thel- wall. Passing through Latchford we come upon a, very sharp curve of the river, and a weir, up to which we are told the influence of the tide is felt. The curve, and weir, with a lock and a little island covered with trees in which is a rookery, form a pretty picture of which one would like to preserve a record. True, the water is filthy, but that could be put all right in the painting. Upon this Latchford section there are about four hun- dred men at work, and two steam navvys of the ordin- ary kind heretofore described. The section is about four and a half miles long, and so far as we inspected tne workin,gs the excavating seemed to be of a remark- ably easy character, the soil being very sandy and soft. Here will be situated a set of locks and sluices, and the canal will be of the normal width of one hundred and twenty feet at the bottom. In the portion of the works under notice the canal will cut across the river either five or six times; and in one place a hugh embankment is being raised with a view to the diversion of the river's I course. We notice a great deal of water in the bottom of the cutting, and ask whether it is from rain or springs? "It conies from the cutting itself," was the answer; " and we are much troubled with it. At one place higher up we chanced to cut through some field drains, with the result that we have quite two feet of water in that part. But you can see'for yourself how it is oozing through the sides." And so it was; coming through, in all directions. Thinking of the long distance from Warrington, we asked, "Do you house your men here ? " "We do not at present ; but you may see over yonder the huts in course of construction, which will very soon be tenanted."' We go across to look, and find quite a street of neat- looking wooden houses running along continuously on each side. They look rather larger than one might have expected, with rooms on each side of the front doors, and projecting portions behind. But then the occupants will be in the-happy position of having no upstairs, acon- dition of things to be envied. We enter one or two near completion, and find some communicative workmen. "When will these rows of houses be occupied?" "They will be ready for occupation about the end of next week; but probably will not be used until another batch is put up." "Where do the men lodge now?" "Many of them at Warrington, some at Latchford. I go to Lymm." A pretty good' walk, too, night and morning. We look round at the internal arrangements, which seem to us uncommonly comfortable considering the temporary purposes of the buildings; but they do not quite satisfy, ourworkman. When is the British work- man satisfied? He commonly uses the privilege of his nationality to the fullest extent, and grumbles at most things. The front door opens directly into the kitchen or common living room, which is furnished with a good fireplace and ovened grate. Opening out of this, to the left, are two littlebedrooms for the use of the family, and to the right is a big room for the lodgers (single men.) At the back are two other doors, the one opening into a scullery, the other into a pantry with plenty of shelving. Our friend considers the living room too small, and thinks a slice might have been taken from the single men's apartment. Also thinks there are so many doors , in the room—there are six, including the front—that there are no proper spaces wherein to fix tables and things. All the same, we think we could manage to make shift with such a house in some one or other North Wales wilderness, during the summer-time at any rate. The roofs are coated with a thick waterproof material. Of course there are upon the section the usual offices and workshops of wood', and steam tippers, and temporary railways running I,ere and there and everywhere. 57 MOORS. Hearing that thereis much going on at Moore, we de- cided upon visiting the works there: but they are some five or six miles distant, in the oppostte direction from Warrington, and stretch on until they nearly shake hands with Runcorn. Hbvrever, the day is fine, the east wind is not quite so bitter as usual, and it is not an unpleasant walk through the- lanes and along the cross-country roads, watching the larks mount into the bright sky, and noting the evident determination of the trees and hedgerows to rush out into masses of greenness at the very first opportunity which maybe vouchsafed to them.
go. Cam

Eventually we read., the canal works, and go along them for some miles, without seeing anything of Moore, but are not surprised We are getting used to that sort of thing, and are quite content with the assurance that the village is somewhere in the neighbourhood. The works are very extensive, are being executed with mense vigor, and we soon note that the excavating is of a different and altogether more difficult nature than any we have yet seen—altogether a contrast to that we have just left at Latchford. Entering at the end nearest to Warrington,we found the lower part of the cutting com- posed of an exceedingly stiff clay, which is cut put with the spades in solid unbroken lumps so tenacious that they are lifted into the wagons by means of two-pronged forks. Thare are no steam navvies at work just here, but crowds of men are slaving away at a great pace. A Little further on you find the. soil somewhat looser and mixed up.with bits of rock, giving warning of what will be found a little deeper down. We are some distance from the.river at this part, but the Runcorn and Latch- ford Canal is not very far away, and the Lordon and North-Western and Grand Junction Railways cut across the line of the Canal. Further on are vast earavations with two or three lines of railway in the bcttem • and there is a long stretch of white sand for some depth, which thanges-into horivontal lines of rock and then into a yellowish sand. All at once, after considerable length of this has been passed, it suddenly runs out to the 3ur-- faco, and is succeeded by a bright red sand material which grows stiffer and harder as it descends, until at the-bottom of the cutting it is tolerably mild red rock. Machines aire.used here, but not for scocping purposes. The cranes used are merely for lifting, and are provided with,great buckets, which are let down, to the bottom and filled by the men, who are working, with pick and' k shovel. Very slow and laborious work it looks, Every- where we see plenty of proof that Mr. ?ember was justi-. fled in stating his conviction that great quantities, of water would be obtained from the sandstone. The diffe culty here is to get rid of it, and steam puircing opera- tions have to be carried on without intermission. Suddenly, as we walk along the edge of the great trench, we here excited shouts of "Stand back! Stand back !." and are made to u9derstand that blasting is being performed at the bottom, and that an explosion is imminent. We quickly get out of harm's way, . expecting to see and hear a miniature Vesuvius. Then there comes a noise something like the muffled bang of a decent squib, there is little smoke, and that is all. We look down into the cutting, and with a little assistance from a bystander at length discover that a too or so of sandstone rock has been cracked and loosened, ready for the men to get out. Passing this portion, the earth again becomes of a loose nature, and we find a steam navvy at work in the usual fashion, scooping away. Next the white sand reappears and we have a weary walk along a white sand embank-
there

ment which might remind one of New Brighton, only there is no sea, no Ham and Egg Row, no photography, no donkey-riding. We are told there is a German steam navvy at work (the only one) nearly a mile further on, and being a novelty to us, we are bound to see it. The machine cer- tainly does a wonderful lot of work where the soil is favourable; but we fancy it is not at all adapted for stiff material. It consists of a series of large %coops—in shape not unlike a flour scoop without the handle—fixed upon endless chains. These descend upside down, and empty; they are reversed in ascending, and each scoop is filled by the time it reaches the top and enters the machine house, where it empties itself into a truck under- neath.

Once again we are set upon our travels by the informa- tion that right away in the far distance are some mar- vellous machines at work, which are styled indifferently as "land-grabbers" or "crabs." They are only another half or three-quarters of a mileaway, and we soon find them. They are truly fearful-looking monsters, doing work amongst stiff material such as we have not seen either of the other machines tackle. The steam-cranes are much the same as those used elsewhere, but bang- ing from the projecting arms are gigantic things, appear- ing, as they dangle in the air, like prehistoric crabs. The claws, curving inwards, six or eight on each side, are open and apart as they descend and stick their points into the earth; then they force their way until the ends join, when they lift out a great heap, which is swung round and dropped into a truck by the side. They are if possible, more ugly than, and quite as fascinating as, the diabolical-looking so-called American navvies. . .

Our quest is naCow ended for the thme-... We are very near Runcorn, but turn ourselves right about and return along the edge of the great cutting just as the signal is given to cease working, and we tramp away to Warring- ton with a string nearly a mile in length of weary. and subdued workers, who are heavily making their way home at the close of their labours for the day.

div.head: EASTIIAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.
div.p: EASTIIAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.

Ferry boats daily take numbers of visitors from the landing stage at Liverpool to the neighbourhood of East- ham and Ellesmere Port,.to view the Ship Canal works. About a thousandmen,and alarge quantity of machinery, are in a condition of constant activity, and their labours have a very marked effect. The connections completed recently with the railway at Ellesmere .Port Station, and with the Shropshire• Union Railway and Canal Companies' docks at Ellesmere. Port, greatly facilitate the carriage of materialto the works.

div.head: INCE..
div.p: INCE..

In the space of three months the population of rural Ince has been about trebled, much to the satisfaction of the local tradesmen, who are not slaw to appreciate the impetus given to business by the canal works. Two steam navvies are getting their work in, here, and are rapidly cutting up the foreshore. Hilts are being erected on the works, but in the meantime the navvies engaged mostly live in the village. The line of rails running the line of the section is nearly completed, the trestle bridge or the river Gowy is finished, and the.connection will soon be complete.

WESTON POINT. There will be a lot of dredging and building on this section. Commencing at the • " Mkgazines," about two miles east of Ince Lighthouse, the canal will run along the southern shore, following the course of the present deep water channel until it comes to the mouth of the Weaver. A large basin will be constructed at this point, in order that vessels can load and• unload cargoes. The Weaver Navigation Company's canal will be connected with this basin, close by the site of which it runs. By I this means goods from the Potteries and the Midlands can be transhipped from the canal boats direct to the ocean-going vessels. There are at present at Weston Point two large docks and two basins that provide ac- commodation for shipping, and vessels of 800 tons can at high tides come up the river to these docks. Not only lighters, but sea going boats, find accommodation here, and it is not unusual to see vessels in port that hail from distant lands. Indeed, vessels. of all descriptions. from a steam barge to a brig, may be seen. The princi- pal exports are salt, china clay, and iron. As yet only about forty men are engaged on this section, and their work is of a preparatory character, consisting of laying rails, setting out the site for the basin, and building store-rooms and huts. The number of men employed will probably be largely increased in a few weeks. Christ Ckurch, at Weston Point, was built in 1841 by the Weaver Navigation Company, who not only supply the stipend of the minister, the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, but also the cost of lighting and warming the church. CADISHEAD AND IRLAM.

On the Warburton section, . close- to Hollins Green, nearly 600 men are now at work, and six locomotives re- move the earth dislodged by the steam navvies. Blasting is shortly to be commenced. The bulk of the men be- long to the midland and southern counties, although em- ployment has been found for much,of the surplus male labour of Cadishead and Irlarn. Only a few of the navvies can find lodgings in Hollins Green, and they go in some cases as far as Cadishead and Liam on the Lan- cashire side, and as far as Lymm on the Cheshire side. Those who live at Lymm have a long walk to encounter, as well as the inconvenience of paying toll to cross War- burton Bridge. MANCHESTER DOCKS: PROPOSED ALTERATION. The Manchester Ship Canal Company have resolved, with the consent of the Corporations of Manchester and Salford, to alter their dock scheme in some material par- ticulars. The effect of the proposed changes would be Ito remove a large extent of dock: area southward into the township of Stretford; but the company have agreed, at the instance of the Corporation, to obtain authority from Parliament to make the centre of the Ship Canal the municipal boundary, by which means the borough will obtain a slight accession of area. They also undertake to construct a dock. not less than 34 acres Hi extent between Messrs. J. and M. Worrall's works and those of Messrs. Goodwin Brothers; that Trafford- road shall be diverted, and that an opening bridge shall be constructed across the Dwell at the bottom of Fair- brother-st. securing easy access from Salford to Chester- road and die adjacent districts. A bill is being promoted to give legislative sanction to the arrangement.

div.head: MR. BRLTNNER ON THE WEA.TER TRUST,:.
div.p: MR. BRLTNNER ON THE WEA.TER TRUST,:.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., has addressed the fol., lowing letter to a Liverpool contemporary. you kindly allow mato call the attention of, your. readers to the necessity for re-constituting the, trust of the river Weaver, regarding which I have given notice of a question to the President of the Board of Trade on Tuesday next? I inter • to ask him to sub- stitute a public trust similar to, the Mersey Docks aad 'Harbour Board for the present self-elected body, and, to stop the taxing of the salt trade for the relief of the Cheshire county rate, The tax upon the salt trade,is a tax upon Liverpool, • trade. Parliament has evidently made up its mind to abolish the Landon coal dues, and thus rid the, coal trade of a wanton tax and it has now become absolUrt tely intolerable that the salt trade,, and with it the, ship,. ping trade of. Liverpool, should be taxed for the *Hetet ' tho Cheshire county rate. 1 In former days Liverpool merchants and shipowners, took a great interest in the question, and I hope. that Liverpool will now, througiii its members, and especialty. through Mr. Forwood and, Baron de Worms, two mesas,. bers Of the Government- intimately associated with, Liverpool, express an unmistakable opinion in tavourcfl this measure of simple,justice. Join; T. BRUNNESt 60, Prince's-gate„,Londen, S.W., April 28th,.1488.; P.S.--Salt pays. a. tell of a shilling a ton on, the. Weaver, while"gods" including alkali—worth. 20., times a much' as salt--culy pay Bd. This toll of, a.slail- ling is far in excess of cost of maintaining, and e van el improving at a rapid rate. the navigation of the Weaver and is charged. solely to relieve the rates. 1,00,0611) tons of salt are yearly shipped from the Mersey. J. TB, TILE,Q,UESTION IN THE aIOUSF4, In the House of Commons on Tuesday, , Mr. Brunner said ::--I beg to ask tzt, . President of the Board of Tradewhether he Is aware that the trust of the ' river Weaver„thelargest inland navigation in thaklisg- dont, is a self-elected body; that its incoin'.is derived almost entirely from the salt trestle ; that its.surplus funds have for more than 160 yeara been wed to relieve tlw county rate; that the salt trade .has in this way and during that time been taxed to the extent of more than .42,000,000)sternag ; that the salt trade is,,,and has long been, in. a,deplorably depressed condition ; that the sour- ces of saltproduction have of lateorears been rapidly de- ' veloped„ and bear no corresponding tax for, the benefit of any pablic authority whilst they.have greatly diminished the demand for Cheshire salt; that the salt manufactu- rers of Cheshire have since 1886-been taxed, ia common with other ratepayers of the county,. under the Cattle Plague Act ; that the cost to the county for-this Act is, for mstahhent of loan and interest, 44;22T 15s per an- num; that this loan will be raid off in 19e,; that under a recent Act the trustees of the River Weaverocontribute £15,000, a year to the countßfund ; . and that the consti- tution of the Weaver Trust has been, repeatedly condem- ned by the Board of Trade, on the, ground that it im- posed a tax upon trade, awl whether lw is prepared to recommend for the management of the River Weaver the• constitution of a public trust rssemblrdng the Mersey Decks and Harbour Board; and that the payment from I the trust to the county pand should cease at the date of the last payment on account of the Cattle Plague Loariin 1896, or at an earlier date? Sir M. Hicks-Beach replied that the history of the Wea- ver Trust was contaioed in a report presented in 18'111by the Board of Trade on the Weaver Navigation Bill, then before Parliament: The Board of Trade had no power to alter the management of this or any other trust in the kingdom. Any proposal for the reconstitution of the trust must come from those interested. Any such pro- posal would receive the beet consideration of thedepart. inent.

- WARRINGTON-STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY. The fifth appropriation 'meeting of , the members of this society was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Legh-st., on Monday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided, and there was a full attendance. The • directors present were Messre, N. Legge, J. Griffiths, W. Crampton, George Lea, D. Sumnere, Thomas Burton, and Robert Sutton. The MA.von said he was asked by their secretary, Mr. Titchett, to take the chair that evening, and as he had always taken a great interest in the conduct and management of building societies, and been connected with them for, he thought, a period of something like a quarter of a century, he was, of course, very pleased to comply with , Mr. Titchett's request. But in taking the chair that night he did not intend to-draw any comparison between their society and any other society, because as a rule, comparisons very often mislead, and they Were very apt to misapprehend many facts and circutn- stances connected with the cases that they entered into. In the few remarks he had to make he should, therefore, simply confine himself to building socie- ties generally. (Hear, hear.) He was of , opinion that a, building society was a very good t hing in- deed for a workingman to take an, interest in, be- cause it enabled him to save his money in an easy manner, awl to derive very great benefit and advantage from it; and were it not for building societies, there is many a man who would probably, never have saved a penny. (Hear, hear.) He was encouraged to save a few shillings, or as much as he could, every week, and he did not feel it, yet in, cdUrse of time he was actually surmised at the result—he was aetonished when he found Mosio. 10e savings had be- come Ouch an important sum in his Wen eyes. (Hear, hear.) Of course, they knew that cleriag the last ten years or so the public had lost, to a very great egeept, confidence In building societies, but this had been en- tirely owil*to'mismanagement. They knew that many building societies Inid been managed and conducted in a very_ reckless fashion. He was not alluding to any society CI Warringtora_but they had often read of socie- ties in other towns suffering very severe loss and coming to grief owing to the recklessness and mismanagement of the managers of the societies. It had been the cus- tom with many of those societies, just for the sake of securing a bonus, to advance money to any extent to ' borrowers, without regard either to the quality or value of the property upon which the advances were made. A society of that kind was bound to come to grief in the end, but he meant to say that any building society con- ducted on sound principles and managed in a proper Manner by its committee or directors was bound to be of benefit to every shareholder who had to do with it. (Hear, hear.) He knew that in a society with which he was connected—it was only a small society in the town—they were very careful how they made their ad- vances. They never thought of making advances upon property to a larger extent than any of themselves indi- vidually would be willing to lend upon it, and he was of opinion that in dealing with other people's affairs`they ought to bees careful as when dealing with their own.: (Hear, hear.) If they acted upon that principle they might be sure that every society, conducted as he be- lieved that Starr-Boerkett Society was conducted, on good principles and under good management, would suc- ceed and be of benefit to those whertook shares in it (ap- plause.) Mr. N. Lsoei(chairma.n of the directors) said he could tell them that the Starr-Bowkett Society was going on very well indeed. They were increasing in numbers every week, and he waa-glad to see that the public were getting more confidence in the society than they had: at first. In fact they were going on at such a rate that the society would very soon be filled up. (Applause). They had now 463 members, holding 1043 shares, so that they only wanted 36 more members to complete the society and these he expected they would have before the next appropriation. (Hear, hear.) He thought, therefore,' considering the short time the society had been in exis- tence it had not done amiss.(Hear, hear and applause.) In accordance with the society's rules Mr. Ephraim Aukland, a member, was elected to preside during the appropriation ballot, and Messrs Owen and Winstanley were elected scrutineers of the ballot. On the first ballot, the number 236 was drawn but it was found on reference to the books that the member whose number this was was in arrears with his weekly payments, and he was accordingly precluded by the rules from receiving the appropriation. Another ballot was tire numberenandth of m enumr-. num- ber 319 was drawn, and this being Henry Whitehouse of Bewsey-road, Warrington, who was clear on the books, that member was declared en- titled to the loan of a sum of £4OO for 14 years free of

interest. The ballot having been complete& Mr. TITCHETT men- tioned that the next appropriation would probably be held within the next one or two months. Votes of thanks to the Mayor, on the motion of Mr. Thomas Burton seconded by Mr. W. Stout, and to the chairman of the ballot and the scrutineers, on the motion of Mr. Griffiths, seconded by Mr. Pillinger, were heartily accorded and the meeting then ended.

div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT NEWTON.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT NEWTON.

The marriage ,of Miss Ada Pearson. youngest daughter of the late 'Mr. John Pearson, J.P., of (.3-ol- borne Park (late chairman of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company) and formerly High Sheriff of Lancashire, to Mr. George Montague Brown-Westhead, only son of Mr. Marcus Brown- Westhead, of Lea Castle, Worcestershire, and Red- cliffe, Newton-le-Willows (chairman of the NeWton Division Conservative Association), took place at St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Monday afternoon. Owing to mourning in the bride's family no invita- tions were issued. There was, however, a large and fashionable gathering in the church. which was prettily decorated with choice flowers. The cere- mony was fixed for half-past two, at which hour the bridegroom, accompanied by his best man, Mr. Percy Kirk, was in waiting for the bride, who entered the church on the arm of her brother, Mr. J. E. Pearson, who gave her away. She was attired in a dress of ivory white corded silk, trimmed with Brussels point lace (the gift of her mother), and sprays of orange blos- som ; a tulle veil, and orange blossom in her hair. Her ornaments were diamonds, and she carrieda magnificent bouquet composed of orange blossom, eucharis lilies, and myrtle, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaid was Miss Clara Gillespie (daughter of Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., of Newthn-le Willows), who was dressed in ivory white surah, trimmed with silk lace; large white felt hat and feathers, and wore a sapphire and diamond fly brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. The officiating clergymen were the Rev. Herbert Monk, M.A. (vicar) and the Rev. Walter' H. R. Pughe, M.A. (curate), St. Peter's, Newton-le-Willows. Amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs. Brown-Westhea,d (the bridegroom's parents), and Miss Brown-Westhead, Mr. J. E. Pearson, Mr. • Thomas H. Pearson, Mr. and Mrs. G. F. Pearson, Miss Pearson, Miss F. M. Pearson, Mr. C. E. Pearson, Miss K. Pearson, the Misses Thompson, Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., and Miss Gillespie, Mr. W. F. Gooch, J.P., and Miss Kingdon, Dr. and Miss Watkins, Mrs. Pughe, Mrs. John Jones, Captain and Mrs. Seton, Captain and Mrs. Royse, Sre. After the ceremony, the -wedding party drove to Golborne Park, and later in the day the happy couple left for Lea Castle, Worces- tershire, where theY will spend tke hodeymoon. The wedding presents included the following :--Mrs. Pearson diamond spray, Brussels lace; Mr. and Mrs. Browne:Westhea,d, -cheque; Mr. J. E. Pearson, fur rugs, book of engravings; Mr. T. H. Pearson, a cheque; Mr. and Mrs. G. F. Pearson, silver revolving dish, silver entree dishes, silver egg stand; Miss Pearson, silver tea tray, plush cushion • Miss F. M. Pearson, four silver can- dlesticks, plush table cover; Mr. C. E. Pearson, diamond marquise ring; Miss Brown-Westhead, case of silver dessert knives and forks; Mr. A. W. Pearson, oil paint- ing; Miss E. Pearson (Cheltenham), Worcester vases; Mrs. Brown-Westhead, diamond bracelet; Mr. H. J. Pearson, oil painting; Admiral and the Hon. Mrs. Tracey, a cheque; Mrs. Livingstone, spirit tantalus ; Miss Thompson, silver crumb scoop; Miss A. Thompson, crown Derby cream and sugar stand; Mr. C. Thompson, silver tea kettle; Mr. Bancroft, silver revolving dish ; Mrs. Edward Jones, Worcester vases; Sir A. B. Walker, Bart., diamond star, diamond ring, ruby and diamond ring, antique silver basket, Louis XIV. china vase; Mrs. Tom Fielden, pearl bracelet; Mr. and Mrs. Harrnood Benner, diamond and pearl brooch, pair of silver-mounted glass scent bottles ; Mr. and Mrs. Edward Fielden, diamond and pearl brooch; Lady Sinclair' of Dimbeath. silver frame; Colonel and Mrs. McCorquodale, silver tea service and spoons; Mr. and Mrs. A. C. McCorquodale, pair of silver muffineers ; Mrs. John Jones, silver entree -shells; Mr. Gooch, pair silver candlesticks ; Mr. and Mrs. Heald, case of silver-mounted ivory-handled carvers ; the Messrs. and Misses Houlgrave, silver tea service; Colonel Moore, grand piano; Mr. Grey, silver salad bowl and helpers ; Mr. Kirk, silver jug; Mr. and Mrs. W. Mayhew, 'antique silver basket; Sir Pryse and, Lady Pryse Jones, pair silver candlesticks; Mr. T. W, Legh, M.P., and Mrs. Legh, inlaid French table, Louis xiv.

• PRESCOT. • Tominnii.ienlVinrrixo.—A meeting of the Church of England Tenipertirtep'Society was held on Monday even- ing. in the Houghton-st. schoolroom. The chairman was the Bey. H. Mitchell, vicar. The meeting was well attended, and an excellent programme was gone through in a very, creditable Manner. • NEW RATES.—OR Tuesday, at the Prescot Police Court, a poor rate of is in the pound was laid for Whiston; and a highway rate of 8d in the pound for Ecclesbon (rural); a peer rate of 2.8 6d in the pound and a lighting rate of, 3d in the pound for 'the township of Rainhill, and for 'Prescot a poor. rate of is 4d in the pound. A FORGIVING' . FATHER —William 'Riley, a young man, described as a collier, of Prescot, was summoned at the instance of his father, John Riley, for corrimitting an as- sault upon him. On the complainant, an old motif ;get- ting into the witness box, he expressed his • &meta' withdraw from the case. as his son had promised never to molest him again. The bench refused to allow the case to be withdrawn, ;and the complainant then stated that on the. night' of the 14th ult.: his son deliberately struck him in the eye., •The defendant had been nine times previously bef6re the court, and he was sent to gaol for a month. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
LONDON. THURSDAY EIGHT.

After the storm of last week there has come in the House of Commons the customary calm. The nearest approach to anything like animated debate arose upon the motion for the second reading of the Bing-Harman Salary Bill. For the rest the nightly proceedings have been decidedly dull, with the usual corresponding advantage to the progress of business. It is a lamentable fact, sad as a commen- tary on human nature, that public interest in Par- liamentary proceedings increases or falls away in precise proportion to the advance or obstruction of public business. The House of Commons has lost, this session, much of its once pre-eminent character as a place of public entertainment. In the golden age of Parliamentary life, to which Sir William Harcourt referred the other day, there was no theatre in London that could compete with the popular House at Westminster. There was no sit- ting without its scene, and the only drawback was thetendency for the long continued excitement to pall on the public taste. Now the House of Com- mons is decorous and dull. The session is already nearly three months old, and not a single member has been suspended. As for an all-night sitting, there is a welling up of sullen indignation, if, after a morning sitting, the exceptional rule is brought into operation, and the House sits as late as one o'clock. Such a sudden and complete transforma- tion was never in the world's history worked upon a public assembly. Of course, the Government and the Conservative party generally benefit by this state of things, made possible by the prudent self-restraint of the Liberals in Opposition. Their satisfaction is tinged by the consciousness that they are purchasing present gratification at a heavy price in the way of future disadvantage. The Liberal party must have their turn some day, and with the new machinery for the despatch of business, will, it is feared, work quick havoc with any relics of Toryism that the present Government may leave on the Statute Book. Mr. Armistead, whose name is coming to the front in connection with mysterious little dinners at I which eminent but long dissevered politicians meet, sat for some time in the House of Commons as mem- ber for Dundee. He left the House because he could not stand the late hours, and may possibly come back again now a new order of things is estab- lished. He is a Russian merchant, and spends some months of every year in the dominion of the Czar. For the rest he lives in a pleasant corner house in Cleveland-square, sharing the quiet and dignity of St. James's Palace. Mr. Armistead has reduced the science of dinner-giving to a fine art. He never has more than eight guests. His invitations are rather deliberate if they give forty-eight hours' notice. When in the House of Commons, he had a genial habit of picking up his seven men in the lobby, and carrying them straight off to the carefully-prepared feast. Now he frequents the Reform Club in search of company. About two years ago Mr. Herbert Gladstone went to dine and sleep in Cleveland- square, and so irresistible is Mr. Armistead's hospi- tality that he has been there eN er since. These are his town quarters, and he is as much at home in Cleveland-square as at llawarden Castle. It was at Mr. Armistead's that some weeks ago Mr. Gladstone met Mr. John Dillon. Now, at the same table, he has for the first time in his life sat down to meat with Mr. Parnell. Mr. Armistead does not spoil his hospitality by incitements to after-dinner speeches. His idea is to make his guests comfortable, and in

this he succeeds. Everything is homely and hand- some in his house, not the least decorative feature being the tall and handsome host. Mr. Armistead is /e veritable Amphitryon ait l'on dine. Among the strange figures which every year emerge from obscurity and flit through the rooms of the Grosvenor Gallery and the Royal Academy, on private view days, is notable that of a little old gentleman with a hat born in the last generation and now diligently brushed the wrong way, an ancient overcoat reaching nearly down to his heels, and a general appearance of business connections with second-hand articles of commerce. I saw him

at the Press View of the Royal Academy yesterday, where in the nearly empty rooms there was full • opportunity of studying hisremarkable personality.B It was Mr. Richmond, R.A., who, sixty-four year ago, entered as a student in the Royal Academy' and had in those early days William Blake for master. Mr. Richmond has since done an immense amount of work, chiefly as a portrait painters He has a much-thumbed book containing the record of 3,800 more or less eminent persons whose portraits he has painted. It is not a rash estimate to surmise that the amount of money he has received would justify the purchase of a new hat, and the parting with an overcoat which certainly was never made for him. Mr. Richmond, R.A., the so i of a painter, is the father of another, who is already an Associate of the Academy, and is pretty certain before very long to maintain the continuity of the R.A. title in the family. Like father and grandfather, Mr. W. B. Richmond is a portrait painter. Last year he had the good fortune to get Bismarck to sit to him, and has produced what to the uneducated mind aeems a i very striking portrait, though some emi- lent critics sneer at t and point out certain de- ficiencies shocking to their cultivated mind. The general public, happily less, educated, will, I fancy, recognise in Mr. Richmend s Bismarck the present- ment of a live man, full of power and energy. Mr. Richmond, A.R.A., should, whilst there is yet time and opportunity, paint Mr. Richmond, R.A., in coat and hat. Apart from its value as a portrait, the subject is full of picturesqueness. One night, in October, 1883, I dined at the Union Club, New York, at a dinner given by Mr. Whitelaw Reid to Lord Rosebery, then en route for Australia. Mr. Reid told me that, with the exception of the two English guests and himself, every man in the reom had either been a candidate for the presi- dency of the United States or was intending to be- come one. Amongst them I remember Mr. Cleve-. land, the present president, who was at that time governor of New York, 'an d Mr. Chauncy M. Depew, who is now in the first flight of the running for the next presidency. Mr. Depew is one of the great railway managers in the United States, and is known as one of the best after-dinner speakers in America, a reputation which he well sustained on Vie evening I met him. The candidates will not even be nominated till the autumn, but I hear from Mr. Depew that he is already overwhelmed with correspondence on the subject of his candidature. Some of these communications are interesting speci- mens of unconscious American huraour. They are also not without their sad side as illustrating the curse which falls over the United States when every four years it is demoralised through all its centres by a presidential election. One elector, whom, of course, Mr. Depew has never heard of before: wrote as follows:—" My rent is due to-day. An inexor- able landlord on Monday morning will put my household effects in the street unless lean pay him. I have no claim upon your generosity except that my grandfather heard yours make his first speech.' Another thus tersely puts his case :—" I owe 1,500 dollars. It is due next week. My credit is first- class in the town, but I don't want to strain it, and so I write to you." This last reads like an extract from Artemus Ward or Mark Twain, which only shows what genuine samples of American humour are to be found in their works. It is a noteworthy and happy accident that Lord Folkestone should sit on one side of the House of Commons and Mr. Lockwood on the other. These two gentlemen have great gifts in the way of immourous portraiture, and during an important ''3te may be seen, one immediately behind the Opposition Bench, and the other at the lower the Treasury Bench, diligently sketching - members. Lord Folkestone's artistic qen somewhat interfered with by the 'ne as Treasurer of the Household. of that important office preai
40et., 'Proxt `end of . sivtuiery kas citeeiganceO 081. *lda. the tit%

heavily upon him, he finds recreation in drawing Mr. W. H Smith with exaggerated mutton chop whiskers, or Lord Randolph Churchill twirling an exaggerated moustache. Mr. Lockwood has more time, and one or other of his sketches is constantly being passed up and down the benches. He has some idea of utilising his talents for the public bene- fit. There is a scheme on foot of starting an evening paper in York, and Mr. Lockwood will contribute illustrations. lam afraid he will find this a, very different thing from occupying an idle quarter of an hour in the House of Commons. The press view at the RA. was held yesterday, and the general opinion of the show was that, though there is not much very striking, the average is good, and outsiders are taken care of. One of the most remarkable pictures is Vicat Cole's "Pool of London," a picture that might be bought by the Corporation. Tadema's six thousand pounder of a classical subject—an avalanche of rose petals let down on guests at a Roman banquet,--hangs next IMillais's beautiful landscape which, with another, he sold for .£9,000, and opposite to Leighton's An- dromeda. This is another of the great pictures of the year. The next most important is Orchardson's widower, who hears his daughter singing, and is reminded of her mother's voice. His face is full of sadness. It is a most pathetic picture. Hon has some beautiful landscapes, and Henry Moore as come to the front with several sea subjects in an amazing way. Of the portraits, there is an excel- lent one of Mr. Gladstone by Holl, with that weird look in the eyes which I have seen so often in the House when his interest is suddenly aroused, and which Millais, with the instinct of a painter, caught in his first portrait. There is the portrait of Bis- marck, alluded to above, and an excellent one of the Speaker. Ten thousand pictures were sent in ; only 1,500 were hung. The Commissioners of the litris Exposition, to open next year, are in communication with Buffalo Bill with intent to induce him to add the charm of his Wild Indians to the other attractions of the big show. Unlike Lord Salisbury's Government, Buffalo Bill is undeterred by political considerations of the association of the show with the fall of the Bastille. He is hesitating, but it is simply on a matter of terms. The bargaining is still going on, the Com- missioners having made two offers, and Buffalo Bill having metkhem with alternative propositions. He is now waiting for the next move on the part of the Frenchmen, and on the whole thinks he will take the Deadwood Coach to Paris.

div.head: WARRINGTON MILLER'S DUST
div.p: A WARRINGTON MILLER'S DUST
COLLECTOR.

At the Leeds Assizes, on Thursday, in the Nisi Prins Court, before Baron Pollock, an action was brought by Van Gelder, Apsimon, and Co., machine makers, of Liverpool and Halifax. against Fair- dough and Sons, millers, of Warrington, to recover £196, the balance of an account for machines sup- plied. Mr. E. Tindal Atkinson, Q.C., and Mr. C. Dodd were for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Waddy, Q.C., and Mr. C. M. Atkinson appeared for the defendants. The delivery of the goods was not denied, but it was claimed that the dust collector supplied by the plaintiffs did.not answer the purpose for which it had been erected. It was worked by water, and the , result, it was alleged, was that instead of collecting the dust as it should do, the machine caused an of- fensive smell, and proved a nuisance, besides being unworkable. A model of the contrivance was pro- duced in court, but his lordship suggested that the jury could not reasonably go into the scientific evidence for and against the machine, and sugges- ted arbitration.—The learned counsel, after consult- ing, said they could not agree'as to an arbitrator.— His L ,rdship : I am very sorry. This is not as it should be. It is not business. It is simply war to the knife of the most savage description. (Laugh- ter.) We all look upon the law as costly ; why not, then, try and do what is best for yourselves ?--An order was made for the matter to be referred to an official referee.

The daily and other papers of last Tuesday gave the number of specta- tors as 3,000, and as that number of people at 3d per head would amount to £37 10s, the supporters of the Runcorn Volunteer Band naturally concluded that we did very handsomely. However, facts are still stubborn things, and I enclose you a balance sheet, which shows that the gross takings were £24 16s 3d, from which you must deduct £5 145 3d (the amount the football club kindly charged us for rent of field for two hours), and £ll 15s id expenses of tea to players, printing, &c., leav- ing a balance of £7 6s lid to pay sundry musical debts and divide amongst 22 bandsmen.—Yours faithfully, RAVENSCROFT, hon. sec. to Band.
