AN ABOMINABLE 1 Sir,—As a ratepayer in the' wish to direct the attention et the members of that authority, and especially one or two ex-officios to the abominable nuisance which is allowed to exist at the corner of Howson's-lane, at its function with the Knuts- ford-road. It is due. to the drainage from a number of houses into an open ditch of both ordinary slop water, and liquid and solid excreta. It is always stagnant, offensive, and liable to become a danger to health. It is no excuse that because. the Ship Canal is going to pro- duce great changes in this district, therefore the removal of nuisances must be delayed. Until this district is pro- perly drained it is the duty of the Sanitary Authority, not only to systematically empty this cess pit, but also to flush and disinfect the sewers already laid down, which have for some time past been emitting most offen- sive gases. It is of little use addressing the Authority in their official capacity, for they are known for their "dilatoriness," complaints-about this nuisance having been made time after time with no effect ; so perhaps a little wholesome castigation in "Touch and Go" may be useful in spurring them en to a sense of their respon- sibility.—Yours, &c.,
ict I
LABOR OIVINIA VINCIT.
MINE RENTS AND MINERAL. ROYALTIES.

Sir,—As a matter of courtesy, I must acknowledge your very kindly and exceedingly able lbader in Satur- day's "Examiner." My pamphlet on "Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties" about which you speak has been and is in enormous demand, and has gone out in thousands to those to whom it is dedicated, namely, the employers and the employed in the mining and iron and steel industries of the United Kingdom. I have received many friendly communications from representatives of men and of masters and from members of Parliament, including Mr. John Morley, Sir William Harcourt, Sir Walter Foster, Hon. Bernard Coleridge, Sir Bernhard Samuelson, Mr. Henry Labouchere, Mr. Thomas Burt, Mr. C. Fenwick, Mr. B. Pickard, Mr. Handel Cossham, and very many others. And the spirit of every com- munication is that the publication of this pamphlet has brought the subject within measurable distance of Par- , liamentary action. I In your leader you quite agree with very many of my correspondents that my views are very moderate, but don't you think that is the great virtue of my pamphlet? We Radicals, good sound robust Radicals, always are moderate men. We always believe in and advocate and very often carry moderate measures of Reform, which, granted in time, avoid the need or possibility of more drastic treatment. The Extremists are those who will not recognise the need of Reform, and the result is Revolution. _ _ _ _ .

I have said in my pamphlet that the Nation gave away all its minerals without lmowing that any minerals were in existence. I have said that the amount already lost by the Nation would about wipe off the National Debt; and that the annual amount the Nation is still losing is about £6,000,000 a year. Still lam no advocate for the Nation enterring into possession. I have said so in my pamphlet, and I say so here. I would not con- fiseate a single pound of coal or iron. But I would adopt such payments as have to be made so as not to hamper our National Industries, and I would reduce the £6,000,000 we now pay per year, one fourth, or one half, or three fourths, or as much as might be found needful to enable us to compete on something like just terms with other mining and iron and steel nations; and whether our annual payments were £6,000,000 or £1,000,000, I would charge the sum with local rates.— Yours, King-st., Wigan, 30th Aptil, 1888.
C. M. PERCY.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 5, 1888.
RUNCORN TEMPERANCE SOCIETE ES AND COMPENSATION TO PUBLICANS.

A specially convened meeting of the members of the Lifeboat Division (Runcorn) of the Sons of Temperance, was held on Saturday night, for the purpose of considering the Local Government Bill. There was an unusually large attendance, and Mr. E. Kay, the W.P., occupied the chair. An anima- -1 ted discussion of two hours duration took place, and the following resolution was unanimously passed on the motion of Mr. D. Bisbrown, seconded by Mr. S. Henderson :—That in the opinion of the meeting the proposal to compensate publicans to whom —for the public good—licenses may be again granted, is unjust and contrary to precedent, and would, if adopted, be such an intolerable burden to the ratepayers as to pre- vent the exercise of the principle of local option which the bill proposes to establish ; and this meeting earnestly appeals to the Government ts at once withdraw the proposal, and should they decline to do so, calls upon all fair-minded citizens to use ei,ery effort to prevent the adoption of such a proposal by the House of Commons." —On the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones, seconded by Mr. W Heatherington, and supported by Mr. John Ince Mr. J. Ashley, Mr. Thomas Heesom, and Mr. T. Cooke, it is further resolved :—" That this meting welcomes the acceptance by the Government of the principle that the ratepayers should control the liquor traffic, but considers that no legislation for dealing with it can be at all ade- quate which does not confer upon the ratepayers the power of preventing by direct vote the issue and re- newal of licenses for the. sale of intoxicating liquors in their respective localities." It was decided to forward , copies of these resolutions to the President of the Local , Government Board, and to Mr. Brunner.

On Monday evening a meeting of the Runcorn Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held. Delegates were present from the Rechabites, the Sons of Temperance, and other temperance organisations in the town. The vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, presided. Interesting speeches were made by Messrs. W. Shaw (missionary), D. Bisbrown, R. Wilson, J. D. Jones, T. Cooke, and others, and ultimately resolutions condemn- ing the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill, and requesting that the ratepayers should have a more direct control of the liquor traffic, were passed, and ordered to be forwarded to Lord Salisbury, Mr. Rit- chie, and Mr. Brunner. At a meeting of the Halton Wesleyan Temperance So- ciety, on Friday evening last, the Rev. F. Homabrook presiding, resolutions of a similar character were passed.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.)
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.)
RUNCORN.

The work of excavation proceeds apace on this section. The cutting is now of great length, but as yet no attempt has been made to increase the depth beyond 20 feet. Last week a start was made at No Man's Land, but the work, as was reported in this journal last week, was most abruptly stopped. The reason then assigned for this circumstance was the fact that the land was almost submerged by the high tides that then prevailed. It ap- pears, however, that this is not a correct explanation. The Mersey Conservancy Board possess certain rights over all lands that are covered by a tide of 21 feet, and as No Man's Land answers that description, it is within their jurisdiction. It was this body that, not having given permission for operations to be commenced on No Man's Land, caused Mr. Walker's navvies •to so suddenly retire. No doubt application will be made to the Board in due form, and work resumed on the land in a short time. The number of men now employed on the Run- corn Section is in excess of 1,000, and the lodging acco- modation of the town is not equal to the demands made upon it. We believe that Mr. Walker has therefore de- termined to erect a number of huts on the section, but their location is not yet fixed upon. For the joint use of this section, and the Weston section, an accident Hospital is to be erected below Runcorn Docks, near the pumping station.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

On this section, Mr. T. Kirkham, Runcorn, has se- cured the contract to erect the large wooden shed, of which mention was made last week. The shed will be a most substantial structure, and have a length of not less than sixty feet. It will be principally used for making Lock Gates. The construction of three more huts for navvies has also commenced. A few days ago the work of pile driving was started on Frodsham Marsh, but as was the case at Runcorn, the Mersey Conservancy Board interfered with their authority, and operations ceased. THELWALL.

The laying of the line of metals to connect the works atThelwall with the Ship Canal siding at Latchford station is not yet completed, though during the past few days workmen have been engaged upon the line near Morris Brook farmhouse. At a meeting of the Dares- bury Highway Board on Thursday, the Surveyor (Mr. Peerman) reported that the rails of this connecting line had been laid across Thelwall-road, Station-road, and Cross-lane, and that every precaution had been taken for the safety of the public. The Clerk also submitted to the Board a draft of an agreement which it was proposed should be entered into with the contractor, Mr. Walker, as to the conditions upon which the latter should be allowed to lay the lines across Grappenhall-road, Knuts- ford-road, and the other roads under the jurisdiction of the Board. We understand that a delay in laying this branch line has been caused owing to the fact that per- mission has not been obtained for the crossing of some land belonging to Mrs. Tunstall, adjoining Kuutsford- road. Rapid progress is being made with the navvies' huts which) are being erected to the east of Morris Brook, and while the first two rows are almost ready for their inhabitants, a start has been made with the opera- tion of roofing the third row. There are also indications of an intention to erect another batch, so that in a few months time there will in all probability be quite a colony of "hardy toilers" in this locality. During the last day or two a good deal of timber, bricks, &c., have been carted on to the ground near to Cedar Lawn, off Thel- wall-roa3, the late residence of Alderman Pickmere, and the foundations of some temporary buildings have , already been laid.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

During the present week the several parts of an " American " steam navvy have been brought upon the works at Statham; and it is now almost in working or- der in one of the cuttings a little distance from the road- way which leads along the banks of the Mersey. A num- ber of men are busily engaged at this point, and the wagons, which are rapidly filled by them with the clayey soil of the district, are shunted to the large spoil heap by the side of the cutting, and there emptied. At some of the workings at Statham, water has been an hindrance to progress, and in one cutting the navvies have been flooded out. ACCIDENT AT NORTON. A serious accident 9ccurrel en the Ship Canal works at Norton on Tliiirgday inornino.. A ganger named Scott, a married man who resiaes in Spring Gardens, Runcorn, was superintending the work of some navvies in the cutting, when a landslip occurred. He was buried beneath many tons of earth, but was quickly dug out, and removed home. His back is most seriously injured, and doubts are expressed as to his recovery.
THE ALLEGED FRAUDS BY A LATE RUNCORN SOLICITOR.

BUILDING SPECULATIONS ON THE MERSEY. Francis John Forsell Kirby, a well-known Leices- ter solicitor, who a few years ago practised in Run- corn, was placed in the dock, at the Leicester Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with obtaining various sums from the Stamford, Spalding, and Boston Banking Company, by false pretences, in August, 1886. The prisoner, who had been in part- nership with Mr. Woodcock, solicitor, Runcorn, ap- peared to feel his position acutely, sitting through- out with his head buried in his hands, and evidently much agitated. The case excited the greatest interest, prisoner having been an assistant clerk to the magistrates and -member a the Town Council until a few days ago. Mr. Fox Wright prosecuted, and Mr. Fowler appeared for the defence. Evidence was given to show that the prisoner had had an account in the, bank from 1885 down to his bankruptcy. At first his overdraft was limited to £5OO, but it was subsequently increased to £750. In August 1886, he applied for an additional overdraft of .£6OO, making the whole £1,350. By way of security he produced the mortgage deeds of land at Garston, and as there were sufficient to cover the amount the overdraft was granted. The prisoner drew cheques against it until his total draft reached £1,580. On him filing his petition inquiries were made, when it was discovered that he had parted with 311 interest in the land before he obtained the additional overdraft, having suppressed the later deeds At the close of the evidence, Mr. Wright applied for a remand, and Mr.. Fowler asked that the prisoner should be admitted to bail, but the Bench remanded him until Tuesday next, and re- fused bail. The statement of the Official Receiver showed that the unsecured claims amount to .£F7,858, the fully secured claims to £19,955, and the partly secured claims to £52,817, the value of the securities being £29,269 The total un- secured debts- thus amounted to £41,406. The securities included a considerable leasehold estate at Runcorn, and also estates at Widnes, Farnworth, and elsewhere. The properties at Farnworth and Widnes were split up into a large number of sub- leases, upon which mortgages had been issued. The net assets were .f.. 5,316 leaving a net deficiency of £36,089. The Official Receiver added that he did not think that large deficiency would ever be fully ac- counted for; but to obtain some light on the subject they must go back to the beginning of Mr. Woodcock's partnership with the bankrupt in 18=. There was no doubt the Cheshire estates had proved a great loss. Some time ago Mr. Kirby estimated that £5,000 was lost in the Runcorn property. There was a third estate at Farnworth, which be (the official receiver) believed to be wholly bad. But there had been no fresh valuation of any of the properties. In the case of the Runcorn property it was put at the valuation placed in the statement of the affairs- of the original leaseholder.. As regarded the valuation of the Whines property, that was valued a great many years ago for the purposes of a mortgage. It was said to have inceeased in value since, but the whole of these estimates must be taken for what they were worth. For the rest, it' appeared that much of the deficiency. a £36,000 was due to the fact that interest had been paid from year to year on money which had Tong ago been hopelessly lost. The balance sheet of 1881 showed a 1 nominal profit of £3,000, but this was fictitious, as in the opinion of the official receiver-the estate had been insolVent ever since 1878.

div.head: MARRIED MISERY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MARRIED MISERY AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Massey, a rougli-looking young fellow, was charged that he being well able to maintain his wife, did desert her. —Mrs. Massey said she had been married five years, and pto the 4th April lived with her husband at a house in Windmill-st. On the 23rd March he came home and said "Is there nothing on the table only this," and she replied " No ; I cannot get much with 135." The defendant thereupon struck her on the face with his fist, making her a black eye, and kicked her on the right side of the body. On the 4th April he turned her and her little daughter into the street, and said they must go to the Workhouse before he would keep them. She had since lived with her mother in Surrey-st. The defendant earned about 2.85 per week at the worksof Messrs. wigg Bros. and Steele. The defendant acknowledged that he had not paid his wife any money for five weeks. She had, he said, got into the habit of drinking, and he used to have to go without food. He lost his employment because he stayed away three days in consequence of not having had anything to eat. He was now working for a man that was sick and received 24s per week, but when that man returned he would have to go into the yard and labour for 2s 8d per day.—Mr. Reynolds said he would be ob- liged to keep his wife and child.—An order was therefore made upon him to pay 8s per week towards their sup- port, and also the costs, 10s 6d.—The Defendant; I can- not do it; she has run me into debt for CO.

div.head: COUNCILLOR BOLTON'S AURICULAS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR BOLTON'S AURICULAS.

At the National Auricula Society's show held in the new Town Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday, Councillor William Bolton, Warrington, was a suc- cessful exhibitor, securing the second prize for six auriculas (dissimilar); second prize for twelve fancy auriculas (dissimilar); first prize and premium for single green-edged auticula; fourth and sixth prize for single grey-edged auricula; fourth prize for single self; and fourth prize for four Alpine auriculas (dissimilar.) At the London show of the Auricula Society, held in the Drill Hall of the London Scottish Volunteers, James-st., Westminster, on Tuesday week, in con- nection with the Royal Horticultural Society, Mr. Bolton took seven prizes; fourth prize for twelve auriculas (dissimilar) ; fifth for six auriculas; seventh for single green-edged auricula; sixth and seventh for single grey-edged auricula; third prize for single self auricula; and second prize for the best seedling self auricula. The premier auricula selected from amongst the whole show was a variety called Edith Potts, raised by Mr. Bolton, in Mersey- street, Warrington, and shown by him at Manches- ter in 1886. Considering the difficulties Mr. Bolton had in raising and growing plants in such a situa- tion as Mersey-st., it is evident that an enormous amount of patience and skill were displayed. But it shows that the best situations do not always pro- duce the best results. Mr. Bolton resides at present at Stockton Heath, and it is due to him to say that he grows these plants himself, without any assistance, and has made Warrington well-known amongst the florists of the United Kingdom.
MYSTERIOUS DROWNING OF A RUNCORN _ _ TRADESMAN.

Yesterday Runcorn was the scene of a very pain- ful sensation. On. Thursday evening, about half- past nine. Mr. William Blythe, tailor and outfitter. High-st., and his brother. Mr. Fred Blythe, left home with the intention of walking to Widnes to escort home their wives, who were witnessing a play at the new Widnes Theatre. On arriving opposite Runcorn Parish Church, rain descended heavily, and at his own suggestion, Mr. Fred returned home to fetch their overcoats and the macintoshes of the , ladies. His brother meanwhile was to shelter near the Hearse House; but Mr. Fred, when he again reached this spot, could not find his brother, and he concluded that he had walked on in advance. He therefore proceeded on his journey alone. Mr. Blythe did not put in an appearance at home that night, nor next morning, and information was given to the police. About five o'clock yesterday after- noon, a waterman named John Owen, who resides at Massey's-court, off Brunswick-st., saw the dead body of a man lying on the "grid" at the bottom end of No Man's Land, and with assistance suc- ceeded in raising it to the bank. He at once recog- nised the body as that of Mr. Blythe ; and P.C. Gibson appearing on the scene, that officer pro- cured a spring cart and had him conveyed to his home. There were no marks of violence upon the body, and the watch which deceased had worn had stopped exactly at half-past ten. It is supposed that Mr. Blythe mistook his way, and fell into the "gut," which is entirely unprotected. He leaves a widow and four children.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Buffalo Bill's Wild West show left Salford on Friday morning for Hull, on its return to America. The'trial of Mr. Condon, M.P., on a charge of conspi- racy, was commenced at Mitchelstown on Friday, before Colonel P ersse and Mr. Irwin. _ . _ .

The appointment of Prince George of Wales to be lieutenant on board H.M.S. Alexandra was posted at the Admiralty. on Friday evening. The Central News learns that a Cabinet Council has been summoned to meet at the Foreign Office at half- past twelve o'clock to-day (Saturday.) Mr. Gladstone will spend the Whitsuntide recess at Hawarden Castle. The right hon. gentleman has not been at Hawarden since the 26th December, when he left for Florence. _ .
During the recent gale on the Southern Irish coast much damage was caused to the English and French fishing fleets. The French lugger Esperance lost her whole train of 110 nets.
Gold has been discovered at Festiniog, North Wales, which on analysis yields the splendid result of five ounces of gold to the ton. These further discoveries have created intense excitement.

THE TRIAL OF MR. W. O'BRIEN, M.P.—At the re- sumed trial of Mr. William O'Brien, at Loughrea, on Fri- day, the third charge against the hon. gentleman was, at the suggestion of the magistrates, withdrawn by the Crown, and the proceedings terminated. A SIGNIFICANT BALLOT.—A ballot has this week been taken of the householders of Padiham on the question of granting compensation to publicans. Mr. Thomas Hull, the chairman of the Local Board, attended as returning officer, and late on Thursday night announced the result as follows :—For 112; against, 1,850; neutral, 117; thus showing a majority of 16 to one against the scheme. THE MURDER BY A MOTHER.—At Leeds Assizes, OR Friday, Mary Holliday, aged 30, was indicted for having wilfully murdered her illegitimate daughter, aged nine years, at Wandsworth. Prisoner lured the child from her grandmother's house, where the child had been living for six years, took her to a lonely place' and threw , her into a canal. The prisoner was convicted and sen- tenced to death.

THE NATIONAL PARTY AGAIN. - According to the "Pall Mall Gazette" Mr. Chamberlain, speaking on Thursday evening at a political conversazione at his brother's house, distinctly declared that he intended no longer to ally himself politically with his former col- leagues in the Liberal party. He spoke of the forma tion of a new party, called, or to be called, the lJnionist or National party, which would unite with the Dissen- tient Liberals and the Tory party. THE WARWICK BANK PROSECUTION.—OR Friday after- noon Kelyn.eGreenway and George Cottell, late bankers of Warwick', were brought up in custody at the War- wick Borough Police Court, and charged, under the Debtors' Act, with being privy to making a false entry in the ledger of the bank on the 6th September last, three days before bankrupts filed their petition. Mr. Thomas Wright prosecuted on behalf of the treasury. Defendants were remanded on bail, themselves each in two thousand pounds, with two sureties each of one thousand pounds.

- GAS EXPLOSION.—SIX MEN KILLED. ROME, FR/DAY EVENING.—An explosion of gas occur- red this morning in a tunnel in course of construction near Messina. Six men were killed outright, and a large number very seriously injured. THE EMPEROR FREDERICK.

The following bulletin was issued on Friday morning : —"The Emperor this morning is free from fever, and is able to leave his bed. His Majesty's strength is gradu- ally increasing. The issue of daily bulletins will be dis- continued until further notice.". _ _
..... BERLIN, FRIDAY EVENING.—The Emperor dined this afternoon with the members of his family.
LIST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock._ _

MrEVELLANEOUS.—The report of amendments on Scotch Roads and Bridges Bill was agreed W.—The Copyhold Acts Amendment Bill, and the Westminster Abbey Bill were read a third time.—The LORD CHANCELLOR, reply- ing to Lord Dunraven said witnesses replying on oath., before a Select Committee were absolutely protected, ex- cept in a case of perjury.—The Land Law (Ireland) Amendment Bill was read for the first time.—The House went into committee on the Musical Compositions Copy- right Bill, which passed through committee.—A Bill to establish Local Bankruptcy Courts in Ireland, intro- duced by LORD ASRBOURNE, was read a first time.—The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE ILLNESS OF THE SPEAKEE.—On the House assem- bling at three•o'clock, the Clerk announced that the Speaker was unable to be present, and Mr. Courtney accordingly took the chair. NAVAL Gows,—Mr. STANHOPE, in reply- to a question, said he knew that the firm of Armstrong and Co. had had foreign orders for guns. He believed the work they t had hitherto carried out for the Italian Government would in future be carried out in Italy. He had no information as to any foreign contracts, such as those alluded to, being held by Messrs. Armstrong and Whitworth. ARMY AND NAYY.—Mr. W. SMITH, replying to Lord Charles Beresford, could not admit that the army and navy were in a state of dangerous weakness_ Lord Har- tington would preside over the Royal Commission which would be appointed to inquire into the civil and profes- sional administrations of the naval and military depart- ments.

ME LICENSING QUESTION.—MT. RITCHIE,. replying to Mr. Caleb Wright as to whether the holders of licenses endorsed for offences against the licensing laws would be entitled to compensation, said no compensation would be given under the provisions of the Local Government Bill to licensed victuallers against whom the licensing justices made an uncomfortable report. STATE itAILWAYS.,—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. WATT called the attention of the House to the present position of affairs with regard to the railway companies of the United Kingdom with a view to the State purchasing them. The Government, he said, had power to acquire the railways on payment of 25 years' purchase based on the average profits of the- previous year; and it had been calculated that if this power were exercised a saving would be effected of 25 per cent, in faro:our of the public. A good stimulus would, be given to our industries owing to the reduction in the-charge for 1 the-carriage of goods, and enable the Chancellor of the Exchequer to a very large extent in future , to develope and increase the recenue of the country. He moved the appointment of a Committee or Royal Commis.sien to take into consideratiorahe ques- tion of acquiring the railways of the United Kingdom, in accordance with the provisions contained in the geneial Railway Act.—Mr. HOWELL supported the ap- pointment of the committee. Other countriea had ac- quired the railways, and the result had been beneficial. I—Sir I. GOLDSMID, Sir B. SAMUELSON, and Mr. I. C. BOLTON opposed, and Lord H. BRUCE supported the ap- pointment of a committee.—Sir M. Btaca could not imagine anything, more mischievous than thestate acquir- ing the railways.—Mr. GLansToss agreed with the Pre- sident of the Board of Trade. He believed railvray com- panies had an honourable record, and had done their work well. It would be highly injudicious to encumber the Government with the management of the railways, which they would have to undertake if they were ac- quired by the State.—The motion for a committee was negatived. SCIENCE AND ART.—Ms, BARTLEY called attention to the desirability of arrangements being made by the Science and Art Department from its present resources for the circulation of small collections of art objects to local musetems.—Sir W. HART' Dims. said this was done at present to the extent of their resources.—After a short discussion the motion for going into supply was withdrawn.

CUMMS BILL.—On the motion for the third reading of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, Mr. GLADSTONE hoped the endeavour of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to restrict the new Wine Duty to ex- pensive wines would prove successful; but whatever was done ought to be done quickly-. He took objection to the condition in which death duties had been left as regarded inequalities of taxation on real and personal property.--The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER defen- ded the Budget proposals. The Bill was read a third time, and the House was counted out at ten /Taunt% past nine,

div.head: LETTER FROM HARRY SPEAKMAN.
div.p: LETTER FROM HARRY SPEAKMAN.

Mr. J. E. Langshaw. secretary to the Runcorn Football Club, has received a letter from Harry Speakman, who is with the English Football team in Australia. A few extracts may interest his nu- merous admirers in Runcorn. The letter, which was written on board the ship Kaikoura, at the Cape of Good Hope, commences :—I now have the plea sure of writing to you from sea to tell you that we are all doing very well. Indeed, we could not do better. I wish Hugh had come; he would never have forgotten the voyage. At Teneriffe we went on shore at 10 p.m. in boats rowed by Spaniards, who could not speak Eng- lish, so we had to make them out as best we could. Many things were Irony cheap here—Oranges, 100 for is 6d; cigars 100 for as.; and tobacco, is 6d a lb. Our team was loaded with things when they returned to the ship after seeing the sights of the town. Tony Nolan said he would go home on the train if he could get there. The shops and bazaars don't shut up at any time, so we stayed in the town until two a.m. We were fairly in it. Dr. Smith, our boss, is a jolley chap, and when we got on board we did not go to bed until the ship sailed at 8 a.m. We saw the sun rise; a prettier sight I never saw. We amused ourselves by playing pranks upon the Spaniards,who were coaling the boat, until we sailed. In a few days we were in the Tropics. It was very warm, and we had to wear our football suits, as we could not bear the heat ; but we managed to keep ourselves alive with fqn. The sea was like a mill pond until we reached the Cape. We have concerts and balls on the quarter deck." Reference is then made to the selection of officers of the team, and the sports in which " Harry " showed so prominently, and he concludes by sendinglis best wishes to the coMMitOe, the team, and Captain Hughes, and expresses the hope that they had won all matches since he left. " Tell Will Carroll," he says, "that this is the place for making them fat." Since arriving in New Zealand the English football team have played two games at Dunedin against Otago. In the first match the bEnglishmen were victorious by two goals and two tries to one goal. Speakman, it is reported, kicked the two goals In the second match the Englishmen were again successful, scoring one goal and one try to a goal.

div.head: GRAND CONCERT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GRAND CONCERT AT RUNCORN.

The Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa choir gave their third and last conceit of the season, on Monday evening, in Runcorn Public Hall. If somewhat slowly, yet surely, the choir are advancing in the estimation of the public, and their efforts to cultivate a taste for music, and at the; same time to please, are meeting with encouraging success. The audience which as- embled on Monday evening was of considerably lar- ger proportions than lent their presence on the for- mer occasion, and another winter may see the choir, per- haps not more firmly established, but more popularly ap- preciated: The programme was divided into two parts. The first part was most appropriately devoted to Mr. T. Mee Pattison's "May Day Cantata," and the second con- sisted of songs and part songs, the principal vocalists being Miss Emily Mowll, Eistedfodd prize winner, of Birkenhead, and Mr. George Butterworth' honours cer- tificate R,A.M., andT.C.L., of Darwen. As to the work of the Choir, taken as a whole, unstinted praise must be accorded, and the only discordant note that may be sounded is that in several pieces the weakness of the tenor parts was very palpable. The choruses were most enjoyable, and on two occasions the audience showed their appreciation by unmistakeable encores, a circum- stance that must have been highly gratifying not only to the vocalists, but also to their able conductor, M, John ITolford. Both the principals were successfulr in win- ning the approval of the audience. Miss Mowll is the possessor of a soprano voice of good quality and exten- sive range, and she sang with a power and expression that caused her to be thrice re-called Mr. Butterworth as a tenor, with a mellow and expressive voice, though somewhat lacking in power„ and the solos and songs set down to his name were admirably rendered, and he was twice honoured with an encore. A most enjoyable con- cert was brought to a conclusion by the choir singing in memory of Piusuti, that eminent composer's song "The Watchword." The duties of accompanist were per- formed by Mrs. W. B.Kay, in good style. WIDNES DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. _

The annual meeting of the Widnes Division Liberal Association, for the appointment of district Council and other business, was held last nigl)t in the Baths• Assembly room. Mr. Eustace Carey occupied the chair and there was a capital attend- ance. The Chairman explained that the Council consisted of 412 persons, of which number Widnes had 208' representatives, and, this number having been electbd, the representatives to serve on the Executive Committee were selected.—The Chairman then made a speech in which he stated that the association had been at work about three years, and had dealt particularly- with registration. The committee who had been appointed to look after that part of the organisation had done their work to the satisfaction of all con- cerned, thanks to the energy of Mr. H. B. Shores, the secretary. (Applause.) By means of public lectures and meetings they had done what they could to keep up the• interest in Liberal matters, and to edUcate themselves and others in Liberal principles, and in subjects which were before the public at the present time, especially that one subject of the government of Ireland. Although their meetings had been compara- tively few, they had been of a successful character' in all the sub-divisions of their parliamentary district. Their finances, however, were not in the position they should like them to • be. A good number of highly respected Liberals had left the ranks on the question of Ireland, calling themselves Unionists, and had ceased to subscribe to the association. In consequence of their withdrawal they had lost about .tl3O per annum in subscrip- tions, but owing very largely to the exertions of Mr. Shores the number of subscribers had increased from , 70 to over 400—(applause)--so that although they had lost in quality and wealth, they had gained satisfactorily in quantity. They were expending less at present than when the association started, and were at the same time doing a great deal more work. (Applause.) With regard to the party generalbr he thought they had no cause for discouragement, and the result of the by-elections in the country he considered extremely encourag- ing. They had net with one or two reverses, but when the circumstances of those reverses came to be considered he thought an unprejudiced ob- server would find that the circumstances were not nearly so bad as they appeared to be, and in the majority of cases they had been victorious.— Subsequently Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, secve- f tary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, delivered a lecture on "Ireland, its natural beauties, past history, and past misery." Tha lecture, which has been greatly appreciated in many parts of Cheshire, was illustrated with views from an oxy hydrogen light, manipulated by Mr. Horace Hand- Icy. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

MESSRS. EDWARD YOUNG & CG., Seel-st. Liverpool, are about to convert their business into a limited liability company. As we understand a prefer- ence will be shown to present and likely business customers, it is highly probable that a very large section of the trade will avail themselves of this opportunity of placing a portion of their spare capital in the enterprise, the business having for so many years held one of the highest positions in the trade.

div.p: FRODSHA3I.

A "Does' ORDER."—On the application of Colonel Hamersley, the Chief Constable of the County, the Eddis- bury magistrates on Monday made an order that all dogs in the division should be kept muzzled or under proper control in consequence of an outbreak of rabies. The Chief Constable stated that at the next quarter sessions he should apply for an order to cover the whole county of Cheshire. _

Do o LICENCES.-At Eddisbury, on Monday, Edward Williams, hawker, of Frodsham, was fined 5s and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Pearson, for having at Bradley, on the 18th March, kept a dog: without a licence.— Thomas Downs, of Helsby, was similarly fined for a like offence at Helsby, on the 3rd of April.—P.C. Roberts proved the offence.—Defendant pleaded that he had only had the dog for about three weeks, and that on approval. —The officer said he had had it since Christmas.

INFRINGEMENT OF BI7ILDING BYELAWS.—On Monday at Eddisbury Petty Sessions, John Alfred Arrowsmith, of Helsby, was summoned by the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority for permitting a house at Helsby, of which he is owner, to be occupied without having a certificate of water supply.—Mr. Farrington inspector of nuisances to the Runcorn Union, prosecuted on behalf of the Authority and explained that he had seen Mr. Arrovrsmith since the proceedings were ordered, and he had informed him that the house had been occupied without his sanction, and he had been entirely ignorant of the law in the mat- ter. The Authority did not, therefore, wish to press the case.—Mr. Higson characterized the proceedings, summoning a person and then wanting the case to be dealt with leniently, as absurd; he thought the matter should have been dealt with out of court.—Mr. Farring- ton said he was acting under instructions, and this case had been brought because similiar proceedings had been taken against other people who had so offended.—Defen- dant was ordered to pay costs. "BUTTERMILK AND TATERS" AT KINGELEY.—At Eddie- bury Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Ravenscroft, far- mer, of Kingsley, summoned a youth named Thomas Powell, also of Kingsley, and latterly his servant, for £2 ss, the loss to which he had been put by defendant leav- ing work.—Complainant said that the defendant, whom he engaged at Christmas at £ll lOs for the year, left hie employment about a fortnight ago, he believed, to get work at the Ship Canal. Defendant had served several employers in this way. Two horses had stood idle during the fortnight through defendant's conduct, and he had been put to much trouble and loss.—Defendant said he was clemmed ;" he had to eat 'buttermilk and taters" twice a day.—Complainant stated that the defendant had four good meals a day. Other servants of his had never complained, and before defendant went away he did net complain. He was willing to take him back, and did not wish to press for the money.—Defendant said he was willing to go back if plaintiff would not give him "buttermilk and taters."—Defendant was fined 20s and costs, and was told that if he went back he was to have the fortnight's wages deducted from his salary.

SERIOUS ILLNESS OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL.

We regret to learn that the member for Warring' ton, Sir Gilbert Greenall, is lying seriously ill et, Walton Hall. It will be remembered that on Good Friday the aged baronet was seized with an attack of faintness, and fell against the church porch. B was deemed advisable that he should refrain frota taking part in the festivities consequent on the coming of age of his son, Mr. Gilbert Greenall. 11e was improving with the rest and care which he, took, when, we understand, he caught a chill, arta has during the past week been confined to his bed by conjestion of the lungs. Ile is, it is satisfactory to state, in a less critical condition than he was few days ago ;. and it is hoped that with an ha' provement in the weather he will recover from the illness which has laid him prostrate.

div.head: STRIKE AT WIDNES.
div.p: A STRIKE AT WIDNES.

The men who are employed as "strike Dickers at the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Works, co Thursday struck work for an advance of wages,' About two years ago their wages were reducea from Is 6d to 2s 6d per week, and the men consider that the time has arrived when their wages should be risen to the former amount. The directors refu!) to grant the request of the men, and they have la consequence turned out. Although they number only 28, no less than 120 men and boys have beea thrown out of employment by their action. It le stated that the men will be early obliged to resurae work, as they have no organisation to supiv them while out of work.

NOTICE. - NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COM- MISSIONERS AND LOCAL BOARD OF HEALTH. di NOTiCE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Newton-in-Makerfield Ymprovement Commissioners will hold a MEETING for the purposes of their special act, and the several acts incorporated therewith, at their offices in Newton-in-Makerfield aforesaid, on MONDAY, THE 7TH DAY OF MAY NEXT, at tour o'clock in the afternoon, and that at such meeting they will make a High- way and Sewer Rate, a General Improvement Rate. a Gas Rate, and Water Rates for the district and sub-districts. A LL FARMERS are specially requested to attend ' a CONFERENCE , promoted by the Warrington Far- mers' Club, at the FARMERS' STORES, CORNHILL, WARRING- TON, on WEDNESDAY, 9TH MAY, 1888, at 5 p.m. promptly, to discuss the following subjects I.—The sale of foreign killed meat, introduced by a short paper describing the evil and injurious effects to the public and to farmers of its present mode of sale. 2,—Fresh outlets for surplus milk, introduced by a short paper describing the actual cost of installation and working a neighbouring cheese factory, which yields to farmers a much higher price for their milk than by sending it to Man- chester and Liverpool. It is hoped that every farmer will attend this Conference on matters most important to the farming industry. GEORGE PERCIVAL, Chairman. JOHN L. STELFOX, Hon. Sec. Warrington Farmers' Club. Lymm, May 2nd, 1888.
